THE INVINCIBLE ARMADA, 1588. [From a Poem, by Lewis Morris, in Murray's Magazine for July.] A fair eve at midsummer, three hundred years ago. Uraks and his bold seacaptains all are out on Plymouth Hoe; Itey are busy at bowls, brave gentlemen, with jovial mirth . •

'td jest, "Melt watching eyes sty far away a sail upon the West. A eai ten sail! a hundred sail! nay nigh two hundred strong! And up the sea they swiftly climb in battle order long; Their high main-royals rake the skies, as in a crescent wide, Like a thick wood, full seven miles broad, they sail on side by side.

Now when they neared the Meman, as he loomed across the I sea. Lord Howard led the English van, a Catholic lord was he. And his great Ark Itoyal thundered out her broadsides loud and long, With Drake and Frobisher hard by, and heroes in a throng. But never a gun the Spaniards fired, but silent pressed and

slow, Ls some great herd of bisons on the rolling prairies go; And behind them close, like hunters swift, with hounds that snarl and bite, The English squadrons followed through the breezy summer night.

Soon as the dawn began to glow, the guns began to roar. All day the thundering navies fought along the Dorset shore, Till Portland frowned before them, in the distance dark and grim, And again the night stole downward, and the ghostly cliffs grew dim. And already, praised be God who guides the patriots' noble

strife, Though not an English flag is lost, and scarce an English life, De Valdez yields his ship and sword, and into Weymouth bay, They tow Oquenda's burning bark, the galleon of Biscay. Day fades in night, mid stress of fight, and when to waking eyes. Freshwater's ghostly sea cliffs, and the storm-worn Needles r' Se, From a score of sheltered inlets on the smiling Solent sea, England comes forth to aid her sons, with all her chivalry. There sails my Lord of Cumberland, and he of Oxford too, Brave Raleigh and Northumberland, and Grenville and Carew. As to a field of honour hasten knights of deathless fame, To meet the blue blood of Castile, the flower of England came. Then with the wind, the foe faced round, andLltissing o'er the t blue, Forth from his lofty broadsides vast his hurtling missiles flew; Long time tke fight confusedly rageds eachiman, for his own hand; St. George! protect our country, and the freedom of our land! See here round brave Rioaldes the English levies press! See there the ships from London town, hemmed round and in distress ' Such thunder sure upon the seas was never heard before. As the great ordnance smite the skies with one unceasing roar! Now when the fifth day of the fight was come, St. James's Day, The sea was like a sheet of glass, the wind had died away. And from out the smoke clouds looming down, churning the deep to foam, Driven by three hundred oars the towering galliases come. . But ere they neared the English line, a furious iron hail Of chain-shot and of grape-shot crashed through mast and oar and sail. No more they could, they turned and fled, not yet upon the
" sea, Was seen such furious hatred, or such stubborn bravery. And upon the steep white walls of cliff and by the yellow sand, With pike and musket hurrying down the sturdy peasants

stand. And the trembling women kneel and call upon the Holy name, And watch the thick black cloud which breaks in murderous jets of flame. Now St. George for our old England, for the Don has turned and fled. With tnany a strong ship sunk or burnt, and gallant seaman
dead, And by the last day of the week, the warring squadrons lie. The foemen moored in Calais roads, the English watching by.
Then came Lord Henry Seymour, with s message from Her
Grace. And Kir Francis read the missive with grave triumph on his

I aee. And he Aware an oath, that come what would, her orders should he .lone Before the early rose of dawn proclaimed the coming sun. And the summer daylight faded. and 'twas midnight on the wave, And among the close-moored galleons, all was silent as the grave, And the bright poop lanterns rose and fell with the breathing of the deep. And silent rode the towering hulls, with the weary crews
asleep. • When two brave men of Devon , for Sir Francis bade them go, With all sail set before the wind, stole down upon the foe; And before the drowsy watchmen woke, the swift destruction
Carte, As with a blaze of wildfire leapt the fireships into flame Then from the close-thronged ships of Spain loud cries of terror
rise. As from their burning ranks the glare flares upward to the
skies. With cables cut, and sails half set, they drift into the night. And many are crushed, and many burn, and sorne are sunk outright. And the watchers on the Dover Cliffs know well what thing
has been, And for noble England cheer aloud, and for her Maiden Queen. No more, no more, great England, shalt thou bow thy head
again Beneath the holy Office and the tyranny of Spain. And the conquering English followed, and upon the Flanders
_ shore, Hopeless the shattered galleons fought, till fight they could no more. And some went down with all their crews, and some beat help-

lessly Upon the yeasty quicksands of the perilous Northern Sea. Then Sidonia with the remnant, shattered ships and wounded men, Fled northward, with the foe in chase, hoping for %pain again; But by the Orkneys, lo ! the Lord blew with a mighty wind, And on the cruel Irish West they left two score behind. . . And the scattered remnant hurrying back to Spain and life a !ain , , • Left fourscore gallant ships behind, and twice ten thousand

men; And when in dole and misery this great emprise was dohe. There was scarce a palace in all Castile which did not mourn a son. Let not their land for.zet the men who fought so good a fight ! Still slytll our England keep undimmed their fame, their memory bright. And if again the foemen come in power upon the main. )[ay she find sons as strong as those who broke the might of Spain!

-- - - The easiest way to find out a girl's age is to aak some other girl. Many a man who imagines that he is a big electric light finds out to his sorrow that he is only a little tallow dip. Nothing sets so wide a mark between a vulgar and a noble soul as respect for and reverential love of woman- kind. A young woman, beidg asked by a politician which party she was in favour of,replied that she was in favour of a wedding-party. Mutual courtesy oils the wheels of life and makes them roll easily. It sweetens what is inevitably bitter, and cannot bring about that result save by making the best

Of things. Musical critic, to young lady pianist, "You make a ' mistake, mein Fraulein, in using the pedal too freely." Pianist: "Well, you see, doctor, that comes from iny having been used to work a sewing machine." A gentleman was giving a little boy some nuts the other day. The good mother said—" Now, what are you going to say to the gentleman ?" With childish sim- plicity the little fellow looked up in the gentleman's face and replied, "More." An old Scotch woman very fond of a gossip and a dram was induced to sign the temperance pledge. Calling on a friend one day, the bottle was produced, and a glass handed to her. "Na, na, Mrs. Mitchell!" said the gossip, " I have signed the pledge n&er to touch or handle a glass again; but if ye'll put a wee drap in a cup I'll tak' it." Man: "Why don't you get married and settle down?" Bashful Friend: "The fact is, I'm afraid to propose to a girl." M.: 'That's it, eh? " 8.F.: "Yes. I wish the thing could be reversed, and the girls would do the pro- posine." M.; "They'll never do that." B.F. "I believe if one would meet me half-way, I might get through." M: "That's easily managed. Court a widow." Two Indian chiefs were at dinner at the White House, Washington, and one of them, ignorant of its sharpness, swallowed a spoonful of mustard. His eyes streamed in agony, which his brother chief observing, said, "Oh, my bother! why do you weep?" The other replied," lam thinking about my son who was killed at such a battle." Presently the other chief took a spoonful of the same stuff, which caused his eyes to stream like his brother's, who in return asked him, "And why, Pray, do you cry?" "I weep to think you were not killed when your son . was," was the impatient reply. The popular idea, and too prevalent practice, of tak- ing a glass of spirits to keep out ,the cold is a great and dangerous delusion. It does the very reverse. The immediate effect, no doubt, is to impart a sort of warm glow and exhilaration, but this is a feeling and not a reality. The nervous system is abnormally stimulated, and the action of the heart excited; but these are speedily followed by depression. Again, the blood- vessels of the skin are fuller of blood, and in conse- quence more heat is radiated away from the surface, while the contractile power residing in the skin is also impaired, and in these various ways cold is able to exert its hurtful action, while the means for resisting it are greatly lessened by the alcohol. A HORSE OF ANOTHER Cotore.—fliggins is troubled with an overweening curiosity about other people's affairs. Occasionally lie gets his comeuppance, how- ever. lie met Sinithers in a street car; doesn't know Smithers very well, but "me boys" him as if he did. 'Busy, eh ? ' he inquired off-hand. "Yes," said Suilthers, deliberately, ' been buying a horse for my wife." "Have, eh ? Well, let me give you some points." "Oh, I've concluded a bargain." "Not without trying him! Was he sound in wind and limb?" "He appeared to be." l'oesn't bulk ?" "No-o, 1 guess not." "Stand without hitching ?" "Y-e-e-s, I think so." Good gait?" But here bmittlers reached his crossing. When he reached the door he called back to Higgins: "I neglected to mention the kind of horse my wile wanted. It was a clothes-horse."
PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE.
BY HUGE BETTE.

XX.—THE SEA. I shipped, dye see? in a revenue sloop, And off Cape Flnisteere , A merchantman we see— A Frenchman guilt' free; So we made for the bold Mounseer, Dye see We made for the bold Mounseer.—Gilbert. The glorious sea appears to command the admiration of everyone, from the nobleman who graces its surface with his yacht to the man who gathers mussels upon its shores. People who live far inland, and who only:come near the sea occasionally, seem to be thrown into the most unbounded rapture in curtemplating the mighty deep, intensified no doubt by the recollection that while they are near it they can procure large mackerel at less than half the price they pay at home. The British youth doesn't view the sea in its gastrono- mical phases; his speculations range higher. By a long and critical perusal of "penny dreadfuls" he is enabled to associate the word sea with storms, pirates, heroism, and all that sort of thing. He sighs as he remembers some picture of the two fast chums sitting on the jibbooni, fishing; or a trio of merry young tars on the forecastle head, on the look out for pirates. He smiles as he recollects how young Tom and his messmates played larks on the skipper; and then he begins to realise that a boy on shore is a very dull and miserable boy. He longs to board the everlasting pirate, and to rescue the lonely maiden. I may as well remark here that I don't believe parents inconvenience themselves as much as they might do to place more of these nautical weeklies in the hands of their boys. The British parent should not lose sight of the fact that these youthful weekly dreadfuls play a very important part in replenishing our naval and mercantile services. When I was a boy I used to spend all my money on these penny weeklies, and no one can charge me with neglect of study, for I have been several times nearly knocked down and run over in the streets through being so absorbed in their pages. At this lapse of time there is one point in those nautical stories that strikes me as being very peculiar. I don't remember a description of any kind of work in them, except sharpening cutlasses, fighting, removing the dead, and now and then giving a haul on the main halliard. Curious, isn't it? I suppose the seafaring men Who wrote the tales had niggers to swab decks and ' strap up dishes. Some sort of depraved humanity must have done it, but to the British youth there is a vast difference between taking a couple of reefs in a main t'gal'nt's'l and helping the cook to peel 'taters, or between cleaving pirates in twain and mopping pans out. It is quite possible that if every other chapter of those adventurous histories had been devoted to a ' description of sugy-mugy, bad biscuits, squee-gees, green pork, and swabs, instead of raking-crafts, clipper- 1 rigged privateers, broadsides, grog, and narrow escapes, I might not have taken the same interest in them. I well remember when I had ripened into an admirer of anything salty I got acquainted with a young sailor who was home for a few weeks, during which time I was his shadow. He spun yarns for me. It is true he never had fought pirates or chased slavers; but then he could chew tobacco and hitch up his pants in a style that I considered to be faultless. Not only that, but the way he hankered after his ship, and how he fretted and fumed for his time ashore to be over, showed that there was no life to equal "a life on the ocean wave." He fairly took I in the slack of my cable by remarking that he was sure I should make a " reglar out'n-out shellback." That settltd the matter, and I proceeded to pack up. Thinking that a parting scene would grieve the old folks, I went through that process of departure com- monly known as " mizzling," intending to send home a 1 black man' with a lot of bullion and a letter of explana- tion, in a few weeks. I must acknowledge that the city of Liverpool didn't holt near so romantic as I had sup- posed; but I consoled myself with the reflection that it was only the introduction to nobler achievements. I .walked down to the docks cogitating as to what terms I should demand of the first skipper who tried to secure n3y services, and had just decided not to be had too cheaply, when a whole forest of masts came into view. I had come expressly to look for a ship, but I was some- what puzzled where to commence. I began to look for the raking craft, but they were all jammed up so close together that I couldn't tell where one left off and the other commenced. I felt certain that none of them could be got out to sea for a good many months; surely I must have come to the wrong place. Anyway, I had a tongue in my mouth, so I walked up a plank, upon which quite an army of ordinary labourers were hurrying to and fro, carrying baxes on their shoulders, and, to use the language of Crusoe's man Friday, "Oh ! joy. Oh! glad." I was on board a real ship. As nobody offered to come and speak to me, I shaded my month with one hand, and shouted, "Ship ahoy !" with all the strength of my lungs, after the approved pattern in nautical literature. I was just beenning to wonder what all those labourer fellows were grinning at, when something happened At first I was under the impression that the vessel had broken from her moorings, under the strength of a sudden hurricane. Then it appeared as though the mizzen gaff had fallen on the right side of my neck. Then as if the spanker boom had slowed round the mast, and was bobbing against the seat pf my pants. The only articulate sounds that I could distinguish amidst the confusion were such expressions as "What the Why the-- Who the-- Where the--," each evidently the beginning of an intelligible sentence, the remainder of which was lost under a thud. As to my leaving the ship, I rather fancy I must have been put into a cannon and fired down that plank, but I am not in a position to state it as a fact. I have read of phantom ships, and whether this was one or not will for ever remain a mystery. for I didn't stop to investigate. I felt too discouraged to go on board any more ships that day. When the shades of evening began to fall I wiled away the time with swallowing a lump that kept rising in my throat, with wondering what the people at home were doing, and yearning. All the glory of my adventure was shrivelled up. and the only thing to be surprised at is that I didn't set off to walk home forthwith. If you exnect a youth who intends going to sea to be scrupulously careful about the lodgings he takes ashore you may be disappointed. Of course the most heroic youth wouldn't think of sleepingi on a telegraph wire when he could pay for a bed, so I took lodgings. I have some little dignity left, so I shall not own up to crying myself to sleep. As you are aware, sleep comes to the weary. I venture to add that there are times and cir- cumstances when other things come to the weary besides

sleep. Of course I don't forget that the subject of this paper is 'The Sea," and I don't know whether I have the right to introduce natural history or not; but in order to convince you how they came to the weary in this case, I have only to state when I got up and turned the clothes down the bed somewhat resembled an animated currant loaf. I don't suppose you will care for me to dwell on this eventful night, and I'm sure I don't want to; so you will please to imagine the curtain rising upon the next act, which is trying to get a berth on a 40-gun frigate. My spirits had risen with the sun • not quite so high as on the previous day I admit. I felt by this time as though I shouldn't snub the berth of a third officer, or even of quarter-master, and if the craft wasn't quite so clipper-looking and /trim, I would overlook it. I went on board what I considered a fine looking ship, on the deck of which there was nobody but a dirty-looking youth about the same age as myself. I asked him•if the crew were asleep. After he had done laughing, he said he didn't know, but he thought the biggest part of 'em would be drunk, as all four of them were ashore. I was surprised to learn that he was in the entire command of that fine vessel. I plied him with questions, and learnt that she chiefly made voyages between Liverpool and he various ports in Wales, with cargoes of coal, pig- , . , iron, &c: This evidently wasn't the sort of ship I wanted. I began to suspect that my reverenced nautical writers had begun their stories in the middle instead of at the beginning "1 want to go to sea," I said to the youth. "What for?' he asked. I was rather knocked out in the first round. In the face of the commonplace, humdrum appearance of the

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1888.

youth, and the pig-iron facts he had put before me, I really couldn't tell him that I wanted to knock Spaniards on the head, and throw carrots at the head of the first mate from the crosstrees ; he didn't look as if he could appreciate such pastimes. When I didn't answer him he put another question. . . .

"Been skipping the slop ?" - I didn't know what that meant, but I didn't wish to appear ignorant, so I said, "Yes !" He winked at me very knowingly, and after a few more interrogations I left him. He was taking more interest in me than I cared for. I next walked up another plank, and reached the deck of another fine ship, where men were bustling about in all directions. Profiting by experience upon a similar occasion, I didn't "hail" anybody. I walked quietly up to a man with a grizzled beard, who VMS standing idle, and said, " Please, sir, is the captain in ?" _ . _
"In where ?" a;lted. the man:

... ....,..,. .........._ ___._, ______. The men about ships seem to take a delight in going to the funeral of a question. I was beginning to stammer when he said, "The cap'n isn't aboard, if that's what you mean; the mate is." "Can I see the mate, please ?" I asked. "I'm the mate," he answered, . .

"Do you want'any boys ? ' I inquired. "What can you do ?" asked the mate. "I can do anything," I replied, thinking I would let him know how willing I was. "Can, eh!" he returned. "Can you clew up a skys'l in a fourteen knots' wind ?" _

I was bound to acknowledge that I couldn't. "Do you know anything about stu'n'sails?" meekly replied that I didn't. "Can you splice ?" "No !" I hadn't yet learned to splice. "Look here, sonny," said the mate, "do you know , which is starb'rd and which is port o' this ship., ' I looked around with a faint hope that I might be able to read the boards in question, but I couldn't see them, so I answered that I didn't. "Then," thundered the mate, "what the deuce d'ye mean by coming here and saying you can do anything, eh?" He didn't exactly say deuce. He used a word in which first mates never drop the aspirate. I was about to explain that I was willing to learn, when he asked me, "Can you get down the gangway in two seconds?' I looked to see if he was in fun. He was. I saw by the mirthful expression in his face that he was in the humour for practical joking, and to show him that I entered into the spirit of the thing, I both found the gangway and got down it in the time specified. The next ship I tried the "cap'n" was " aboard." The first thing he asked for was to see my discharge. I told him I never had been discharged in my life, whereupon he told me that it was quite evident I had never been to sea. Then he told me that boys who hadn't been to sea were a nuisance. He next wanted to know if I had a character, and when I said I had he wanted to look at it. I hadn't any written character; I thought it wouldn't be required. He couldn't talk to me if I had no character. Here was I, a British youth, volunteering to risk life and limb on the perilous ocean, being checkmated for want of a paltry character. It wasn't at all like the penny weeklies. All that day I walked up planks, and said, "Is tl.e cap'n aboard ?" and the speed and method with which I came down the planks varied as the square of the humours in which I caught the said "cap'ns." Then came the long shadows of evening again; yearning; lump swelling; rest that comes to the weary, and other things that come—not much. I resolved that I come what might there should be no more natural history studies for me that night; so I rambled about till I got into a large yard, and, coiling myself up in a corner, I slept the sleep of the just. When I awoke next morning I spent 'about half an hour in trying to persuade myself to unstiff en. After a cheap breakfast at a coffee tavern I started the in- teresting pastime of looking for a ship. If ever I write thrilling sea stories I shall make it a point to say a few words about the ship-finding business, but in the meantime I don't think I am justified in pestering you with any more failures. I will briefly tell ' you how I got a ship, and how I rivalled the heroes in the "penny dreadfuls." [To be conlcucled next week.]

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. MI ROOASEY. 0, ther's mony a posy i' yon green fields As sparkles breet wi' dew ; An' ther's mony a fleaw'r yon garden gay, 0' gowd, an' red an' blue. An' deawn th' owd loyne, th' green thorn hedge, Wod bonny blossoms grow; Bud mi Rooasey's t' fleaw'r:as mi fond heart likes,— Iloo's bonnier than 'em o! Yon throstle sings on to th' hollin bush, An' whistles to id mate • Ther's a linnet, at's heeard id song, joins glad th' chorus, peearkt on t' gate; An' t' lark comes deawnards wi' weary wing, To ged back to id nest; Tho' t' brids sing sweetly, yet aw'd rayther hear Her voice,—id suits me th' best ! Ther's pratty places, and mony a scene, Like fairyland th' sun; But ov o ther is, these two eon o' mine, They nobbut keer for one. That's just bi th' oak tree at th' bend o' t' loyne, Wheer fleawrs peep eawt o' t' grass; Hey, it's t' prattiest place i' this world to me-- It's theer aw meet mi lass. Let others brag o'er ther forrun maids, So chartnin', fresh, an' fair; Wi' ther beauteous cheeks, an' rooagish eon, An' dark unbraided hair. But nooan o' t' lot con be hawf as nice As Rooasey, kind an' true; Hey, aw like mi lass rest weel, bekose. Aw know hoo likes me too! Just look on th' hillside, among yon trees, Yo'll see a little cot ; It's like a lamb as hod wandered theer To rest i' th' shady spot. That's wheer boo's lived o her cheerful life, Contented as con be, An' boost has' a hooam at's as snug as thad When hoo gets wed to me. But afooar thad comes, wod a dreesome while Aw'st hey to mope an' wait; We tawked things o'er last neet till th' moon Showed id wur geddin' late. We sattled t' job, an' ther's nooan as knows But Rooasey sweet, an'—well— Wed words wur sed, an' wod fond lips met, Hoo knows—beside miser ! Aw'll donee an' sing, for awst be so fain, When twermonth slips away, But aw'll bide as patient as e'er aw con, Thro' t' winter. cowd an' grey. An' then, next Summer, when hay-time's o'er— Owd Time, thee hurry on ! Aw'st tek mi bonny Rooase hooam wi' me, For we'st be med i' one! JACK 0' ANN'S

MILK ADULTERATION AT WIDNES. HEAVY PENALTY.

William Kihg, farmer, llalewood, was summoned before the Widnes magistrates, on Thursday, to an- swer three summonses charging him with selling adulterated milk.—Mr. J. T. Allen prosecuted on be- half of the Local Board, and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended.—A plea of not guilty was entered.—Mr. Allen stated that the defendant was in the habit of sending milk to Widnes twice a day, and he was informed that he sold about 10 or lö dozen quarrs daily. On the 2nd June, Mr. Dickson, the sanitary , inspector, saw the defendant's cart standing before a milk shop. He entered the shop and purchased a quantity of milk from a tankard that had just been deposited there. The inspector then took two samples trom two other tankards that were in the cart. These samples were divided according to law: and had been examined by the Public Analyst, who certified that in two of the samples there had been 10 per cent. of water added to every hundred vans of the poorest milk. To the third sample 13 per cent, of water had been added. Mr. Allen said he need hardly point out to their worships that in Widnes, where there was a large juvenile population, it was important that the milk should be as pure as possible.—Mr. Knowles stated that the defendant was entirely unable to account for how this was wrong. On the day in question Mr. King was away at Liverpool, and left the management of the milk to one oi his men ser- vants. He had no intention of selling poor milk to his customers or of defrauding the public. This was the first charge brought against him, although he had been bringing milk to Widnes for five years. —Mr. Muspratt said adulteration of milk was a very serious offence, and the defendant would be fined .£5 and costs in one case, and have to pay the costs in the other two cases.—The total amount of the fine and costs amounted to .£6 7s. ROSE FESTIVAL AT LOWTON.

On Saturday the fourth annual rose festival o: Lowton and district was held, and all the country side came to do honour to the Queen of the Roses. The weather was in agreeable contrast to that which , prevailed at last year's festival, and although the day was as unlike a typical July day as it could well have been, the 'day must be regarded as a fine one. But if the weather was a trifle dull, any ill effect which such a circumstance might have pro- duced was more than counterbalanced by the extra zest and spirit which both participators and specta- tors threw into the proceedings. Messrs. C. E. Arnott and T. Berwick acted as Masters of the Ceremonies. Mr. J. Bromley was hon. sec., and the following gentlemen formed the Committee of Management: —Mr. W. H. Arnott (chairman and also honorary treasurer), Messrs. W. F. Arnott, P. Ashton, W. Glover, J. Henshaw, T. Cook, W. Yates, E. Marsh, J. Dearden, J. Blears, E. Bennett. J. Evans, and P. Clayton. The Cricket Field, opposite St. Luke's Church, was the place of assembly. The procession, marshalled' by Mr. J. Adamson, left the ground at 2-45 p.m. for Fir House Field, higher tip Church-lane. After the marshal and the Lowton Common band came the Rose Pole dancers, then a bevy of older girls who were known as the Scotch dancers. Next came a Jack Tar sitting astride a miniature 81-tonner, drawn by hale-a-dozen youngsters in nautical at- tire, and followed by as many more. Flower girls, bakers, gleaners, were next in order, and then came a basket carriage, in which were seated the oldest couple in Lowton—Mr. and Mr. James Hill—and a child of four summers, the figure represented I ein "Old age and childhood." There followed Gipsies, , Red Ridinghoods, and milk maids, and girls dressed in costumes indicative of the various seasons of the year. The procession also included Sleeping Beauty and the Prince, a company of Highlanders, Police Constable A 1. and the Rose, Queen, preceded by sword and sceptre bearers and the archbishop. She was seated in an open carriage drawn by a pair of fine greys. Iler dress was a ruby velvet, with train of scarlet silk, and was trimmed with swansdown and roses. In her hand she carried a bouquet, and covering her nearly from, head to foot was a long tulle veil. Behind were carriages bearing pages and maids of honour, and the ex-queen with her train bearers. Then, seated on a car, came Dri annia surrounded by characters representative of Eng- land, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, the Army, Navy, and Volunteers, India, Australia, Canada, and Africa. Following came hospital nurses, Swiss girls, shep- herdesses, jockeys, Mother llubbard, colliers, flower girls, bakers, and a number of other charac- ters. Brannigan's band of darkies bringing up the rear. On reaching the field the Queen took her place on the throne, and the imposing ceremony of coro- nation was gone through. The part of Rose Queen was taken b 5, Miss Mary Alice ilenshaw, aged 12, with quiet dignity and few indications of nervous- ness. The other principal characters were—Bri- tannia, Miss Annie Renshaw (sister of the Queen) ; , ex-queen, Miss Battersby ; archbishop, Mr. Rklyard ; sword-bearer, Mr. William Stanley •, sceptre-bearer, Mr. J. Ward. Lowton Common and the St. Joseph's 'bands were upon the ground, and played capital music for dancing. Amongst other attractions dur- ing the afternoon were dances by the Rose maidens, Scotch girls, and Highlanders ; bayonet exercise by the Highlanders. and a hornpipe by the sailors. As a grand finale, the whole of the performers made the circuit of the enclosure in procession. Dan- cing was afterwards commenced, and kept up until dusk.'

Another curiosity in weather matters has tobe recorded. Snow fell in considerable quantities in North and East Derbyshire on Wednesday morning. The hay harvest is entirely suspended. It is stated that Prince Bismarck has advised the Queen of Servia to yield to the wishes of the King, as, in case of a legal decision against her, the German authorities could not refuse to give up the Crown Prince. Replying on Wednesdayto a deputation from the Par- liarnentau Colonisation Committee, Lord Salisbury pointed out some of the difficulties connected with schemes of emigration, and did not encourage the hope that the Government would, for the present at least, guarantee interest on money subscribed towards a colo- nisation land rent charge stock. THE COERCION ACT—Mr. Patrick O'Brien, M.P. for Monoghan, was on Wednesday released from Tullamore Gaol, at the expiration of the sentence of three month's imprisonment which was passed upon him for a speech cieliverecl at the Four Roads, Roscommon. He was im- mediately rearrested and transferred, under escort to Kilkenny goal, to undergo a second term of imprison- ment for a speech delivered at Goresbridge.

A Greenock telegram states that the Marine Hotel and Royal Clyde Club-house, situate about two miles from Dunoon, were burned down on Thursday afternoon. The loss is estimated at £9,000. The fire originated in the club-house, and the wind blew the flames into the hotel adjoining. A FRATIDELENT SOLICITOR.-At the Leicester Assizes, on Wednesday, Frances John Forsell Kirby, solicitor, formerly a town councillor and deputy magistrates' clerk at Leicester, who had pleaded guilty to several charges of fraud, including one of obtaining £l,OOO from the Stamford Bank by false pretences, was sentenced by Mr. Justice Hawkins to five years' penal servitude. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., was entertained on Wed- nesday night by the members of. the Irish National League of Great Britain at a banquet in the Holborn Restaurant. Mr. Justin M'Carthy, M.P., occupied the chair, and referred to Mr. Mandeville's death, contend- ing that he was one of Ireland's martyrs who had suf- fered and died that Erin might really be a nation. FRENCH AooaEsstoN.--The African Trade Section of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce resolved on Wed- nesday to seek an interview with the Colonial Secretary lin reference to "the aggressive action of the French at Abeokuta." Lord Knutsford has informed the Chamber that Her Majesty's Government are in communication with the Governor of Lagos and the French Government on the question.

div.head: FROM LONDON LETTERS, ac.
div.p: FROM LONDON LETTERS, ac.

I understand that the title of the new edition of his book upon which Sir Charles Dilke is engaged will be "Greater Britain: Twenty Years Afterwards." The title was suggested by Lord Tennyson's second version of Locksley Hall. Returns compiled in London show that there are now building at several shipbuilding ports of the kingdom over 600,000 tons of merchant shipping. This indicates a greatly increased activity in the industry as compared with the state of things a year ago. M. Worth, in reply to an interviewer lately, said, "I find that every country produces beautiful faces, graceful figures, and lovely dispositions, well as their contraries. I suppose Russian ladies are the greatest dancers in the world ; English- women are justly proud of their perfect complex- ions the French lead the world in real elegance; and the American ladies impress me by the easy way in which they wear gorgeous gowns. Nothing overwhelms them." Great indignation is expressed in many quarters at the publication of the most sensational and wildly improbable story that the Empress Victoria is a prisoner in Friedrichskron. The modve for the circulation of this monstrous fable can only be guessed at, but there are those who say that there is an evident intention to raise between England and Germany a feeling of estrangement to the possible profit of Russia. The announcement of the "Times" of the ap- proaching marriage of the Master of Trinity with Miss Augusta Ramsay, the senior classic of last year, takes many friends greatly by surprise. Dr. Butler is 56 years old, Miss Ramsey 22. The union of two senior classics is an event which we may safely pronounce an uprecedented one even in the long and varied history of the institution of mar- riage. Dr. Butler, formerly head master of Har- row, is a son of Dr. George Butler, who also was head master of Harrow in his day, and was subse- quently Dean of Peterborough. The " Times" has acted very generously towards Mr. O'Donnell. At first the authorities of the lead- ing journal were exceedingly annoyed at having been put to tile expense of bringing so many wit- nesses from Ireland to no purpose; but, after re- flection, and possibly because they knew there was no chance of getting their costs out of the ex-mem- ber for Dungarvan, they have intimated that they will not press for the same. I understand that Mr. O'Donnell has, at great personal sacrifice, paid all the costs which he had incurred to his own legal advisers. Mr. Ruegg, Mr. O'Donnell's counsel, is a great authority on the Employers' Liability Act. The camp at Wimbledon is in a horrible condition I have a letter from there to-day which says that the ground is of the consistency of gruel, and that the marvel is that all the tents were not washed away in the tremendous downpour of Wednesday night. All night long residents in more settled regions than Wimbledon had to listen to the wind soughing among the trees, and to the, everlasting plash of rain on the sodden ground. In Wimbledon the downpour has damped everybody's spirits except those of the men who have come up to compete for the Queen's I'rize. For this there are this year no fewer than 2,363 entries. The pioposal made by Mr. Smith on Thursday, which strikes out an independent line cutting out the varied suggestions of what he was prepared to do, is-accepted with general satisfaction on the Liberal benches. Immediately after the conversa- tion arising on Mr. Smith's notice had terminated, Mr. John Morley had a conversation with Mr. Par- nell, in the course of which he found the Irish lea- der eagerly ready to accept the Ministerial offer. The proposal is absolutely novel, necessitating the introduction of an Act of Parliament to bring it about. It will probably be necessary that the terms of the appointment of the Commission shall limit the inquiry to the specific charges raised by the "Times," and shall not degenerate into a " fishing " inquiry, ranging over the Jest twenty years of Irish political warefare. The fact that court mourning is worn influences the fashions in circles which have no pretensions to high connection. Hence black amd grey are fashion- able colours this summer and it must be said in apology for so sombre a tint that so far it has well fitted the season. Again, if it were not for the bene- ficent offices of grey as a softener of harsh colours we should suffer this summer from a surfeit of green. Green is, or may be, a beautiful colour, but it is one of which we may easily have too much. Cream colour and white are always /suitable for young girls in summer; but hitherto, owing to the inclement weather. these have not been worn as much as usual. The same cause has given tweeds and other stout woollen fabrics a prominence which they do not often attain in the month of July. Such a meeting as that held in St. James's Hall on Wednesday afternoon is seldom seen. Its com- position was written on the faces of those who attended. A glance at them betrayed their calling. They were the London publicans, met to protest against the invasion of liberty and the advent of coercion involved in Mr. Stevenson's Sunday Clos- ing Bill. Mine host presented himself in a hundred disguises,but he was always unmistakably mine host. Tall or short, stout or thin, old or young, fair or brown, he was always the publican. The pioceed- ings were very enthusiastic. There was a general feeling that England's future would not be worth ten years' purchase if the public houses were shut on Sunday. Mr. Bung is not in want of rest one day in seven. But this afternoon it was only the publican who protested. There was no public present. A romantic story about the Glasgow Exhibition is going the rounds. An official, it is stated, picked up the other day a lady's pocket book purse at the moment a gentleman was passing. The latter naturally stopped and assisted the official in looking for a clue for the owner of the purse. " Oh," exclaimed the official at last, " here is the owner's photograph, anyway," and then hastened to add, as he took it out of the wallet, "Why, no, it isn't ; it's not a lady's photograph at all. It looks— you'll excuse me for saying it--extremely like one of yours, sir," and he turned to thegentleman who had beenassisting him. The latter at once admitted that it was his photograph, and said he thought he could find the lady to whom the purse belonged. And he did find her, the romance of the story being that the discovery of the photograph revealed to him the young lady's secret. They are to be married next month. Our Orkney centenarian is gone. I confess to be- ing a sceptic about centenarians in general/ but for certain reasons the Orkney stories are generally we i rthy of credence. There s a significant phrase in the paragraph chronicling the demise of this par- ticular one. "Being good at telling atoeies in con- nection with things he had seen, he was a great favourite with the community." That faculty of "telling stories" is very common among old Orkney men, One old fellow I have heard of was the stand- ing joke of the youth of the community, who amused themselves by drawing him on to tell his biggest whoppers. One of his choicest was that he had served on board a ship of "fifty thousand" tons. "The Great Eastern would be nothing to her," re- marked one of the mischievous youths. "Only a tow-boat," was the unabashed reply. Another of these garrulous old chaps used to say be had been all over the world—ay, to the end of it. "And what did you see there?" Oh, there was a big wall, and when I lookit over it they were breakin up auld moons and stars."

div.p: A GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
• BY JEAN MIDDLEMASS. Author of " Lady Muriel's Secret," "The Spider and the Fly," "Poisoned Arrows," " Wild Georgie," &c., &e.
5P9i

CHAPTER XXVI. NO TIDINGS. Mr. Stanhope's straw, to which he has been clinging so desperately of late, has not developed into a raft on which he can float. Nothing has hap- pened to postpone the dreaded marriage with Sergius Lenskoff, and it is fixed for to take place on the morrow. "Geoffrey will be safe, safe in his birth- right of elder son; Fedora, his beloved wife, will be spared the pang of a terrible exposure; but his darling Irene, how will it be with her ?" he asks himself repeatedly, as he wanders like a ghost about the rooms, replete with preparations for this great festivity. Every circumstarice seems to have combined to keep Henry Stanhope's secret, not only Sergius Lenskoff's promised silence if he marries Irene, but Simon Knight's opportune death without leaving I one word behind that could tell tales. No; Mr. Stanhope is mistaken. In his death-bed murmurings Tom Chilton caught just a sound or' two, which, if repeated, might awaken the past. But Tom Chilton is either reserving them, or does not think them worth telling. How can he know for certain that Simon Knight was the only witness to that false marriage in Russia, that on his return to England he came to Warleighlto bully Mr. Stanhope, whom he tracked there, and that the first money Henry Stanhope raised on his estate was the sum with which Simon Knight started the business at Wandsworth, paid under the solemn promise that he would never reveal to mortal man what he had seen in Russia? And Simon Knight, coarse and hard though he was, had kept his word. "He was a tradesman before everything," he would have said. "Money's worth for money's value was the only reg'lar mode of proceeding." And so the wedding-day was about to dawn. The bride's dressof embossed creamy velvet dim- med with point d'Alengon, which had been in Prince Sergius family for years, was the most ex- quisite garment that Laferriere had ever produced. The diamonds, which Sergius Lenskoff had elected should be scattered among her flowers as though they had been rained there in a shower of magni- hence, would be the talk of London. Sergius Lenskoff intended this marriage to be I heard of far and near, and in carrying out his luxuriously grandiose ideas he had an able coadjutrix in Lady Fedora. On her own account her habits were perhaps rather retirin,o• but she loved pomp and grandeur for her child. If she could only have awakened her husband to the belief in the great hap- pine,ss that had come to them, she would have been quite satisfied; but this was so impossible that she gave up making the attempt, and trusted to the future, when she felt quite certain he would be com- pelled to acknowledge how mistaken he had been in his judgment of the man whose delight it was to encircle their child with every luxury and gilded pleasure that wealth can command. Whether Lady Fedora or her husband is the better judge of character the sequel alone will prove, but there LS little doubt that there are others besides Mr. Stanhope who will murmur "Poor Irene," when decked in her bridal sheen she stands at the altar by

Sergius Lenskoff's side. Yet for the nonce she is radiantly happy. How can she be otherwise. She loves the Prince with all the strength of her young gushing affections, and he devotes himself to her with a constancy and an almost omniscient knowledge of what will please her; this from the. man she loves cannot do otherwise than touch a girl of Irene's temperament very deeply. She is dressed for the wedding now in her jewel besprinkled garb, and Sergius himself in his simple morning dress, it l' Anglaise, drives round to the Eaton-square house for a moment before going to the Greek Church where the marriage is to be cele- brated with all pomp. He would see Irene and bestow on her one last gift more costly than its predecessors—a bracelet, in which an empress might have gloried. He clasps it himself round her fair wrist. Ah, it would have paid twice over all Henry ,Stanhope's liabilities. Prince Sergius does not speak while he fastens it, only stoops and kisses the arm round which he leaves it—then he looks up and meets Henry Stan- hope's eyes as he watches the little scene from his post of observation on the hearthrug, his back to the fire. It is scarcely a pleasing 'expression that those eyes convey, nor are Prince Sergius' as they return the glance wholly free from malignity. The only diffe- rence is, on one man's face there is triumph, on the other despair. Irene surprises this somewhat ominous eye tele- graphy and utters a little cry as she seizes almost pleadingly, the Prince's arm. Yes, he is to shield her now ' • the father knows it and turns away with a surpressed sigh. _ My own, my beautiful, you are nervous ' • there is nothing to disturb you, my Irene ; in less than an hour you will be my wife, and then I shall defy the world." Defy the world ! Ay, will lie? , Turning then to the disconsolate father, he says very pointedly: We shall meet again, Stanhope—we shall meet again." Mr. Stanhol4 quails. The only active part he is called on to take in reference to this dreaded mar- riage is that he must himself give Irene to the man he would rather see dead at his feet than the husband a his child. Lady Fedora has arranged all about the settlements, seen the lawyers, done everything that is possible herself, but Mr. Stanhope must give the child away, she says. It is a torture for Henry Sta.nhope,in which Sergius Lenskoff delights, a part of his revenge for the want of a seeming encouragement to his suit which his old friend has most assuredly not troubled himself to affect. They will meet again. Another half-hour, and Henry Stanhope with Irene on his arm, his step so tottering that it seems as if he will scarcely reach the altar, walks up the aisle of the church, a bevy of smiling bridesmaids following ' in the bride's wake. The Prince, with his best man, is waiting for them. There is no chance now of a reprieve. As a man in a dream, Henry Stanhope feels rather than hears that the service is proceeding he does his appointed part of it without being conscious that he is perform- ing anything out of the way. The organ and a choir of fresh young voices break out in a rich and melodious anthem. The ceremony is over. The fair young girl, who has been the joy of the Stanhope's home for years, is Princess Irene now, and the sacrifice is complete. She takes her husband's arm and they pass into the sacristy to sign the books. Of course Henry Stanhope is a witness; with a trembling hand he affixes his name. "Why don't the carriages come up more quickly —will this terrible ordeal never be over—if he could only get away or not see the pageant he would not perhaps be so sensibly alive to the fact that Irene is really married." People are beginning to notice how strange and dreamy he looks. Lady Fedora makes excuses saying he is ill, but sotto voce bids him rouse himself for only a short time longer. Once more Prince Sergius places Irene's hand on his arm to lead her to the carriage,as he does so they are assailed with a torrent of compliments, she with kisses. While the tumulVof glad voices is at its height the Prince hands Henry -Stanhope a paper. He unfolds it with those long thin fingers of his which are never steady now. The certificate of Damitri's death and burial ! The telegram announcing: Damitri's sudden death had been received by Sergius Lenskoff in the club hall that night lie had dined with Henry Stanhope. He had kept his own counsel; till now told no one, first he must gain the prize he sought—lrene's hand. He hated Henry Stanhoir for mistrusting him, and resolved to give him this terrible coup with full force when all the world was by. The Englishman's pluck was greater than Sergins Lenskoff had thought. He did not flinch when he read those lines did not fall down struck to the earth, as might have been expected Though he was now doubly certain that Sergius ' Lenskoff was no mate for his beautiful loving child, yet he would not proclaim it to the by- standers, but let him take her forth to the carriage without uttering one word of surprise or reproach. Only by his weary, pained look could those who knew him well see how much he suffered, and when they saw him almost crawl out of the church, leaning on Ferdinand, whose arm he had clutched, fearing lest he should fall, the general opinion was that Henry Stanhope wouldnot live long to witness his daughter's happiness. No, the weight of his by-gone sin was crushing the strength out of the strong man, and the terrible saciifice of his child, rendered still more terrible in
what now proved to be its utter uselessness, ad iet! tenfold to the mental agony Henry Stanhop,? had been,

suffering of late. No brain, no frame can stand such tension long, and with the departure of the guests, Henry Stanhope's last flickering gleam of endurance ended. He lay prostrate in his study chair and neitho- noke nor moved. Lady Fedora, beside herself with anxiety, sent fo- the family doctor. He shook his head and looked grave. No, the ena would not be yet; still it had begun. Henry Stan- hope would rally from his present torpor, but never again would he possess his old energy. " Geoffrey—l want to see Geoffrey," was his re- peated prayer. And so they started for Italy to join their eldest son, Lady Fedora hoping almost against hope that the warm, bright sunshine would restore her husband. For a time it almost seemed as if her hopes might be realised; sitting in Geoffrey's painting room or walking slowly with Geoffrey in the sun- shine, Henry Stanhope looked brighter than he bad looked for months. He had told Geoffrey all, confided to his son what from the tongue of gossips he had partly guessed, for the secret was not altogether as close a one as Mr. Stanhope believed; and Geoffrey and he had agreed that since Damitri was really dead, the painful storY might with justice be concealed from Lady Fedora, Geoffrey reserving the right to tell her the' whole Ai truth if any portion of it should reach her after hio PV father's death. And thus the trio passed thewinter together, a full account of Ferdinand's marriage being sent them. They had excused themselves from being present, Mr. Stanhope was too ill, but the Princess Irene Lenskoff was there, radiant in her acknowledged beauty. The honeymoon had not yet waned, Irene' letters still teemed of happiness and love. The" were just starting for Russia to a castle belonging W Prince Sergius on some barren steppe. What would his life be there? The father quailed as he contemplated it. He only kneW what Lenskoff was ; but even Lady Fedora begins to regret her child. Weeks pass wearily into months, and the tidings from her are so scarce,the letters so fax between and so uncommunicative that if the mother had her way she would start for Russia herself to learn what is being enacted there. But her home tie is too strong. Mr. Stanhope ie failing alowly, dying of that canker, remorse, thee, which there is scarcely a more agonising disease. Every day he asks after Irene, every day Lady Fedora shakes her head and whispers—no tidings. "It is a just retribution," he murmurs almost with his dying breath, holding Geoffrey meantime the hand. "I let her go from me to save mysefr —it is just that she should not be with me at lig last."

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tussnsr. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m. THE LIFE PEERS BILL. The Marquis of SALISBURY formally moved the second reading of this bill. Earl BEAUCHAMP did not object to the principle of the measure, but thought that some explanation of its pro- visions was necessary. The Earl of DERBY could not see why valuable public servants should not be elected to life peerages, and he believed that such election would be beneficial to the public service. He thought it best to leave qualifications to the discretion of the Minister of the day. The bill was a step in the right direction. Lord COLCHESTER approved of the principle of the bill, and hoped it would pass.—Lord Mineurroir also sup- ported the bill. The EARL of DUNRAVEN accepted the bill as an instal- ment of future legislation. EARL GRAM-ILL/I hoped ,that in Committee all the fancy safeguards and restrictions would be swept away. The EARL Of FRVERSHAM did not consider that ade- quate cause had been shown for making the proposed rhanges. The Earl Of ROSEERRY said the bill had met with a very tool reception, but he anticipated a very warm opposi- tion for it when it reached the House of Commons. The House would be turned into a kind of legislative hydro- pathic establishment, where these noble persons would take BIM care of their connections than of the constitu- tion of the House. (Laughter.) Ile wished the reform of the House should go much further than this hill. The Marquis of SALISBURY gathered from the debate that there was a unanimous feeling in favour of the second reading. He would not discuss details, which would be better discussed in committee. It was the in- tention of the Government to pass the bill into law this sesslon.—The bill was then read a second time.

AN AUTUMN SESSION. Tag COURSE OF BUSINESS.-STATEMENT BY MR.
SMITH.

The questions had concluded before 3 45, at which time a considerable number of members were in the House, in view of the announcement that was expected, as to the course of business, from the Leader of the House.

Mr. Smits, in me;eing that for the remainder ef the Session, the Government business have precedence of all other business on all days, pointed out the great necessity for proceeding with the Local Govern- ment Bill, and said that the Government were determined to main the bill a workable measure, although they might not insist on the carrying of all its provisions, and might leave, for instance, the District Councils to be dealt with in the future; setting up for the present the County Councils, and putting them in going order. The House would not be asked to spend time on any particular clause; but he hoped thst assistance would be given which would en able the bill to make much more rapid progress. What he had said applied to the London clauses, as well is to the others in the 'bill. As to Supply, it was neces- sary that the votes should all be taken before the. H6llse, had any rest. He hoped, therefore. that the Local Government Hill would be got through this or next week, and Supply taken day by day after- wards; unless, indeed, it became necessary to redeem the obligation to bun, members in reference to the Sun- day Closing Bill. '(Heer, hear, and laughter.) There was other important work to be done, however, and, in view of the annortance of the Railway Rates Bill, the Emplevers Liability Bill, and other measures which had been before the Grand Committees, the House would be asked to .place them on the statute book this year. Then there was the provision to be made for imperial defence. the larrlFO for dealing with the BCOVC4I Pniversities, and the proposal, not yet introduoed, tor the constitution of a Ministry of Agriculture The Tithes Bill must, also be dealt with this year; the Land Commission 1311; but the Irish Drainags Bills would not be forced through against the wishes ed the hon. gentlemenfrom 'lreland. Amongst the measures to be dropped were :the Lunacy Act Amendment Rill; the Parliamentary Under-Secretary Irish cheers)—the Judicature (Ireland) Rill; and the Technical Education Bill. To do the necessary work which remained, an autumn session would be necessary. He proposed that the House should adjourn in August, until the end of ,October or beginning of November. which, he thought, 'was a recommendation which hon. 4-entlemen would 'readily accept, in view of the public need for mach an arrangement. He had one modest request to make, and he,hoped the right hon. gentleman would satisfy hint that,the time of the House, exhaused as members were. would not be taken up either beforethe adjournment or after the adjournment by the discussion of proposals for the reform of another branch of the legislature He unconditionally expressed this hope in order that bon.rneinbers might be assured they would not be canal upon to grapple with a subject which tuust either be reducedto dimensions unnaturally small and frivolous in their character, or that would, in its natural dimen sions,,certainly require the virgin energies of the House. --41augiiter and cl teert.)— Mr. W.. 11. Tile right. hon, gentleman had met the proposals of the Government in a most consider- ate manner, and with regard to othor lion. gentiemon who had complained of the likeonverr.enee of an autumn session, ire could only say tint lie was fully aware of the extreme incotivettienee in Meted. and he looked forward to an autumn sitting with very considerable regret. THE LOCAL 60VEHNMENT BFLL—SIR U. KAY- snlyrri,EkvonTirs AMENDMENT.

Eir U. KAY-SHUTTLEWORTIr moved an amendment to the proposed method of adjusting the financial relations between counties and boroughs. Speaking especially in the interest of Lancashire, he suggested that the proposed equitable adjustment should, with a view to doing jus- tice to the county as contristed with its boroughs, in- clude the distribution of tffe proceeds of the transferred licenses, local taxation licenses, probate duty grant, and all others. . . .
--AIi:if:FOWLER (Wolverhampton) objected to the ap- poiutmeut of commissioners as proposed in the amend-

merit for the purpose of revising the financial relations between counties and boroughs. Lord CiaiinonNe on the other hand, argued that ~,reat injustice would be 'done to the counties if tlie readjust- ments in question were not made. Sir W. HAR.COBRT said that both the noble lord and the right honourable baronet had tried to seduce the Presi- dent of the Local Government Board from his pledges, and to take the money of the boroughs and give it to the counties. • .Mr. Hiram said it would not be right that the boroughs should retain all the revenue thus obtained ; and it was, therefore, only right that there should be such a readjustment of revenue as would be effected under the amendment which he had proposed, strengthened and made clearer, as it would be. by the amendment of the member for Clitheroe, which he was willing to accept on behalf of the Government. Sir HENRY JAMES opposed the amendment. The MARQUIS Of HAUTINGTON said there could be no doubt that unless some readjustment of the distribution of the new revenues as between counties and boroughs was made, the counties and boroughs not included in schedule 4 would suffer by the extension which had been given to schedule 4. Besides that, there would be great injustice as between different boroughs. Sir LYON PLAYk'AIR opposed the amendments both of the President of the Local Government Board and the member for Clitheroe. The discussion was continued by Commander Bethell, Mr. Neville, Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. Maclsan, Mr. P. Wil- liams, and Mr. Leake. Mr. RITCHIE stated that, in order to arrive at a clear understanding, he should propose to insert some such words as these: "In the adjustment of the financial ar- rangements other than the distribution of the licenses and probate grant, no borough shall be rendered liable to contribute in a greater proportion than at present." He proposed to consider where those words could be most conveniently introduced. Upon the understanding that those words would be in- serted, Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth's amendment was agreed to. The amendment 'was further amended on the mo- tion of Sir LYON PLAYFAIR (with the assent of Mr. Ritchie). Clause 31 was then agreed to, with some amendments inserted, on the motion of Mr. Ritchie. Clauses 32, 33,, 34, and 35. were agreed to. On clause 36, application of the act to the metropolis as county of London, Mr. James Rowteens proposed to add the following provision :—" That there shall be no selected councillors in the county of London.." After some discussion on the amendment progress was reported. The Liverpool Overhead Railway Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelvel o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS. WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes after twelve o'clock. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. The consideration of the Local Government (England and Wales) Bill in Committee was resumed, when the amendment proposed by Mr. J. ROWLANDS to clause 32, that there shall be no selected councillors in the County of London., prompted considerable discussion.—Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, Mr. Baumann, Mr. S. Buxton Mr. Cans- ton. Mr. R. G. Webster, and Sir W. Harcourt took part in it, and some of the speeches were lightened by humor- ous touches that provoked laughter. The amendment was rejected by 192 votes to 148.—An amendment re- ferring to the appointment of sheriff was rejected.—Mr. LAWSON moved to leave out the sub-sections treating the city of London as a separate county.—Mr. RITCHIE, while unable to accept the amendment, pointed out that the present bill was not a final settlement of the problem of London government.—Sir W. HARCOURT declared that as the bill was only put forward as a temporary solution of the question of London government discus- sion on this point might be deferred until next session. —The amendment was by leave withdrawn.—Mr. Rxrcius moved an amendment with the object of allow- ing the Parliamentary boroughs of the Metropolis to re- turn to thetounty Council double the number of mem- bers they returned to Parliament, and it was agreed to.—Mr. S. BurroN proposed an amendment providing that the selected county aldermen should not exceed one-sixth of the whole number of elected conncillors.—The amendment was accepted by Mr. RITCHIE and agreed to.—Mr. CAUSTON proposed that selected councillors should be selected only from among the elected councillors.—After discussion, in the course of which Mr. Loma intimated that it would be impossible for the Government to accept the amendment, Mr! CAUSTON'S proposal was rejected by 246 votes to 145.— Progress was reported. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Oaths Bill as amended was considered, and the third reading fixed for next day. Amusement was caused by Mr. RITCHIE'S reply to Mr. TALBOT, who asked when the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors (Sunday) Bill would really be considered.—The PRESIDENT Of the LOCAL GOVERNMENT Boum said it would be impossible to fix any date until they saw how public business progressed.—The oill was postponed.— The Friendly Societies Act Amendment Bill was with- drawn.—Mr. R. REID brought in a bill to amend the law of marriage • and the House adjourned at twenty minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. TIM IRISH POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.—The Duke of ARGYLL moved that the Government deserved the sup- port of Parliament in securing for the Queen's subjects in Ireland the full enjoyment of personal freedom in their lawful transactions, and in protecting them from the coercion of unlawful combinations. He held it to be only reasonable that their Lordships should show affirma- tively their confidence in the administration of the Gov- ernment, and he characterised Mr. Gladstone's conversion to the principle of Home Rule as sudden and violent.— The LORD CHANCELLOR' finding that no other member of the House rose to speak, put the question. A division was not challenged, and he declared "The Contents have it." "Nentine contradicente," added Lord SALM- WRY, and there were cheers from the Ministaialists. Their Lordships adjourned at a euarter-past five o'clock.
HOUSE OF CONLMONS.—TIIIIRSDAT. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. The Manchester Ship Canal Bill was read a third time. THE CHARGES AGAINST MR. PARNELL. A COMMISSION OF JUDGES. _

Mr. PARNE.I7-Irbe-g--t.-o---aSk- the First- Lord of the Treasury, whether he will afford facilities for enabling the judgment of the House to be taken on the motion for •a select committee standing in the name of the hon. member for Cork in the list of notices of motion for to-day. Mr. W. H. Swine: Sir, the Government maintain the opinion which they have expressed, and in which the House concurred by a large majority last year, that the proposed tribunal is altogether unfitted to deaf with the question, limited as it is in scope and character, that the hon. gentleman proposes to refer to it. The Govern- ment are, however, willing that Parliament should pass an Act appointing a Commission which should be wholly or mainly composed of judges with full powers, as in the case of other statutory commissions of inquiry, into the allegations and charges made against certain members in the recent case of O'Don- nell v. Walter and another. It has always ap- peared to the Government that the proper course for hon. members concerned was to appeal to the courts of law for a complete examination of those charges, but if, for reasons of their own, they were unwilling to avail themselves of their right to take this course, the Gov- ernment are prepared to offer the alternative which I have proposed. The Government, however, are not willing to give a day for ithe consideration of the motion of the hon. gentleman., ' Mr. PARNELL : Will the hon. gentleman put his notice on the paper ? Mr. Smrra Yes, if the hon. member is prepared to accept the offer that has been made, I am prepared to I put on the notice paper a motion for leave to bring in a bill with reference to the judges. Mr. GLADSTONE : Will the right hon. gentleman put the notice on the paper so that we may see the terms of it ? _

Mr. Slum: Yes ; I will put it on the pallier for Mon- day. LAND PURCHASE IN IRELAND.—Mr. BALFOUR told Mr. W. P. Sinclair that the Government intended to make proposals during the session for preventing the lapse of the system of land purchase established under Lord Ash.- bourne's Act. The announcement was a surprise to Mr. Gladstone, who, rising soon afterwards, said he had under- stood from Mr. Smith's stateme.nt the other night that the only new measure of importance the Government in- tended to introduce was that relating to the appointment of a Minister of Agriculture. But if the Government in- tended to introduce a bill renewing and e-xtending Lord Ashbourne's Act, he could only say that that would mean a considerable extension of the system of creditorship on the part of the English Treasury, and that was a mea- sure that would be regarded by many members on his side of the House as a measure of the utmost importance and one likely to lead to a long and rigid discussion. - -

Progress was reported after a number of amend- ments had been rejected, and the House resumed. div.head: RIOT IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: RIOT IN MANCHESTER.

A serious collision between Orangemen and Catholics took place in Manchesteron Sunday afternoon. The mem, hers of several prominent Orange lodges in the city gathered near the Royal Infirmary for the purpose of pro- ceeding to St. Mark's Church, in Holland-street, where a special service was announced to be held. The members, to the number of about 120, were wearing the usual re- galia, and when the proe-ession had been formed they proceeded to Ancoats, in which district the church is situated. Passing along Canal-street, a narrow thorotmh- fare populated chiefly by Irish Roman Catholics, they met with extraordinary opposition. A band of Catholics rushed from a yard, armed with hatchets, knives, pokers. and bottles, and made a desperate onslaught on the pro- cessionists. Being utterly taken by surprise and over- whelmed by superior numbers, the Orangemen made a feeble resistance, and as they ran along the street they were knocked down with hatchets, pokers, and bottles thrown by infuriated women. Two of their number, Joseph Walmsley (Bradford) and Daniel Ritchie (Pendle- ton), were badly injured, and others received seriods scalp and body wounds. The regalia was torn from them, and but for the timely arrival of thirty policemen, who had been telephoned for, the affray would have had probably a fatal termination. The ugly weapons with which the assaulting party were artuned placed the Orangemen almost at the mercy of the Catholics, and they were pitilessly cut down as they attempted to get out of the streets,. or knocked down with heavy pokers wielded by savage Irishmen. The riot, however, was quickly quelled on the arrival of the police, and the ring- leaders were taken into custody. A large number of the Orangemen were taken to the Ancoats Hospital, and al- though many ghastly wounds had been inflicted, it is not anticipated that any fatal result will ensue. Up to last night the police were busily arresting prominent members of the aggressive faction, who had evidentl organised the attack for several hours before the Orneee. men arrived at the scene of their ambush.

At Manchester Police Court, on Monday, J. Me.Mahon, Patrick WHugh, Mary Ann M'Hugh, Margaret Martin. Mary Lawson, Alfred Efarlow, and Mary Lowry were rumvicted of attacking and wounding several members of an Orange procession. and a.,eaulting the police, on Sunday. Mc Mahon and M'Hugh were sentenced to two months' imprisonment, with hard labour; two others were fined £2 each, and three others 21.5. each, the Bench remarking that the streets of the city should be rendered safe for everyone.

div.head: W IMBLEDoN MEETING.
div.p: THE W IMBLEDoN MEETING.

Most of the intending competitors for this year's meet- ing had arrived on Sunday night.. Amongst them is a team from Canada, but there is no other body of volunteers from the colonies. The entries on the whole show a falling off from the numbers recorded last year. when representatives came from India, the Cape, and Australis, in addition to those from Canada. The time for post entries, however, had not expired, except in the case of the Queen's and SL George's. The competitions have much the satne features as last year, but there is a very interesting new competition for cyclists. The prize list amounts to £16,500. divided amongst 10-5 separate contests, this being the largest sum that has ever been offered at Wimbledon or anywhere else in the trines of rifle shooting. Last year being the cele- bration of the Queen's Jubilee, brought about—or at all events that is the reason assigned for it—a very large increase in the number of entries for the Queen's Prize and the St. George's. On this occasion there is a falling off in point of numbers. In 1837, 2,477 competitors were entered for 'the Queen's, against 2,363 this year; and for the St. George's there are 2474, against 2,370. In the Alexandra, which began on Monday. the Windmill, the Martins, and the Daily Tele- graph, there is also a falling off; but this fact is in no way traceable to any diminution in the interest which Volunteers take in rifle shooting. It is due more than anything else to the uncertainty which prevails respect- ing the holding of the annual meeting, and the sooner this question is settled the better will it be for the good of the force in general.

About 40 competitions began on Monday, amongst them being the Alexandra, regular and auxiliary officers, Humphrey Cup, St. Lower, Secretary of State for War, Armourers, Halford, Curtis and Harvey, Henry Atkin- son. Schuppisser awl Co., Coventry Machinist, Company, Steward, Robin Hood, Kynoeh. Graphic, Gregory, Ise. The only competition that ended with the day was the Alexandra, which 'v.as won last. year by Pr:vate Ward, 4th V.E. Devon, with the splAndid total of 68 out of a possible 70. In addition to these competitions pool at 500, 600, and 800 yards went on briskly, and those able to pay a shilling a shot for revolver practice had the opportunity afforded them. . . .

The inter-University match between teams of four for the Humphrey Challenge Cup ended in a victory for Oxford, with 626 points, against 569 by Cambridge. The match between the auxiliary officers' team of eight and the army officers' team resulted hi a victory for the auxiliaries with 1,485, against 1,366 by the regulars. Though the illooting in the Alexandra com- petition, the principal event of the day, finished at night, the statistical department found it impossible to give further information concerning the result than that CoL-Sergt. 'Vicars, 131 h Middlesex, stood first with 31 points at 500 yards. 33 at 600; a total of 64. Col.- Sergt. Semmence, 4th Norfolk, and Corp!. hildorran, sth Lanark, also each made 64, but with only 30 points .at the longest distance,. The shooting at the 200yds. range in the first stage of the Queen's Prize Competition commenced yesterday morning. The weather was dull, with a light breeze from the rear of the targets. The sun oame out in the afternoon, and gladdened the hearts of those who suffered by the heavy rain that fell during the night. No highest possible hut been put on in the first stage of the Queens; but the shooting all round was of a very high order, end far above the average. Lieut. Warren, of the Victoria,s, the winner of last year's Queen's Prize, put on 26 at 200 yards—exactly the same score he made twelve months ago. The prize list in the Alexandra competition was posted late on Tuesday afternoon. Colour-Sergt. Vicars 13th Middlesex, took the first prize, £3O; Colour Serge. Semtnence, 4th Norfolk, £2O : Coml. M'Morran, sth Lanark, and Sergt. Palmer, Ist Warwick, £l5 each. '

On Wednesdiy, in spite of wind and rain, the scores generally were higher than in previous .years, especially in the competition for the Queen's Prize. At the 500 yards range Private Lewis, 4th Devon, Lieutenant Mac- Intyre, Dumbarton, Sergeant Crompton, 3rd Liverpool, and Private Hart. Birmingham, each made the highest possible score. Lewis now stands at the head of the list, with an aggregate of 68 points out of a possible 70. Highest possible scares were also made for the Holford, Perrinet, and Windmill prizes. At a meeting in the even- ing, a resolution was passed unanimously in favour of Richmond Park as a site for future meetings. On Thursday, the winner of the highest prize of the Wimbledon meeting announced Iso far was Lieutenant Barrett, of the sth Volunteer Battalion Argyle and Sut- herland Highlanders. His total score in the first stage of the shooting for the Queen's Prize was the largest made-96,—and he takes the bronze medal. Lieutenant Barrett is an Englishman, and formerly belonged to a Rochdale corps. No competitor with a lower score than 86 is entitled to shoot in the second stage of the Queen's Prize contest, in Which stage last year 39 men who only made 83 points took part. The Martins Challenge Cup and £l5 have been won by Captain Timmins, 2nd Cheshire, with the" best possible" at 600 yards.
