div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Load Randolph Churchill has arranged to leave Eng- land in about a fortnight's time for a tour in the Pyre- nees and Spain. The lion. Philip Stanhope will, in Committee of Supply, move the reduction of the vote which includes the Attorney-General's salary by the amount of such salary, for the purpose of discussing Sir Richard Webster's action in the case of O'Donnell v. Walter. The Grand Committee on Trade met again on Mon- day, and proceeded with the consideration of the clauses in the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill dealing with canals. Mr. Mundell& said by the mere effect of compe- tition we should get good results, provided always that the canals were not under the control of the railways. Canals were at present too much under the control of the railway. (Hear, hear.) If the canals were entirely independent, then competition would regulate the rates, but at present they were not all independent, and what the Committee wanted was to bring those canals which were not independent under the same law as those canals which are independent.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AT DOLL'S HILL
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AT DOLL'S HILL

The garden party given on Saturday at Hollis Hill by Lord and Lady Aberdeen was very numerously attended. Among those present were Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, Countess Spencer, Countess Granville, Lady Harcourt, Sir Arthur and Lady Hayter, Sir Charles and Lady Russell Mr. and Lady Fanny MajorilsAnks, Mr. and Mrs. Campbell-Bannerman, Mr. and Mrs. Mundella, Countess Compton, Lord Sandhurst, Countess Tolstoi, Mr. and Mrs. Grove, Mr. and Mrs. Hoare, Sir Chas. and Lady Tennant, Hon. Mr. Hugessen, Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P.: Mr. R. M. Ferguson, M.P., and a very large number of members of Parliament, Liberal candidates, cnairmen of Liberal Associations in London, and the presidents and secre- taries of the various branches of the Women's Liberal Federation.
THE O'DONNELL LIBEL ACTION.-A CHALLENGE
FROM MR. DAVITT.

Mr. Michael Devitt. speaking on Glasgow Green on Saturday evening, said Mr. O'Donnell in taking a certain course during the recent trial acted on his (Mr. Devitt's) advice, with the view of obtaining a fair and impartial hearing. Mr. Parnell was not consulted in the matter. When the Lord Chief Justice had decided that there was no case against The Times, he should, in the interests of fair play, have prevented the Attorney-General making out a case against others. If the letters which had been read were genuine, then The Timm held proofs that would convict Mr. Parnell and others of conspiracy to murder. He challenged the Attorney-General to put him (Mr. Devitt) and Mr. Parnell in the dock. THE RETENTION OF IRISH MEMBERS AT WEST- MINSTER,

Correspondence is published which has taken place between Mr. Parnell and Mr. Rhodes, ex-Minister of Cape Colony. now in London, on the retention of Irish members at Westminster. The latter wrote to Mr. Parnell as a sympathiser with the claims of Ireland to self- government, but said the exclusion of Irish members from Westminster seemed to be considered in England and the Colonies a step in the direction of pure repara- tion, while the tribute clauses were degrading to Ireland by placing her in the position of a conquered province, and were also opposed to the first principles of constitu- tional government. Mr. Parnell, in reply, admitted that he considered the exclusion of Irish mem- bers from Westminster a defect in • the proposed Act, and that such exclusion might have given colour to the accusation that the bill had a separatist tendency. He /said this while asserting and believing that the measure was accepted by the Irish people without after- thought of that kind, and as a satisfactory settlement of the dispute between Great Britain and Ireland. He agreed that there should be effective safeguards for the maintenance of Imperial unity. If the next Home Rule scheme provided for the retention at Westminster of Irish members, he would cheerfully aerree to it. Mr. Rhodes in a further letter offered £lO,OOO to Mr. Parnell as a contribution towards the funds of the party, and enclosed a cheque for £5,000 as the first instalment.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.
Two young men, John Kilkenny and Kilkelly, were drowned, on Monday, in Lough Lee, near Athlone, by the accidental upsetting of a boat.

The eviction ot the 65 tenants on the Vandelour estate, county Clare, who have adopted the Plan of Cam- paign will commence at the end of this month. At Armagh Assizes, on Tuesday, Bettina Prior, daughter of the late Col. Prior, J.P., was indicted for the murder of a child named Flaven, whom she enticed into the kit- chen of her house, and, it is alleged. deliberately drowned in a boiler. The prisoner pleaded not guilty, and the case was adjourned. On Monday, cause was shown, before Mr. Jastice Monroe, against making absolute the conditional order for a mandamus, directing the resident magistrates to state a case with the object of quashing the conviction of Davis Barry and three others, under the Crimes Act, for the Killeagh conspiracy, to put them in a position to bring an action against the justices. Judgment was reserved. Mr. Healy, M.P., supported the conditional order, and Mr. Ronan was for the justices. Four members of a Nationalist excursion party were arrested in Belfast (m Monday, on a charge of causing a riot. on Saturday in Temple Patrick village, about nine miles distant. It appears the excursionista, after reach- ing Temple Patrick, quarrelled with the villagers, and caur.Ad serioui disturbances, which the polies were un- able to quell, with the result that several shots were tired from revolvers, and a young man named Charles Ross was dangerously wounded. A number of other persons were also injured, and for several hours there was much excitement.

A vsry strong feeling exists amongst Nationalist mem- bers in reference to the sudden death of Mr. John Man- deville, which, it is alleged, was accelerated by a disease of the throat contracted at Tullemore Gaol. An informal consultation took place on Monday afternoon, and the question of raising the matter in the House by moving the adjourtament forthwith was seriously discussed. Eventually it was decided to defer Parliamentary action until sworn information should have been given. It was also decided that Mr. Mandeville's funeral should be the occasion of a great demonstration, and to this end a communication was forwarded to the deceased's relatives, asking that the ceremony should be postponed until Sunday. THE HEALTH OF MR. DILLON. Private letters received by the leaders of the Home Rule party in London give a satisfactory account of MT. John Dillon's health. He is being very carefully treated by the prison authorities, who, it is said, are sensibly impressed with the peril of applying the prison rules in all their severity to a man of his delicate constitution. It is confidently expected by the Irish leaders that, in consequence of the death of Mr. John Mandeville, the authorities would be doubly careful with respect to Mr. Dillon. THE MURDER IN A CHURCH. 71At Armagh Assizes, on Tuesday, a young man named William Thompson was indicted for the murder of his hrother-in-law, Thomas Thompson. in Knockarnuckley Church, near Portadown, on March 2nd. The prisoner's sister, who was the deceased's wife, died 12 months ago, and the widower became engaged to a young woman named Moffat. The prisoner, who had accused Thomas Thompson of ill-treating his first wife, became enraged at the projected second marriage, and swore he would prevent it. On the day appointed for the mar- riage he went early to the church, and on the bridal party entering stepped forward, and shot the bridegroom in the back, inflicting a wound from which the unfor- tunate man died within a few hours. The prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to be hanged on the 1301 of August next.

TERRIBLE MURDER OF A BOY. • At Killarney, on Saturday, Johanna Doyle was com- mitted for trial for the murder of her little son, 10 years old, deaf, dumb, and a cripple. After the murder she and all the other members of the family, except the father, were placed as lunatics in the asylum. On Satur- day they were all released from the asylum, and the woman was brought before a magistrate with her eldest son, Thomas, both being charged with murder. A state- tnent she made in the asylum was given in evidence against her. It was to the effect that when the cock crew after midnight she found the deaf and dumb boy was not her son, but a wicked fairy. With the aid of Thomas she carried him out of the house and threw him into the manure heap, and then, getting a hatchet, dealt him three blows on the head, after which she went back to the house, and they all prayed. Thomas was dis- charged from custody.

div.head: ADDRESS TO ARCHBISHOP VVALSH.
div.p: ADDRESS TO ARCHBISHOP VVALSH.

Archbishop Walsh has received from the dean and ehapter of his diocese an address of welcome, on his re- turn from Rome, recognising that the Pope took him into council on the temporal concerns of Ireland, and lamenting the persistent perversions and abso- lute falsehoods published concerning the confidential relations between his grace and his Holiness, despite authentic denials, expressing confidence that every in- terest, of Ireland was safe in his grace's care. Archbishop Walsh, replying, says that at no time was an archbishop ..1 Dublin engaged in a work more directly tending to tie advancement of the best interests of the diocese and its people; his anxiety arising only from the falsehoods circulated to shake the foundations of Irish Catholicity and their confidence in the Holy Father, who was no less anxious to learn the truth abeut Ireland. His grace made the freest use Of the occasion of putting before the Pope, in the fullest detail, the true character of the claims and aspirations of the people, whether as regards the move- ment for national autonomy, or the national struggle for redress of the cruel injustice which, notwithstanding the adoption of so many measures for reform, still oppress the agricultural tenants of Ireland. The Pope has grasped them in all their bearings; and while in matters purely of politics it is hot for his Holiness to interfere, he was authorised to make it, known to the people of Ireland that in every legitimate effort they might count upon his fullest sympathy. No one feels more intensely than the Pope the miseries under which Ireland still suffers, and he desired that the country may soon receive the blessing of a lasting peace, based upon prosperity.

Percy Jackson, son of a Bolton ironfonnder. died a Cheadle Asylum, on Monday, from injuries attributed las a football accident, which also deprived him of his reason.

A respectablv-dressed woman, who had been drinking during Monday, walked into the soa at Sandgate. in the evening, with her two children. The mother and eider child were rescued, hut a baby is missing.

The steamer Velinora, of Swansea, was returning to Ilfracombe with a large party of excursionists yester- day, when she ran into and sank a small smack. The crew escaped. A panic ensued among the passengers.

At Bow-street Police Court, on Saturday, Walter Hay- Hugs, alias Benj. Brooks, private in the Grenadier Guards, was remanded, charred on his own confession with the murder in April, 1879, of a man unknown, whom he arid he threw into the Herrington Reservoir at Aston, Bir- mingham. Robert Yorston, shoemaker, died at his house, Victoria- street., Kirkwall, on Sunday night, at the advanced age of 101 years and six months. He had been confined to his bed for some time. Only a few years ago he was working at his trade of shoemaking. He was a native of KirkvOall. _ _ _ _

Among the saloon passengers on board the Cunard steamer Aurania,which arrived at Queenstown on Sunday morning from New York, were the Duke and Duchess of Marlborough, who were recently married in New York. The Duke and Duchess proceeded in the steamer for Liverpool, en route to Blenheim House. . .

On Monday, at Rochdale, Luke Kelley was charged with fighting in a field, on Saturday night, near Mitchelt Heyrnill. The fight was prearranged in Manchester, and it had gone on for a quarter of an hour in the presence of about 1,000 persons before the police arrived. Kelley and his opponent jumped into the road, but the former was captured. He was bound over to keep the peace. himself in £lO and two sureties in £5, with the alterna- tive of 14 days' imprisonment A terrible death from hydrophobia was investigated by a Liverpool coroner's jury on Monday. A clerk named Branthwaite was administering some medicine to his collie dog on Jnne 3rd, when the dog bit his thumb. He had the wound cauterised, but on the 13th serious symp- toms set in, and he went to the doctor, who ordered him to bed, as acute symptoms of hydrophobia set in. Ile suffered terribly from the most aggravated form of the disease, and died in convulsions. The dog was de- stroyed. A Mitrrarty DIVORCE SUIT—In the Divorce Division, on Monday. Sir James Barmen and a special jury had before them the divorce suit of Maunsell v. Maunaell and Duthv, which was the petition of a brigade-surgeon in the Royal Artillery for dissolution of marriage on the around of his wife's adultery with Major Archibald Edward Duthy, of the Royal Artillery, from whom dam- ages to the extent of £lO,OOO were claimed. The suit was practically undefended, and the jury awarded the petitioner £2,000 as damages. THE JEWISH New YEA 12.—The New Year of the Jews commences five weeks hence. According to the tra- ditional chronology of tho synagogue this will be the 5645th year since the creation of the world. Autumn commences at three ,a'dock in the morning of the 6th October, winter at half-past ten in the morning of the sth January, coring at six o'clock in the evening of the 6th April, and summer at half-past one in the morning of the 6th July. The year 5645 is the 1816th since the destruction of the Second Temple.

The Mancbester Coroner held an inquest on Monday on the body of E. Mitchell, a constable in the county police force. The deceased, who joined the force 11 years ago, was seen to take two or three glasses of drink while on duty on Saturday night. The circumstance was mentioned to him at the police station, and he went straight home rind hanged himself with a rope fastened to the bannister of the staircase. His wife was the first to discover the body, on her return trom shopping. A verdict of "Suicide during temporary insanity" was returned.

• Loss OF a FISHING BOATLAND Two MEN.—On Monday, Mr. Webster, coroner, hed an inquest at Parton, Cum- berland, on the body of Harry Humphreys, whose body was found on Sunday afternoon on the beach. The de- ceased and Robert Griffin went out herring fishing, and, as the weather was unsettled and stormy, it was feared that their boat had been swamped and both men drowned. This fear was confirmed by the finding of the body of Humphreys. Tloth men were married, and Humphreys leaves a large family.—A verdict of " Found drowned' was returned.

FATAL f.var.—On Sunday, an excursion train was run from Sheffield to Cleethorpes. After the train had passed Retford station, and.whilst it was going at a great pace, a man leaped out of one of the carriar.zes and died shortly afterwards. He had fishing, tackle with him, and upon his clothes was found a card of the Sheffield Angling club, containing the name of "C. Oates. Pearl-street, `zheffield." It is thought that, the man's destination must have been Retford, and whether he had got into the wrong train or had honed that the excursion would stop, at that place has not transpired. MURDER BY A SOLIMER.—A serious case of murder by a soldier is reported from Dore. Early on Friday m irninc Gunner Kelly, of the it battery (3rd riencle) of Rural Artillery, while on sentry duty, left his post and went to the quarters of Serceant-Major Burton, of the same tvittery. He found the sercermt-msjor asleep on his cot, with his child near him, and deliberately shot him. The bullet shattered Burton's face, but he menaced to reach the guardroom and obtain PAA;stance. A Mina° was sent for, hut just as the sergeant-inajor was about enter Kelly came up suddenly and shot him through !lie back, killing him on the spot. Kelly then gave him- self up, expressin.g satisfaction at the deed. The motive fcr the crime was rerence, the serceant-major having - caused Kelly to be removed from the position of orderly- room clerk.

" MA RRY Mn on ME."—A sensational scene occerred Saturds.y in the court-room at Dordo.ne. A poacher named Ilaymend was on trial for the murder of a young girl, Marguerite Gonthier. A LAICCASRIRR VISITOR nROR'RED TN DOTTILAS BAT. On Monday afternoon. two yonng men hired a boat, 'and rowed across Door;las !lay The wind freshened, and in their anxiety to reach the shore an oar was lost. 'rhey were being rapidly carried out to sea, when Frank Me.Larney, coxswain of the Douglas lifeboat, ..who was in a sailing 'yacht, some distance off, saw their plight, and sailed alter them. fie came up with the boat about a mile from the iron pier, and shouted to the occu- pants to keep their seats until he got a!ong- ,:ide. Roth, however, rashly stnroi up,, and, as the yacht neared the boat, tried to leao on board the yacht, with the result that only one succeeled in getting aboard with Mc.Larney's help. and the tither man, named raylor, fell into the water. McLarney two' threw a rope to him, the second Time touching his head, but Taylor disappeared, and was drowned. 'l'aylor is stated •o have gone from near Oldham, and was the only sup- nort of aged parents. Art ADVENTURFSS.—Miss Esther Hounsome, about 30 ,ears of are, who has just been admitted b. the work- louse at Eltha tn, Kent, has, according to her own account, had a remarkable earner. She arrived at Hythe about 15 months ago, and, it is alleged, took a handsomely furnished house on the bank of the canal. The fact of occupying suei a residence enabled her to get credit. She now and then displayed a roll of wlAt purported to las bank notes; hut what, chiefly brought her into notice was a story she told of her having recently come into a fortune of £40,030. She subsequently removed to still more pretentious premises in Douglas Avenue, furnishing the place sumptuously on the credit system. In the meantime she was received in the best society, and drove about with the principal ladies of the town; she gave afternoon tea, and altogether moved in !ocal society as a lady of position and wealth. At one drapery establishment she ran up a debt of over £lOO. At length, through the instrumentality of a pressing creditor, the crash Came. She was besieged with appli- cations for money, her furniture was seized, and she baa now been removed to the workhouse. Although of lady- like apnea. ance, Miss Hounsome is by no means an edu- cated person, and she new confesses that sloe has been a domestic servant, her last position being that of lady's maid. She owes nearly £l,OOO to Hytbe tradesmen alone.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1888.

evening if he had not understood from the leader of the House of Commons that it was not one of the measures that he was going to abandon. He had, however, just heard that the right hon. gentleman, in a not unnatural panic under a threat of obstruc- tion of any bill on the suhject which was not intro- duced at the beginning of the session, had decided to abandon it. and under those circumstances he should not detain their lordships longer. (Hear, hear, and laughter.; Really the way in which Lord SALISBURY tosses over Mr. SMITH is delightful. Mr. SMITH LS said to have been in a state of "panic" because Mr. GLansroNs, in his blandest manner, expressed the hope that the Life Peerages Bill would be aban- doned. Poor Mr. SMITH; there are none so poor as to do \him reverence. And observe how the PRIME M4ISTER calls Mr. GLADSTONE'S request a "threat of obstrtiction." It was a threat which he seems to have anticipated, and to which he was obviously prepared to yield. It was a case of "whispering {he'd] ne'er consent, consented." But the climax was not reached until Lord SALISBURY himself moved the discharge of the Bill for deal- ing with the "bad lot" in the House of Lords. When questioned by Lord ROSEBERY as to whether the " threat " of obstructiod applied to this second bill, the PRIME MINISTER replied—" To all reform of the House of Lords." As a matter of fact there was no threat at all, and the second bill was not even' referred to by Mr. GLADSTONE. But the second bill was withdrawn; and on the motion, too, of Lord SALISBURY. And so the farce ended.

THERE has been a good deal said 'from time to time about the retention of the Irish members at Westminster in case of granting Home Rule to Ire- land. It was regarded by many politicians—and particularly Liberal Unionistsr—as a blot upon Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill that no provision was male for Ireland being represented in the Imperial Parliament. There are difficulties what- ever course is taken, but the balance of opinion seems to be in the direction of letting Ireland be represented in an English parliament—even in the case of the creation of an Irish parliament; and Mr. GLADSTONE has shown that he has quite an open mind on the subject. Some correspondence which has just taken place between Mr. PARNELL and Mr. C. J. RHODES, a member of the Legislative Assembly, and an ex-Cabinet Minister of Cape Colony, reveals the fact that, so far as the leader of the Irish party is concerned, he is in favour of Ire- land being directly represented at Westminster. Mr. RHODES, in writing to Mr. PARNELL, said : "The exclusion of the Irish members from West- minster seemed rightly to be considered, both in England and' the colonies, as a step in the direction of pure separation, while the tribute clauses were on the faceeof them degrading to Ireland by placing her in the position of a conquered province, and were opposed to the first principles of constitutional government by sanctioning taxation without repre- sentation." This puts the objection to exclusion in a nutshell; but it IS due to Mr. GLADSTONE to say that if his bill :had Made the provision now deemed desirable, there are some critics who would have been ready to urge that it was preposterous to provide for Irishmen having Control, not only of their own affairs, but of the affairs of England. Mr. PARNELL is like Mr. GLADSTONE in regarding the issue as of minor'importance ; but replying to Mr. RHODES, he says :----" I am convinced that it would be the highest statesmanship on Mr. GLAD- STONE'S part to devise a feasible plan for the con- tinued presence :of the Irish members here, and from my observation Of public events and opinion since 1885, I am sure that Mr. Gladstone is fully alive to the importance of the matter, and that there can be no doubt that the next measure of autonomy for Ireland will, contain the provisions which you rightly deem of such moment." This declaration has given Mr. RHODES great satisfac- tion, and, as it clears the way in his judgment, he offers a contribution of no less than £lO,OOO to the funds of the Home Rule ,party, at the same time sending a cheque for £5,000 as his first instalment. This must be'very gratifying to the Parnellites, the contribution coming, as it does, at a time when the Parnellites are being grossly misrepresented and shamefully abused. Since the correspondence, which is naturally regarded as of considerable im- portance, Mr. PARNELL has been interviewed by, a representative of the "Pall Mall Gazette," and has made further disclosure of his views on this particular phase of the Irish question. Referring Hto the rejected bill, he said:—" It was a bill establishing dualism. The Irish members sat in the Irish Parliament and the British members in the 13ritish Parliament, neither having anything to do with each other. The new bill will proceed upon a different principle, and will provide, I imagine, for the retention of the Irish members in the Imperial Parliament, while leaving the Irish Parliament at Dublin free to control the affairs of Ireland. After Ireland has had some experience of Home Rule, the Scotch will probably require to have their Parliament at Holyrood, but they will certainly insist upon their continued representation at Westminster." He might have added that the Welsh, too, will require Home Rule; and thus we get, as the way out of the many difficulties which beset the matter, four Home Rule Parliaments and one Imperial Parliament—an evolution which, as we have for some time contended, is the natural outcome of our progressive development in legislation. It may be, as Mr. RHODES and as Mr./PARNELL suppose, that when the battle for ,the federal principle is over as to Ireland., thel way will be paved for a federation which shall include all the colonies. And why not? If we are to have Imperial Federa- tion, it will certainly have to be on SOMA such basis. Sir HERCULES ROBINSON is reported to have said:—" The Irish will save the empire yet. Nothing but Home Rule co* uld ever compel the House of Commons to delegate its powers or to enfranchise the colonies by admitting them to share in the government of the empire, and as an empire you must federate or perish." It would be strange if the struggle for• Home Rule in Ireland should, after all, prove to be the great- est conservative movement of modern times. Yet things quite as strange have happened in the past. Let the Tories and Liberal Unionists take warn- ing; they may find that the stars in their courses are fighting against them.

We understand that the prospectus of the Belle Vue, Liverpool, Limited, will be issued in a few days. This is a unique opportunity for investment in ' a project which ought to be highly remunerative to its sharehol- ders, and we have no doubt the prospectus will be awaited with interest.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1888.
" TOI7CII AND GO."

- - - It is no use telling the farmer to "make hay whilst the sun shines." , He will answer that the sun does not shine, unless it be in the night, and then it shines on the other side of the world. Still, there is an average being struck; last year it was all sheen; this year it is all shade. And how cold it is 1 It is the summer of furs and overcoats. '

'The "unspeakable Turk" is breaking out in a fresh place. It is actually stated that a pamphlet advocating a Turkish Parliament has found its way to the Yildiz Kiosk and to the cabinets of certain exalted officials at the Porte. A Par- liament! They will be talking of Home Rule next.

Ann Williamson, who appeared in the Waring- ton Police Court with a black eye, was fined 58 for being drunk and disorderly on the previous night. She was not sure, she said, about being drunk; but she may be excused for being hazy on sub- ject. A woman with a black eye cannot be ex- pected to see clearly. •

The Keswick and District Footpaths Association have secured +he right of way to the top of Lat- rigg. The hill is taken in the ascent of Skiddaw ; it is about 1,200 feet high; and commands splendid views. The victory is a victory not only for to- day, but for all time; and the thanks of all lovers of lovely rrcenery are due to the Footpaths Asso- ciation.

The cotton trade must be doing pretty well, or the operative spinners of North and North-East Lancashire would not have secured an advance of five per cent. without a blow being struck. Spin- ners are not a large body compared with weavers; but they are well officered, and well organised. We congratulate the employed on the advance, and the employers on being able to concede it.

Mr. Brunner is showing an active interest in the Local Government Bill. He has from the first given close attention to the measure; and has sought to Amend it in several important particu- lars. His name, it may be added, is amongst the list of English M.P's. who joined in sending a wreath for the grave of John Mandeville, who was done to death by coercion in Ireland.

General Boulanger has got more than he bar- gained for. He worked up a scene in the Chamber on Thursday to enable him to resign, but it didn't come off quite as he expected. lie called the Prime Minister a liar; but M. Floquet is a Frenchman with as much fight in him as the General.' The result was a duel, in which the French Jingo has got very much' the worst of it; he is badly wounded.

With an autumn session provided for, the Local Government Bill is pretty certain to become law this year. But with the abandonment of the licensing clauses, and of the District Council pro- visions, it will be a maimed and mutilated thing. It is understood that the first elections for the County Councils will take place next January. As there is yet much to do in the shape of preparing the way for the elections there will have to be sharp work to prevent a elections, collapse.

Warrington has missed its chance of be- coming a Town County. The clause limitino the privilege to towns of 50,000 and upwards passed.the Blouse of Commons on Tuesday; but last evening it was arranged that the Isle- of Ely should be' a separate county It is a pity that; whilst the matter was still open, there was no one to put in a word for Warrington. Where was the borough member, and what was he doing?

The marriage of the Duke of Marlborough to the rich American widow is being discussed by the Yankee papers with true Yankee freedom. ome of them make it out that the ceremony was illegal because the Duke is a person who has been "divorced abroad for his own guilt." But, as the new duchess is to reside in England, she will not trouble herself as to New York law. She has made up her mind to take her chance; a dukedom is in one respect like charity—it covers a multi- tude of sins.

William Dia-enson, buifder and contractor, Accrington, is an unusual sort of bankrupt. His assets are expected to realise a surplus of over £5OO after paying his creditors 20s in the pound. But perhaps receiver, lawyer, and accountant will relieve the Court of any trouble as to the surplus. If Dickenson, in the way of contracting, had been careful to contract fewer debts he might have had a free hand, and kept the surplus to himself.

'There are certain milk-dealers who well make use of the cow with the iron tail, though it is a fraud upon their customers and a breach of the law. Wm. King, farmer, of Halewood, was fined £5 and costs in one case, and ordered to pay costs in two other cases, for selling milk adulterated with water to the extent of from 10 to 13 per cent. Mr. Muspratt rightly observed that the offence was a very serious one, and he rightly followed up his, observation by inflicting a serious penalty. Fraudulent farmers can afford to laugh at the law when for a big offence they are let off with a little fine.

Sir John Millais exoresses his ," Thoughts on our art of to-day" in the current issue of Cassell's "Magazine of Art." It is a capital article, and may be rem' and re-read with advantage. He has no sympathy with those who insist on brown, even in grass, and says—" God Almighty has given us green, and you may depend upon it it's a fine colour." This mode of expression suggests the story of "the lady Marechale" referred to by Carlyle, who said— Depend upon it, sir, God thinks twice before damning a man of that quality." But Sir John talks sense, and the lady talked nonsense.

On Thursday an inquest was held on the body of an elderly man named George Taylor Ward, who committed suicide, in the Mersey, at Runcorn. It is an especially pathetic feature in the case that the poor fellow, who was a joiner, seems to have been drivolin out of his mind through being out of work for ten weeks. In Germany, it is under con- sideration to make provision for workmen 17 a species of insurance, one third of the premium being provided by the State, 'another by the em- ployer, and the third by the workman himself. Would it not be as well to try something of the kind in England? The best amongst the poor I will die rather than go to the workhouse.

A good deal has been done by strict regulations to prevent accidents in coal mines; but it would seem as if the regulations required to be more stringent. There have been no less than three acci- dents in the St. Helens district within the past week. In one instance a man had his ribs broken; at another colliery a miner had his thigh broken; and at a third mine two men were killed outright. In every case the injuries were from falls from the roof. It is a matter of course to say that when the utmost precaution is taken accidents will happen ; but the point to consider is whether more precaution can be taken than is being taken.

Bad work has bad results. Charles Goodman, a sailor, who had had too much drink, fell into the Weston canal the other night and was drowned. A woman who saw the accident, tried to assist him with her umbrella; "but she was not able to keep him up owing to the ferrule, which she had hold of, coming off in her hand." If that ferrule had been I put on Iroperly the man's life' miqht have been , saved. The Prince Imperial lost Ins life through I bad workmanship. When the Zulus were in pur- suit he failed to mount his horse because of the saddle giving way; the result was that he was im- mediately overtaken and slain. Workman, what- ever thine hand findeth to do, do it with all thy might.

The Duke of Argyll—" that portentous politi- cal pedagogue," as Lord Rosebery happily styled him the other day, was holding forth in the House of Lords, on Thursday, in favour of coer- cion. Seeing that his own crofters have had their rents reduced, not by the Duke, but by the Corn- missioners, it is quite intelligible, if not wholly

creditable, that his Grace should assist in holding down those who are stru;gling against landlord tyranny in Ireland. 'lt is suggestive of the little influence he now possesses that no one in the House thought it worth while to say a single word in reply to his long lucubration.

The Duke of Argyll made one point in his speech, but to do that he had to substitute fiction for fact. He said Mr. -Gladstone's conver- sion to Home Rule was sudden and violent, and •was as reruarkable as that of St. Paul. As the Duke assumes to know everything, he knows, or ought to know, that before the election of 1E435 and before the so-called conversion—Mr. Glad- stone said that if the Irish people were united, under the extended franchise, in demanding a cer- tain thing, it might become necessary for Parlia- ment to make such changes as would go to the very foundation of the constitution. It is obvious to those who are not wilfully blind that Mr. Gladstone had Honie Rule in his mind then, and, if so, his conversion was the result of evolu- tion—not of miracle.

Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight" frde on application.—Advt A SUCCESSFUL WIDNES MUSICIAN.—MiSS Gertrude Owens, daughter of Mr. Samuel Owens, Widnes-road, has passed the Trinity College (London) Junior Exami- nation in musical knowledge, gaining 89 marks out of a maximum of 100. She is the pupil of Mr. Thos. Sherratt, of Lugsdale-road. FARNIVORTH PARISH CHURCH.—As announced some months ago, the Rev. W. Edmondson, formerly curate of Parr. St. Helens, has now taken charge of the living of Farnworth, in place of the Rev. G. Bond, who is sus- pended. The Rev. James Lawton, curate-in-charge, has departed to a new curacy in Gloucestershire. SUCCESSFUL RUNCORN VOLUNTEER AT WIMBLEDON.— Captain Timmins, of Runcorn (2nd C.R.V.), on Thursday won the cup and £l5 in the Martini's competition at Wimbledon, with the best possible score of 55 points at 600 yards. In the Queen's Prize competition Captain Timmins reached a total of 81 points, and fails to get into the 300 by five points. RUNCORN STARR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY. In connection with the first society an appropriation was held in the office of the secretary, Mr. W. Handley, on Monday night. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. J. D. Jones was voted to the chair. Mr. William Betney and Mr:, William Booth were appointed scrutineers of the ballot. The first number drawn was that of a person who hadwithdra,wn from the society, and, a second bal- lot was taken, with the result that Mr. Joseph Newall (415), carpenter, of Stanley-st, is entitled to the loan of £2OO free bf interest for 121 years. CAMDEN SUNDAY &moor,. ItromogN.—The teachers and a few friends of this school, in all about 60 persons, on Monday had a pic-nic to Comberbac.h, near Budworth. They left Runcqrn about ten o'clock in the morning, in three brakes supplied by Messrs. Yarwood, and after a pleasant drive arrived at their destination. With the exception of one heavy shower during the afternoon, the weather was fine, and the party passed a most enjoyable day amid the scenery of Marbury Mere, Dinner and tea were provided in Comberbach school. The return jour- ney was occornplished by nine o'clock in the evening. POLICE hiseectioisr AT RUNCORN. The honourable Captain Legge, H.M. Government Inspector, on Mouda.y inspected the members of the Runcorn Police Division. There were on parade Superintendent Hollingsworth, In- spector O'Donnell. and Sergeants Woolley, Gosling, Booth and Nield, with 19 constables. Five constables were on duty. The clothing and accoutreMents of the force were closely examined by Captain Legge, and afterwards In- spector O'Donnell put the men, who presented a smart appearance, through a course of drill. The Government Inspector then visited the cells, courtroom, and offices. and examined the books, and it is pleasing to record that everything was found in a very, satisfactov condi- tion. Williams 6B THE RUNCORN STORES MEN ON Pic-mc.—The enyloyes of the Runcorn Co-operative Stores were enabled to have a holiday on Tuesday, through the kindness of the com- mittee. They took advantage of their liberty to have a pic-nic to Chester, and a party of 40 hada pleasant drive to the ancient , city in two breaks supplied by Messrs. Yarwood. Arriving at 12-30, the visitors at once sat down to a capital dinner provided by Mr. Hewitt, of Foregate-st., and afterwards they divided into small companies and went to view the curious and interesting sights of the city. At 8-30 tea was provided, and two hours later the return journey was commenced, and safely accomplisned at eleven o'clock, a most enjoyable day having been spent. The arrangements were carried out by a committee consisting of Messrs. A. Ashbrook, J. Leach, W. Ashton, J. Shipley, W. Cartwright, R. Owen, , J. Cropper, J. Whittington, W. Powell, J. Shaw, and W.

Lacy. HALTON LADIES' ann.—The seventy-second anniver- sary of the above-named club, which r is the oldest, wealthiest, and has the largest number of members of , any club of its kind in England, was cetebrated on Mon- day afternoon. The club is under the patronage of Lady Brooke, who has in the past taken a great interest in the welfare of its members; and it was universally regretted that she was unable to be present. The balance sheet, 'which had been audited and approved by Mr G. J. Knight, accountant, of Runcorn, showed that the amount expended during the past year in sick allowance to mem- bers had been £B4 6s; funeral money, £2O; surgeon's fees, £37 12s. The member's subscriptions amounted to £139 us 6d; and the money in the Runcorn Savings' Bank to the credit of the club is shown to be £157 12s 3d; in London and North-Western stock, £615 18s 8d; in the Halton Burial Board, £196 8s 8d; in Parr's Bank- ing Company, £57 12s 4d; and after deducting a balance of £2 16s 4d which was due to the treasurer, the total amount of funds of the club is £1,027 15s 4d. It will thus be seen that the club is in a sound financial posi- tion. The members, to the number of 250, met at the Castle, and walked in processional order to the Parish Church, where an appropriate sermon was preached by the Rev S. L. Laidman, vicar of Barnton. After the ser- vice the members again formed in processional order, and, to the music of the Runcorn Volunteer Band, marched to the 'gates of Norton Priory. At the head walked Mrs Charles Reynolds, Mrs Henry Reynolds, Miss Reynolds. Mr Talbot, Mr C. Reynolds, J.P., Dr Carru- thers, Messrs Gannon, Wright, and J. Stokes. and the Rev S. L. Laidinan and Rev J. Lockwood. On return- ing to the Castle, the members partook of an excellent tea in a tent erected by Mr Cooper, of Runcorn. Mr Howard, of the Castle Hotel, was the caterer. Subse- quently a brief speech was delivered by Mr C. Reynolds, and votes of thanks to the various officers were passed. Tim NEW ItoNeoax MAGISTRATES.—Dr. Steele and Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg took their seats on the Bench at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday for the. first time. ACCIDENT TO A FLATMAN AT WIDNES.—There now lies at Widnes Accident Hospital a flatman named Platt, who is suffering from a 'fracture of the skull.' The man was assisting in working one of Mr. Cooper's flats, and in throwing out the anchor the windlass struck him on the head, causing the injuries mentioned. He is progressing under the care of Dr. McDonnell. WELSH WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The anniversary of this chapel was celebrated on Satclay evening last, when the Rev. Hugh Owen Hughes, of Machyullath, South Wales district, preached an eloquent sermon. On Sunday the rev, gentleman, and also the Rev. D. Jones, of Bagillt. preached to good congregations. The collec- tions in aid of the trust fund realised over £9. NEW WESLEYAN MINISTER FOR WIDNES.—Next month thq Rev. R. Burdon, superintendent minister of the Wid- nes Wesleyan Circuit, leaves the town for Pocklington, near York. During the three years he has resided in the circuit Mr. Burden has earned the affection and good will of all with whom he has come in contact, by his earnest yet unassuming labours in the cause of Christ. He will be succeeded by the Rev. Thomas Law, of Ripon, who is mentioned by the "Ripon Gazette." for his faithful and acceptable services in chapel and school work. THEFT BY A LODGER AT RUNCORN.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Michael Hedley, a labourer, was charged with stealing a watch and a pair of boots, worth 355, the property of ,John Moore, fitter at Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele s, who resides at 2, Ann-st. The prisoner had lodged at the house of Moore. On Friday he left, andllie watch and boots were missed. Evidence was given that the prisoner had pawned the watch with Mr. E. Imison, and the boots with Mr. Craddock. The pri- soner admitted his guilt, and he was sentenced to a month's hard labour. DISTRIBUTING INDECENT LITERATURE AT RUNCORN:- Harry Williams and Peter Garritty-, young men, were were brought before Dr. Steele and Mr. Lloyd Wigg, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, charged with haying on the previous day distributed indecent literature in the town. Police-clerk Sutherland proved the case. Su- perintendent Holting,worth said these men were sent out by a firm styled Longest and Co., Liverpool. There were no less than six men distributing books and bills on the previous day, when there were thousands of visitors in the town. The Chief Constable had issued instructions that the practice should be stopped.— The prisoners were each fined 40s and costs, or a month. ROBBING UPPER MERSEY COMMISSIONERS: At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Moses Peers, of Cartwright-st., was charged with stealing a spade belon- ging to the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners. It appeared that about a month ago the prisoner borrowed a spade from Thomas Houghton, engineer on the "Buoy Boat," stating that he had a job that would take a few hours. He promised to return it, but instead of doing so, he sold the spade to Ann Simcock, general dealer, of Appleton-st., Widnes, and he was apprehended by P.S. Gosling.—The prisoner said he took the spade back, but the boat had gone.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said this was the prisoner's 58th appearance., A sentence of a month's imprisonment was passed upon the prisoner. INSANE THROUGH DRINK AT RUNCORN.—A man named James Farrell, described as a tramping tailor, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, un- der circumstances stated by Superintendent Hollings- worth. On Monday night he was brought to the police station in a "dripping wet" condition, charged with being a wandering lunatic. He had jumped into the Old Quay Canal, and swam across to the other side. He however, left his hat in the water, and he again jumped in, and brought it out. Dr. McDougall examined the prisoner, and said he was suffering from various hallu- cinations, the result of excessive drinking. The prisoner had since been six days in Walton gaol, and a warder gave evidence that the man was now all right; The prisoner was discharged with a caution. BITING A MAN'S LIP OFF AT WIDNES:. kt Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Timothy Mitchell, of Eliza- beth-st., Moss Bank, was charged with causing grievous bodily harm to Patrick Kelly, Charlotte-st. On Satur- day night the men had a quarrel, and were fighting in the street. Whilst wrestling on the ground Kelly called out in pain, "Oh, he's biting my face off," and a man named Ryan pulled the prisoner up. Kelly was bleeding profusely from the mouth, and Dr Hutchinson was sent for. That gentleman dressed the wound, and displayed in court a bottle containing three-quarters of an inch of Kelly's lip.—lnspector Keighley informed the magis- trates that he saw the injured man on Sunday. He could not talk distinctly, and his lip was paining him very much. He Was unable to eat anything.—The pri- soner was remanded in custody for a week THE MASONIC HOTEL. RUNCORN.—Before ,Mr. C. Rey- nolds, Dr. Steele, and Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph Grundy, landlord of the Masonic Hotel, Devonshire-place, was charged with having, on the 16th June, unlawfully permitted drun- kenness to take place on the premises.—Superintendent Hollingworth informed the Bench that the defendant had taken no actiori in regard to an appeal against a sentence passed upon him a •fortnight ago on a charge of a similar nature. With their Worships' permission he would withdraw this case. He did not wish to harass the publicans if they would endeavour to keep within the law.—Mr. C. H. Lewin said the superintendent had given the landlord an excellent character, and the con- viction in the previous case would be sufficient warning to him.—The Bench allowed the case tiz be withdrawn, the defendant paying 8s 6d costs. A VIOLENT DRUNKARD AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Barratt was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Fryer-st., on Sunday night, also with wilfully damaging, the cell at the police station to the extent of Be, and further with damaging the dwelling-house of Thomas Kelly, of Vicar-st., to the extent of 45 6d, by breaking the window-sash and panes of glass. P.C. Ratcliffe deposed that about eleven o'clock on the previous night the prisoner was very drunk, and making use of beastly language in a loud voice. He brought him to the police station, and there he was very violent and committed the damage complained of. They were obliged to pull his boots off. Catherine Kelly said the prisoner created a fearful disturbance in her house, and when he went outside he smashed the windows with his foot. The prisoner, who denied the three charges, was ordered to pay a total sum of £1 17s 10d, or go to gaol for 21 days. • WIDNES FREE LIBRARY CororrrritE. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall yesterday. Mr. Wade Deacon, J.P., presided, and there were present— Messrs. Morrison, Pankhurst, B. Brown, S. Sadler, W. Sadler, and J. T. Allen (clerk.)—The Chairman reported that he had made an application to the secretary of the Gilchrist Trust for a course of lectures to be delivered in Widnes next winter. Should the application be success- ful six lectures will be delivered in January, February, and March--one every fortnight. A charge of penny would be made for admission. He (Me. Deacon) had asked that they might be free, but the Secretary objec- ted,—The tender of Mr. T. S. Swale for printing a sup- Vementary catalogue of the Library was accepted.—The Librarian reported that during June there had been bor- rowed or consulted in the reading-room 4545 volumes being an increase in the lending department of 978 over the cor- responding month of last year, and of 77 in the lending department. The average daily issue was 175. During June the reading room was open 26 days, and the total attendances were 12,478, being a daily average of 480. The attendances show an increase of 2,699 over the cor- responding month last year. THE WIDNES ENGINE DRIVER'S ADVENTURE.—Before Mr. E. K. Muspratt and Mr. J. Brock. at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Andrew Doyle, a young man, of 18, Charlotte-st., was summoned for assaulting John Harrington, engine driver, of Travis-st. Mr. .11 W. , Knowles appeFed for the complainant, who stated that on Saturday night, about half-past eleven, he was pass- ing along Widnes-road, near the Board Schools, when he evertook the defenda a and another young man, and a young woman. Fro .n their conversation he thought the young men were undei the influence of drink, and he was going past them when the defendant made a remark to him and then struck him about a dozen blows on the head and neck, lie did not strike in return; lie merely defended himself This statement was not sup- portea by witnesses.—The defendant called William Griffiths and Elizabeth Lockett, his sweetheart. These witnesses stated that the complainant was very insulting to the defendant and his sweetheart. The defendant told him to go about his business, and complainant walked about five yards away and then called the defendant to him. He then struck the-defendant, who returned the blow in self-defence.—The case was dis- missed. A RUNCORN WATERMAN HEAVILY FINED.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. Charles Reynolds (chairman), Dr. Steele, and Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg, William Smith. landlord of the Duke of Wellington Hotel, Perci- val-lane. and Joseph Smith, his son, were charged with assaulting George White, a waterman, who lives in Brunswick-St. Across summons had been issued charging White with having been drunk and quarrelsome in the hotel, and refusing to quit when requested by the land- lord. He was further charged with assaulting Joseph Smith. Mr. C. J. Lewitt appeared for White, and the Smiths were defended by Mr. J. W. Knowles. The case for White was that on the 30th June he went into the hotel in a perfectly sober condition, and was served with a glass of beer. He was accompanied by a friend and several other persons. While he was standing at the bar Smith senior suddenly came round, and, seizing hold of him by the neck, said "Come out of this you ' —." Smith struck him on the face and kicked him, and then the son came up and did likewise while the father held him. He wits then thrown into the street. He went to a doctor an had the wounds dressed, and afterwards took out the summons. Two days later Smith took out cross summonses. The allegations of the Smiths and several witnesses was that White was very drunk, and was in a very quarrelsome mood. He made use of mostfilthy tannage to Mrs. Smith, and attempted to create a disturbance with a man in the taproom. No beer was served to him, and he was requested to leave but refused to do so, and not more force than was necessary was used to eject him. He was very violent, and struck the son several severe blows. The Bench, after hearing the whole of the evidence, dismissed the charge against both Smiths, and fined White 20; and costs for being drunk, &c., and lOs and costs for assaulting Joseph Smith.

A CENSUS or WIDNES.—The Widnes Local Board in committee, on Tuesday, decided to take a census of the town in order to ascertain how many representatives Widnes would be entitled to send to the County Council, as proposed by the Local Government Bill. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES, FIVE CROSSES.—On Sunday two sermons were preached in the Five Crosses Wes- leyan Chapel by the Rev. John Shipham, of Frodsham. The collections at the close of the services realized £2O Os 6d, and were in aid of the Sunday school funds. AN UNFORTUNATE YOUNG MAN. A son of Mr. Kyle, the architect at Messrs. Hutchinson and Company's works, was getting into the carriage of the Rev. Mr. Woole, the rector of Ditton, when the horse became res- tive and the young man was thrown with such violence against the side of the conveyance that he sustained a fracture of the arm lust below the elbow. The rev, gen- tleman drove the injured youth down to the surgery of Dr. Hutchinson, under whose treatment he is progres- sing as favourably as can be expected. Not long ago this youth was in the act of performing some gymnastic feat when both his arms were broken, and he was just getting over the effects of that illness when this unfortu- nate accident occurred. COMMITTAL OF A SHOPKEEPER TO PRISON.-0/1 Wednes- day, at the St. Helens County Court, before his Honour Judge Thompson, Frederick Coogan, grocer's manager, Runcorn, but formerly a shopkeeper in Church-st. St. Helens, was summoned to show cause why he had not obeyed the order of the court to pay £9 8s 9d, owing to Richard Seddon, hay and straw dealer, Baldwin-st. Mr. Mearns appeared for the plaintiff, and stated to his Honour that some months ago Coogan kept two grocer's shops in St. Helens, and in connection with his business he had two horses. The defendant got his hay and straw from the plaintiff, and accumulated a debt of £9 8s 9d. After keeping the shops for a short time, without any warning to his creditors Coogan sold the contents of his shops, realising upwards of £lOO, which he pocketed, and left the town. As the defendant did not appear, his Honour committed Coogan for 40 days.

WOUNDED BY A, SWIEPING BRUSH AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Elizabeth Broxton, of 14, Arthur-st., was again brought up on remand charged with having, on the 26th June, inflicted grievous bodily harm to Mary Schumann, aged 13 years, whose home is .at 54, Kent-street. • Mr Knowles appeared for the prisoner. The circumstances of the case have been previously reported. The prisoner's husband was very ill In bed, and the noise of the children playing opposite the house caused him much annoyance, and the woman ran them away several times. On the last occasion she saatched a sweeping brush from the hand of one of the children and gave the complainant a blow on the head, , inflicting a wound that bled profusely. The girl was afterwards confined to bed 16 days with inflammation of the brain, and Dr O'Keeffe was her medical attendant The prisoner was committed to take her trial. • A Row AT A WIDNES WC:MRS.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, before Mr. E. K. Muspratt and Mr. J. Brock, Patrick 'Treacy, 23, Pitt-st:, was charged with assaulting Thomas Lynch. Mr. Knowles appeared for the defendant.—The complainant said he was put to work a furnace at the works of Mr. Thomas Snape on Saturday night. About midnight a number of men, amongst whom was the defendant, commenced to tan- talise him, and the defendant struck him on the jaw with his fist. He became senseless, and did not know how many blows and kicks he received afterwards.— Michael Nlligan, said he was at the burners when he heard Lynbh call out "Oh, God, don't kill me." He saw Byrne pull the defendant off Lynch. Lynch was not drunk.—A labourer, named Johnson, corroborated.— Inspector Keighley said Lynch came to the Police Station at Midnight, and complainedthat he had been assaulted. His face was swollen, he had a black eye, and a scar under the chin that he alleged had been done with a kick. Lynch was quite sober, and said he dare not go hack to the works that night.—The defence was that Lynchwas drunk, and that he must have received his injuries by •falling. Mr. Knowles stated that the defendant was a respectable man .who had lived in Widne.s. for 23 years. —Mr: Muspratt, said it was a serious assault, and fined the defendant 20s and costa 225, tetal £2 2s.—The Defen- dant : I will go to prison before I will pay it. STUBBS FURNITURE CREAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with half the UMW labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles, hi., 2d., and 3d—lsaac Stubbs. Lowlands-road. Run corn .—Advt.

SMUGGLING AT RUNCORN: HEAVY PENALTY. Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court,before Dr. Steele and Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg, Geo. Stoneman, captain of the vessel Fleetwing, from Hamburg,. was charged with having, on the 12th inst., smuggled 5 11-161bs. of cigars; 4 4-161bs. of cavendish tobacco, and 5 6-16Ibs of other manufactured tobaccos, and also 15 hundredth parts of a gallon of perfumed spirits. The defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. Mitchell, super- intendent of customs, said the goods were found in a false locker underneath the bunk in the captain's cabin. The single duty of the tobacco and spirits was £7 lls, but as this was an aggravated case he asked that a fine of the treble value and duty should be imposed.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay £22 18s' or go to gaol for three months. The money was paid. HEAVY SENTENCE ON A FORMER. .RUNCORN SOLICITOR.—Francis John I'ot-sell Kirby, solicitor, formerly town councillor, deputy magistrates' clerk, and deputy coroner, pleaded guilty, on Wed- nesday, at Leicester Assizes, before Mr. Justice Irawkins, to several charges of fraud, including ob- taining .Cl,OOO from the Stamford bank by false pre- tences. The prisoner obtained overdrlifts on deeds of property which had been sold, and afterwards failed, with £BO,OOO liabilities, He was sentenced ,to five years penal servitude. The convict formerly practiced in Runcorn. , COUNTY COURT STATISTICS.—The business of teh 1 Warrington County Court (hiring the last twelve mouths comprised 5,304 plaints entered for trial, representing debts amounting to £9,925, against 4,865 plaints and £10,312. Of these 3,387 were de- termined, and judgments obtained for .C 7,460 against £3,395 and £6,389, exclusive of costs in the former year £624 and fees .C 1,551. The amount paid in to the credit of suitors was £6,692 against £6,934, and that paid out to them .C 6,674 against .C 6,800. There were 1,296 judgment summonses is- sued, 643 heard, 302 warrants of commitment is- 'sued, no debtors imprisoned, 1,625 executions against goods issued, and 10 sales made. During the same period there were at Runcorn County Court 1,451 plaints entered for trial, representing £3,432, against, 1,450 and £3.464. Of the former 1,014 were determined, and judgments obtained for £2,073, against 923 and £1,892.. In the former the costs amounted to .C 164 and the fees £522. The amount paid in to the credit of suitors was £1,834, against £1,799, and that paid out £l,BOO against .Cl,BOB. There were 187 judgment summonses is- sued, 137 heard, 42 warrants of commitment issued, 6 debtors imprisoned, 286 executionsagainst goods, and 9 sales made. SAILOR DROWNED AT RtiNcOßN. Mr. H. B. White, the deputy coroner, on Saturday afternoon, held an inquest at the Runcorn Burial Board Office, on the body of Charles Goodman, 32 years of age, a seaman, who was a native of Wicklow, in Ireland.— John Doolittle, a sailor, identified the. body. On Friday night about half past eleven he was going' to his vessel at the docks in company with the de- I ceased. They had both had some drink, auel he (witness) was "the worse for it". He went in front, and when crossing the bridge across the Wes- ton Canal, near. Parr's Lock, he heard a splash, and he turned back. He saw a young woman whom he I had passed running to his ship-mate in the water. She handefl him her umbrella, but she was unable 'to stick to it, and the deceased sank and did not rise again. The body was recovered by means of grap- pling irons.—Louisa Spencer said she passed the two men near the bridge in question. They had both had drink, but were not drunk. When about 30 yards away she heard a splash, and someone called out "Oh, Jack.' She ran back and put down her umbrella, which the man grasped, but she was un- able to hold him up owing to the ferule, which she had hold of, coming off in her band. He went down and she saw him no more. She thought the man must have missed his way to the steps to cross the bridge and walked into the canal.—A verdict of ac- cidentally drowned was returned. A WAIF OF THE STREETS.—A lad about twelve years of age, named James Quinn, who made an ap- pearance before the borough magistrates on Mon- day, is apparently more sinned against than sin- ning. Ile was charged with vagrancy, his offence ' consisting in having been found sleeping in the Market-place, shortly before three o'clock on Sun- day morning without having any visible means of subsistence. It turned out that a policeman, in the course of his rounds, foung the youngster asleep under a stall in the Market, and took him to the bridewell. It afterwards transpired that he had been away froni his home in Widnes for over a week, and that his parents are more to blame for his conduct than is the lad himself. Mr. George Riley, the School Attendance Officer, who was in court when Quinn was in the dock, threw some

light upon the matter by a statement that he made to the magistrates. He told them that the boy's parents formerly lived at Warrington. having only recently gone to Widnes, and that the father had been sumnloned eleven times for neglecting to send his child to school. The parent's utterly neglected their tamily. and when they went away from War- rington they left the prisoner and anotherlittle boy behind them. ' It was added by the Chief Constable that they left because the police and the School At- tendance Officer were looking sharply after their lads. He had reason to believe that the prisoner, who was "as hard as had been sleeping for about a week in a box in the market. The magis- trates remanded Quinn to the workhouso.

IMPORTANT SALE OP PROPERTY.—From an adver- tisement in another column, it will be seen that on Monday evening next, at the Central Hotel. Wid- nes, a most extensive sale of property will take place. Mr. Thomas Sutton, of Warrington, will be the auctioneer, and no fewer than 70 houses and eight houses and Shops will be offered in eleven lots. The property is in various parts of the town- ship. A NAVVY FOUND DROWNED AT RI7NCOEN.-071 Tuesday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at the Cemetery Lodge on the body of a navvy un- known, which was found in the Old Quay Canal on Sunday evening. 15, m. Byfield, of Ellesmere-st.. Runcorn, deposed to seeing the body floatiug in the canal on the day named. P.C. Thompson said with the assistance of Byfield he got the body out of the water. The body was thatl of a stoutly-built man five feet eight inches in height, and apparently be- tween fifty or sixty years of age. There Was no evi- dence as to how the deceased had got into the water, neither had he been identified. A verdict of "found drowned" was returned. THE ISLE OF MAN STEAM PACKET CO., DOUGLAS. —The royal mail steamers of the Old Manx Com- pany will commence their double daily service to- day (Saturday), so that their services hereafter will be from Liverpool at 10-30 a.m. and 1 p.m., with an extra steamer on Saturdays at 4 p.m. This extra steamer returns from Douglas every Monday at 1 am. The steamer " Mona's Isle" will make the double journey each day from Liverpool at 10-30 a.m., returning at 4 p.m., allowing day excursionista I about 14 hours ashore at Douglas. It will be seen from our advertising columns that the Company are advertising cheap excursions from Douglas to Glasgow in connection with.the successful Glasgow Exhibition. SUCCESSFUL LOCAL ATHLETES.—At a meeting promoted by the Manchester Athletics Club, which came off at Old Trafford, on Saturday, H. Allen, of Warrington, rode second in the one mile bicycle handicap. At the same meeting T. Locker, of the Warrington Athletic Club, won the three-quarter mile steeplechase, while Morris, of Widnes, came in third. At the annual athletic meeting of the Den- ton Cricket Club H. Barber, of Widnes, ran second in the one mile handicap. The annual sports of the servants of the Cheshire Lines Committee were also held on Saturday. L. Scott, Warrington, took the front place in the quarter-mile handicap, J. H. Whitham, Warrington, was third in the one mile handicap, and J. H. Fair, Warrington. took a con- solation prize.

DARES/WRY HIGHWAY BOARD.—A meeting of this Board was held at the Sessions House, Dares- , bury, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Cliffe (vice: chairman) presided. and there was a full attendance of members.—Messrs. R. Davies and Co., solicitors, of Warrington, wrote on behalf of Mr. John Darby- shire, lately the surveyor, and now a member of the Board, asking for the payment of .£1 for the stor- age of pipes belonging to the Board on Mr. Darby- shire's premises between July, 1887, and July, 1888 —Mr. Jones moved that the letter be allowed to he ' en.the table.—Mr Aaron said he would propme that they don't pay Mr. Derbyshire a penny, but that they take legal proceedings for detaining the High- way Board's property. He remarked that if they paid Mr. Derbyshire they would have to pay all the farmers who allowed pipes to lie on their premises, and the pipes were scattered all round the district. —Mr. Burgess proposed that they pay Mr. Derby- shire 16s 6d, which was the ..el claimed, less 3s 6d, the cost the Board had been put to in sending for the pipes when Mr. Derbyshire refused to allow them to be taken away.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded this proposal.—Mr. Long characterised the whole affair as a very childish piece of business, and sug- gested that if Mr. Derbyshire would not look at the thing in a different light that they subscribe the sovereign and pay it to him, because he did not think the auditor would sanction the payment out of the Board's tunds.—"The motion that the letter lie on the table was carried, and the subject then dropped.—The next business of public interest, which had reference to the Ship Canal, will be found along with other canal news.

taken an active part in the discussion of the mea- sure. Several of his suggestions have been accepted, and on Tuesday last he proposed an amendment to the clause with regard to the control of the police. He objected to the interference of the Home Office as regarded the members of the police. After some discussion, Mr. Ritchie agreed that the control of the police should be in the hands of the County Councils. That the congregation the vicar of Widnes left in Dublin have presented him with .£lOO upon a silver salver, and that the temperance society and the bible class have each presented him with a valuable, gift. That this evidence of the value placed upon his services by his former flock has given considerable satisfaction to the parishioners of Widnes, and they are already Singing the praises of the "New Vicar"

That it is a matter for sincere congratiflatiOn that Widnes Local Board are able not only to provide an abundant supply of water for the town, but also to sell the precious fluid to the Liverpool Corpora- tion on terms that will considerably increase the proftts of the waterworks.

RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. The annual meeting of this Board was held at the Cemetery Lodge on Wednesday. Present—Messrs. W. Whittaker, H. Coleburn, W. Littler, W. H. Roger- son, W. Mellor, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The secretary took the chair pro. tem.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN, ETC.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN, ETC.

On the proposition of Mr. Coleburn, seconded by Mr. Whittaker, it was resolved unanimously that Mr. E: Imison, who had occupied the vice-chair during the past year, should occupy the position of chairman during the ensuing year. Mr. R. Morris was appointed vice-chair- man_ on the motion of Mr. Rogerson, seconded by Mr. Littler. Mr. Littler proposed a vote of thanks to the retiring chairman, Mr. Rogerson for his services during the past year. Mr. Rogerson had attended the meeting's regularly, and had always been ready and willing to aid in anything that had been brought forward to further the interests of the Board. Mr. Whittaker seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. Mr. Rogerson acknowledge the compliment.

STATISTICS. The Secretary reported that the interments for the three months ending June 25th numbered 80; correspon- ding period last year, 61; increase 19. The fees received for the same period amounted to £77 12.8 6d; last year, £6O 13s; increase. £l6 19 6d. viLrkiiiiiro AT THE CEMETERY.

. . ... Mr. Thomas Blease, of the Mersey Vaults attended the • Board with regard to the robbery of a ballet of flowers from the grave of a relative by a girl named Mary Man- nering, of 55, Surrey-st. He wished to know what steps the Board would take. The girl's parents were willing to apologise through the newspapers. and to have some small bills printed and distributed. The Board informed Mr. Blease that they could not be responsible for baskets of flowers and loose globes, &c., that were placed on graves in the cemetery. He was the party aggrieved, and it was at his discretion whether he prosecuted the girl or not.
THE FEES.
The question of reducing the fees for burial, &c.. to persons in the out townships was deferred until the next meeting.

div.head: FIRE AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: FIRE AT STOCKTON HEATH.

On Thursday night, about ten o'clock, a man on a barge, moored in the Bridgewater Canal, Stockton Heath, noticed flames and smoke ascending from stabling and outbuildings belonging to Mr. Dallow, and on the left bank of the canal. lie aroused Mr. S. H. Dallow, who was in bed in the adjacent house The tire-bell at Wilderspool Brewery was rung, and in little more than half-an-hour from the discovery of the fire, the fire engine from the Brewery was lon the spot, and began to play upon the buildings. Mr. E. Dallow, the owner of tbie premises, was away in Warrington, but soon returned, having been in- formed of the tire. It was found impos- sible to save the stables, the roof of which soon fell in, and the efforts of the men were directed towards saving a shippon cart-house and some other buildings adjoining the Istables, and to prevent the house—about eight yards distant--catching fire. In this they were fortu- nately successful. There were three horses, a cow, and a large number of fowl in and near the burning premises, butthese were all safely secured with the exception of some\of the fowl. The place continued to burn until after one o'clock. The scene around the premises was one of great confusion, as a large - crowd collected to watch the progress of the fire. The cause of the tire is unknown, but it is believed -to have originated in the loft above the stables, where there was a quantity of dry hay and straw. The damage is estimated at from ..EBO to £lOO, and is covered by insurance.
