TOWN HAWKERS. BY A WARRINGTON TOWNSMAN.

Another class of individuals who, judging from their numbers, seem to thrive amazingly in War- rington is Town Hawkers. Some of these gentry are really only beggars in disguise, but the majority are true specimens of the race. The beggars who try this role are old hands who know the law pretty well. At least they know that while they represent to the police that they are trying to earn a living , they are secure from being "run in" for following their true vocation—that of begging. Consequently , these dilapidated beings make a house-to-house visitation on the pretence of selling periodicals or pins; but, if any occupant shows an indisposition to purchase, they are not at all anxious to "push trade," but at once commence to "spin a yarn" which ends with an appeal for "a copper." Many times have I been in a newsagent's shop and heard these weather-beaten "travellers" ask for "back numbers," on the ground that they "must have something to show, if the policeman watches them." What with hawkers at the front door and rag- gathers at the back, housekeepers in quiet neigh- bonrhossels have a lively time of it. Early in the morning come the rubbing-stone and salt merchants from the alleys of To onis-end, pushing their wares in nondescript vehicles that threaten to collapse at every turn of the wheels. The merchants are usually women and boys, the men presumably staying at home to break the stone which the weaker and younger members of the family sell in their per- ambulations. Constant refusal has hardened the stone dealers to such an extent that they always reckon not to hear what is said to them. Whenever they get a chance, they yell out "Any rubbing- stones, any chalk-stones, any salt 1" with an awful drawl on the last word ; and while you are telling the mop-headed taterdertnalion you don't want any of his wares, he runs on with " Four-a-penny rub- bing-stones, three-a-penny chalk-stones, threepence a lump • s-a-1-t,' " samples of which commodities he carries, mixed together, in his arms. "I tell you I don't want any," you remark, and the young ruffian complacently observes: "I'll let you have this lump (salt) for tuppence." "Did not I tell you, I don't want any ?" you say somewhat ruffled, but still the dirty urchin stands his ground with "You might buy these rubbing-stones, I'll let you have them for ." "how many times do you want telling," you irritably inquire, and the young merchant responds with, "Well, you might have these chalk - stones, they're reglar big uns !" Out of patience with his pertinacity, you at last hopelessly inquire "Are you deaf?" to which the salt seller instantly replies "No !" and seizing your opportunity you heartily ejaculate "Well, heed then!" Finding all attempts to trade are vain, the youthful merchant with provoking slow- ness turns round and leisurely shuffles off, to repeat the same performance at the next door. Then you are called in the presence of a swarthy complex- ioned, dark-haired gentlemen, of decidedly Hebrew appearance, who carries a prodigious bag on one arm, and on the other a collection of wash leathers, one of which he holds up for your inspection as he inquires: "Any vash ledders to-day ?" " Shust veel at it," he says, as you tell him you are not in want; but, as you decline to do so, and he sees it is useless wasting words on you, be bids you "good day," and moves on, time being an object with him. Sometimes a man of like facial aspect, but well dressed, and evidently in a better position in life, will make his appearance with a small but heavy bag. "Any shewelry, to-day?" he inquires, as he unfastens his bag and produces a watch. 'Now, there's a beau- tiful vetch," he exclaims, opening the case back and front, and turning the article round for your inspec- tion and admiration. "But, I don't want one, thanks; I've got one," you reply. "Oh, indeed," he says, "yell, perhaps you know of some vriend who vents one." "Oh, dear, no; I've no friends in that line.' "Yell, could I sell you a chain or a brooch ?'' "Nothing at all, to-day, thanks; jewel- lery is nothing in my way." Seeing you mean what you say, he reluctantly picks op his " shew- elry," and as he departs he again demands whether there is really no one you know in want of such a thing as a vatcb." There you are! Seven and six for a chair like that! Why it's giving it away at the money!" ob- serves an old-headed youth as he spreads out a folding chair before your astonished gaze. "No chairs to-day, thank you; I've no time to sit on them," I respond. and folding the chair as quickly as he set it out, he swings it across his shoulders and walks off, Then come men carefully carrying delicate look- ing " what-usts," in all the beauty of fresh veneer, or labouring under the weight of en)rmous tin trunks (as if you wanted to go for a holiday in the depths of winter!') or laden with a variety of tin- ware—from hangers to toasting-torks. Of hawkers of emallwares there is no end. Some are of mournful disposition, but others are of the "Mark Tapley" type, and can be cheerful under the most depressing circumstances. I remember one little man, bollie 4ft 6in, high, about as broad as he 'was long, laying down his box as he cheerfully en- quired "Any pins or thread to-day ?" "No, thank you; I get mine at the draper's down the street !" "Oh! all, things are dreadfully quiet. I haven't worked for about 26 weeks, and as I haves wife and six children I've taken to selling pins. But things are dreadfully quiet! Good day," he said smilingly, bowing his way into the street. Always in the evening, when you are thinking of donning your night attire rather than making your toilet, a man will call round selling combs. These articles are always of the very, very beet manufacture, and if bought in any shop would be sure to cost four times the price asked for them. "Now, here's a splendid comb," says the man, as he runs his fingers along the teeth, "I'll guarantee you wouldn't get a comb like that in any shop in this town, under Is 4d, and here I offer it to you for a paltry fourpence !" "But I don't want it. I've combs enough to last as long as my hair will, without buying another." "All, but you haven't one like that; it's a real beauty. Just look at it." "Its no earthly use to me, I tell you, I don't require one at any price." "A nice rug, to-day?' queries a spruce looking middle-aged man, spreading a white rug before him, and turning it over to show that it is lined. "Dirt cheap, and a really good article. Just feel at it." But as you assure him you are not contemplating a trip to the Arctic regions, and therefore have no use for such an article, he folds it under his arm and sets off in search of some one more reasonable. For weeks now we have been favoured with the weekly visit of a tall, well-built fellow, too lazy to work, and almost too lazy to talk. "Want any oranges?' he hisses, almost inaudibly, through his teeth. "No, thanks; who wants oranges this weather, I should like to know? I don't, certainly; I know that; and look here, you'll save both your time and mine by not calling again." This has been the man's answer week after week, and still he calls. " I thought I told you not to come again?" "Oh, I forgot; you see, I cannot see well." "I should have thought you could see a place like this, anyhow; you've been often enough to know it." "I did not know it," says the old hypocrite; who can see well enough to walk in a bee line down the street. In . _ .

the summer one is pulled out of the house by thick headed greengrocery boys and girls who call day after day, as regularly as clock work, to see if you are not dying for want of radishes, gooseberries, or strawberries. All the fruit and vegetables that are in danger of "turning" before the next market day are placed in baskets, and boys and girls are pressed into the service in order to get rid of the stuff be- fore it becomes bad stock. Their efforts to sell, however, are entirely wasted on me. as all hawkers get the same reply. Of all articles offered for sale, surely the most extraordinary is "poetry." Yet I was offered a dose of this the other day by a man who briskly observed, "Poems composed by myself while in Walton Gaol. One penny each!" The very thought of prison poetry was enough, and I replied, " No.poetry to-day, thank you." The fellow imme- diately turned on his heel and was gone, though I took a good look round to see that nothing had ."gone" with him. Every beggar and every hawker meets with a blank, and often pointed, refusal from the writer. Experience has taught me that it is the only safe course to p ursue,and it saves me now from what would otherwise be endless trouble. All the tramps. and hawkers who " work" the district in which I re- side well know there is no business to be done with me, and,consequently,don't waste their time or mine in calling. They are all more or less in league, and, when they compare notes, they place a black mark against my house. i recently removed to a new house, and for the first four or six weeks hawkers,' &c., swooped down upon me like moths to a candle. But a persistent refusal to every person soon caused them to drop their visits, and now we see them pass our house on their way to others higher up where the inmates are not so "hard hearted." All hawked goods are like Franklin's whistle— decidedly dear; in fact, they can he bought fresher ' and cheaper in shops. Besides, the purchase of such

THE SHIP CANAL WORKS,
AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO. 26.—WARBURTON, &c.

I Having now followed the course of the canal to its commencement in the estuary of the Mersey at Eastham, we propose to resume our account of its eastward course towards Manchester, which, it may be remembered,we broke off when in the neighbour- hood of Warburton, a little•to the 4astward of Lymm. The quiet and pleasant village of Warbur- ton lies on the south bank of the Mersey aS that river, in one of the numerous sinuosities of its course, takes a bend northward. The traveller who approaches it from the direction of Lymm passes along some typical Cheshire lanes, that is typical in their fresh natural beauty, and just before reach- ing the substantial modern-looking church turns to the right and, having duly paid the very moderate toll that is demanded., crosses the bridge and at once finds himself on the soil of the county Palatine "proud Lancaster." As he proceeds down the lane which, if be go far enough, will bring him on to the main road between Warrington and Manchester, he has full in front of him the Ship Canal works in steady but continuous progress. That is as things are at present, but in this article we are more concerned with anticipating as far as possible what is to be in the future. We will then suppose that our traveller, like another Rip Van Winkle, slumbers I profoundly for the next four or five years, and on some fine afternoon in the July of 1892—0 r it may, I perhaps, be convenient to fix some even later date— re7visits the scene of his former peregrinations. Approaching Warburton from the direction of Lymm, we may well suppose that he will not be struck by any remarkable changes in the hamlet, for Warburton is a place which even in this nine- teenth century preserves the "oven tenour of its way," and is not likely to undergo any very rapid metamorphosis. The church may be a little more weather-stained, and some of the -cottages may display visible signs that they are somewhat nearer their final stage, but that most probably will be all. Going in the direction of the bridge, how- ever, it is more than possible that he will be strongly impressed with the fact that this after all is a world of mutations, for it may be that the bridge itself will have gone, and the river it spanned no longer flow in its old channel. That this is a pos- sible contingency seems to be indicated by the fact that :the lands and properties which may be ac- quired by the Ship Canal Company under their Act of Parliament include at this point the bed of the Mersey, the bridge, and the toll-house, which is erected on the southern or Cheshire side of the river. Such a contingency seems to be also pointed to by a clause in the Act for the "protection of Rowland Eyles Egerton Warburton," an owner of land in this locality, which provides that "if the present bed of the river Mersey" "be filled up" hereabout, certain things shall be done. Continuing his journey, however, either across the bridge, if it still exist, or, if it be abolished, along the new cause- way laid on the filled in hed of the river, our traveller will in a few minutes be upon the southern bank of the now completed canal for the broad channel of which the road will have been broken up and in- tersected. The means of crossing the canal will be a swing bridge which, according to the words of the Act of Parliament, will be "provided with all necessary machinery and apparatus" to carry the road over the canal. If the old channel of the Mersey has been filled up Mr. R. E. E. Warburton will have a legal claim to a wharf on the south side of the canal and near to this awing bridge, at which he and his tenants and workmen shall be at liberty I to embark and land, free from wharfage rates, a variety of materials to be used in the cultivation of his estates. The user of this wharf will, however, be subject to the reasonable bye-laws which may from time to time be made by the Canal Company and approved by the Board of Trade. In case the old channel of the Mersey is not filled up, the existing rights of wharfage upon any land belonging to Mr.Warburton adjoining the Mersey in the township of Warburton are not to be prejudiced or interfered with, but even these rights are to be exercised subject to anti in accordance with the bye-laws of the Canal Company for the regulation of private wharves. It may here be mentioned also that no canal tolls are to be demanded for a variety of materials to be used in the cultivation or fer- tilization of the estates of Mr. Warburton in this locality, provided that this material is Carried on the canal or river in vessels either belonging to or hired by Mr. Warburton or his tenants. TIIE RIXTON AND WARBURTON ROAD.

The level of the road leading from 'Warburton to Rixton will not be altered by the making of the canal, but a matter which will naturally attract the attention of an observer who passes along this way some years hence will be the depth of the canal beneath the level of the surrounding ground. Two or three miles away to the west the comparative levels of the canal and the land on either side will be such that embankments will be necessary at some points, but,as we go eastward, in the direction of Manchester, the ground rises, and at the Rixton and Warburton road the waters of the canal will be about eleven or twelve feet beneath the level of the roadway. In close proximity to the road on either hand the disparity between the two levels will be even greater, for the surface of the canal will be over rather under twenty feet lower than the natural surface of the ground. Away to the right of a person proceeding to Rixton or Hollinfare from Warburton, the Mersey, in another of its twistings, bends northward, and its channel will again be struck through by the canal and for a short distance the bed of the river will be the bed of the canal. To the left of the road the farm buildings scheduled as being in the occupation of Mr. John Worthington lie just outside the limits of deviation and will, therefore, not be molested. Near to Cadishead, however, houses described as being owned by Mrs. Mary Hardy, and the farm buildings in the occupation of Mr. Aaron Toft, come within the limits of the land that may be taken by the Canal Company under their compulsory powers. Across the Mersey from Cadishead lies the quiet village of Partington, into which the limits of deviation extend, and include a house and garden ' described as belonging to Mr. Thomas Winstanley, and a house and farm buildings owned by Sir Win. , Cunliffe Brooks, M.P. The offices, stores, huts, joiners' shops, &c., are on the Weston side of the river, and near to Weston Point Docks. ' THE FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday afternoon, Mr. H. B. White, dePuty coroner, held an inquest at the Burial Board office, Run, corn, upon the body of Charles Newnes. a navvy, who was killed on the Ship Canal works at Old Quay on the previous day. Mr. Gregson, agent for the Runcorn sec- tion, watched the proceedings on behalf of the contrac- tor and Inspector O'Donnell.—Evidence of identification having been given, the ganger under whom deceased was employed stated that the man WWI working at the steam navvy, when a landslip occurred, and he was buried under about five tons of earth. He was dug out as quickly as possible, but he was quite dead. Wit- ness attributed the slip to a land drain which ran behind' the clay.—James King, driver of the steam navvy, de- posed that the deceased was engaged cleaning soil from behind the wagon. Witness noticed a small fall of earth and he cautioned the men. In about a minute a large quantity of earth fell, and he called to the men to get out of the way. The deceased was buried underneath the clay, and when he was got out his body was dread- fully mutilated, and he was quite dead.—The Coroner expressed the opinion that the slip had been caused by the land drain and the heavy downfall of rain.—The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death."

Cor- coran. It appeared from the evidence that the prisoner was creating a disturbance at Daley's common lodging house, in Scotland-road, and when the constable ap- peared on the scene he struck him a violent blow in the face. The prisoner was fined 5s and costs in .each case, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment. FIIIDAY.—Before Mr. John _White, Dr. Gomall, and

Alderman Harrison. Hill, with intent to avoid a distraint for rent owing. div.head: NEW RECTOR OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE NEW RECTOR OF WARRINGTON.

In bidding farewell in a Wellingborough Church periodical to his old parishioners, the Rev. F. W. Willis intimates that, although he shall be in Well- ingborough from time to time until the end of the month, he shall take his leave of them to-morrow (Sunday.) On behalf of Mrs. Willis and himself the reverend gentleman heartily thanks the parish- ioners for their help during his ministry of seven- teen years. Practical evidence is given of the high esteem in which Mr. Willis is held by his parishion- ers. The teachers and scholars of All Saints' Day Schools recently presented to Mr. and Mrs. Willis a handsome silver cruet set bearing the inscription— " Presented to the Rev. F. W. and Mrs. Willis, by the teachers and scholars of All Saints' Day Schools, Wellingborough, 1888." In making the presenta- tion Mr. Styles, the headmaster, remarked that it was a slight token of the love and respect which they all bore to the recipients. It was the wish and the sincere hope of both teachers and children that Mr. Willis might be as successful, and become just as much beloved in Warrington as he was in Wellingborough. Mr. Willis, in reply, said that he always felt that whenever anyone gave him a pre- sent he did,not deserve it, and he did not feel he de- serve the one they had just given him; but he was happy to think that he had gained the affection of rich and poor, old and young, and it was a great de- light to carry away that feeling with him to War- rington. He hoped to visit them from time to time, and wherever he was he should never forget them. He trusted that some day, when he came back to Wellingborough, 'he should see them growing up to be men and women, who would be carrying out in their daily lives what they had been taught in that school. Mrs. Willis joined with him in thanking them for their kindness.

The key. T. A. Easterling, the new rector's senior Curate, has only been at Wellingborough six months, prior to which he was curate of East Teignmouth, Devon. During his brief stay at Wellingborough he has shown much ability in the pulpit and taken an active part in parochial affairs. He has already preached his farewell sermon.

ADVANCE IN SPINNERS' WAGES.—On Tuesday afternoon. at the Mitre Hotel, Manchester, a conference was held between the employers' committee of North and North- east Lancashire and representatives of the operative spinners' association of North and North-east Lancashire, who were accompanied by Mr. Mawdsley, the general secretary. They also had an interview with the card- room hands. The spinners' deputation consisted of representatives from Preston, Blackburn, Darwen, Accrington, and other districts, and the cardroom hands had delegates from the same districts, along with the president and secretary of the amalgamation. The spinners applied for an advance of 5 per cent., and the cardroom hands of 10 per cent, for males and 5 per cent. for females. After the deputation had withdrawn, the employers considered the application, and then announced that they would grant an advance of 5 per cent, to spin- ners where the Oldham list is not adopted, and 5 per cent, to cardroom workers—the increases to take effect a month from the next pay day.

HE DTHERITED THE TENDENCY.

Mr. W. L. Notton, of 114, King's Cross-road, King's Cross, London, suffered for years from a disordered liver. He tried several medicines at various times, but could get no permanent relief. In a letter to Messrs. H. H. Warner & Co., he says:—" I was un- fortunate enough to inherit a tendency to liver com- plaint, which my occupation, being entirely an indoor one, with long hours, naturally served to increase. About every two weeks I was obliged to undergo severe vomiting and purging, accompanied with terrific head- aches. 1 as told that the fault was entirely due to an inactive liver, and as long as I kept at my business there was no hope for me. I found the attacks increasing in- stead of diminishing, and finally resolved to try pro- prietary medicines. I saw a testimonial in one of the newspapers, detailing a similar case to my own, in which a complete recovery had been reached by the use of Warner's SAFE Cure. I had known of this medicine, but had an impression it was only for kidney disease. I procured and commenced taking it, together with War- ner's SAFE Pills. The first bottle did not seem to benefit me. I, however, persevered, and at the expiration of two months discontinued it, believing myself thoroughly restored. Since that time I have had no return of my old trouble. My liver, kidneys, and skin are now in good working order, and I consider myself permanently cured. I shall be pleased to answer any inquiries con- cerning my case."

div.head: EASTHAM AND ELLESMERE PORT.
div.p: EASTHAM AND ELLESMERE PORT.

The water—especially after the recent heavy rains— has given a little trouble in the deep cuttings at the im- mediate commencement of the Canal, but the large sump is expected to be finished shortly, and will then afford a place for drainage of the whole section. The brickyard has been removed from its position on the natural level, on to the top of the new level formed by the tip. The former site of the yard will now be filled in with earth, which will complete a larger level tract of land formed entirely of the material taken from the cuttings. The banks across the first bend of the river are being rapidly pushed on from both ends, and will afford a large and convenient tip for earth, clay, and stones, which cannot be utilised. The bulk of this cutting, however, is good hard rock, and will be used in building the sides of the embankment. The new hospital at Ellesmere Port is now complete, and what few patients there were in the temporary one have been removed to the more commodi- ous rooms of the new building. INCE.

The first cutting of this.. -section, where the landslip occurred last week, is now cleared, and as the cutting gets deeper the earth is found to be more solid. Most of the huts at Stanlow Point are now complete and inhabi.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT
div.p: ACCIDENT AT
MOORE.

On Thursday afternoon a serious accident happened to one of the men employed on the Moore section of the canal. He was walking along the railway line in the cut- ting, when some waggons which were being shunted by an engine knocked him down and crushed his thigh severely. He was taken to his house in Dutton-street, Warrington, and attended by a doctor. LOWER WALTON. At the meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board, on Thursday, an application was made to the board, on be- half of Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal contractor, for, per- mission to divert a road through Lower Walton, and plans were submitted showing the proposed alteratibns. Some discussion took place as to the condition on which the permission should be granted.—Mr. J. Darbyshire thought the Board ought to sec that people who might have occasion to use the road were not put to any in- convenience. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Burgess said that there were about half-a-dozen people particularly interested in the road in question, and he believed that even if that Board did consent to the application, there was a clause in the Act of Parliament which protected the interests of some of those concerned. He thought that it would be better if these people were consulted before anything was done. The road at present was so steep as to make a heavy pull for horses, and he was afraid if the proposed alterations were made it would be made steeper still.— Mr. Parr thought Mr. Walker ought to get the new roads made and then nobody would interfere with him.—Mr. Walker, junr:, who was in attendance, in reply to Mr. Parr, said ho did not think it would be six months before the new road from Walton to Warrington was made. The road would be made as soon as they begun with tho river diversion across Arpley meadows. The soil from the new river bed would be used to make the new road, which would need to be very high, through the meadows. —The Chairman suggested that Mr. Walker might make an arrangement with the five or six persons who were most interested in the road it was proposed to alter.- -Mr. John Darby-shire thought the interests of the travelling public should be carefully provided for by the Board.—Mr. Long thought they could not avoid put- ting the travelling public to soine inconvenience while such a big project was being carried out, and he believed they were quite willing to put up with it.—lt was at length agreed that a committee be appointed to confer with Mr. Walker on his application, with power to settle the matter. The following gentlemen were appointed to form the committee, viz. :—Messrs. Burgess, Beswick, Jones, Knowles, and John Darbyshire.

THE ARTIFICIAL LIGHT. While the work is being carried on by night, on some of the sections people will have noticed, in passing, the brilliancy of the artificial light employed, and the unini- tiated will no doubt, very naturally, have put it down to some new installation of electricity. It is not so, how- ever, but is produced from the combustion of oil-gas from a cheap form of refined tar, supplied by the makers of the lamps, after distillation from aniline dyes and other products. A correspondent, who has minutely gone into the matter, gives the 'following description of the method and means whereby the result is produced. The apparatus may be briefly described as a wrought- iron drum of substantial make, weighing, when fitted, about 1401 b., and being 24 inches in height and 18 inches in diameter, fitted with convenient handles for moving from place to place. The burner itself consists of an in- geniously formed casting in one piece, a hollow chamber in which forms the gas generator, the oil in the reservoir being conveyed thereto through the pipes mentioned, and at once turned into gas by the action of the heat. This gas is then conveyed through spaces in the casting, all provided with brass screwed stops, for purpose of cleansing, to the jet from whence it issues in a small stream for about an inch, in the atmosphere, becoming there thoroughly mixed with air, into a combustion chamber, some three inches long, and tapered from two inches to one inch. Hence, the flame passes through some eight cast-iron fins. These fins becoming heated by the flame, assist very greatly in keeping up the tem- perature of the generating chamber. The pump which supplies the needful amount of compressed air (not less than 71b. or over 221 b.) is of very simple construction, and having a short length of rubber hose attached to it, serves also as the means of supplying the drum with oil. It is worked by hand with a cross handle, and has only a plain clack valve. Complications of all kinds are avoided and for such a light as it produces, the apparatus is sim- plicity. itself. The cost of oil for a lamp giving equal to from 2000 to 3000 candle-power, does not exceed 3d per hour; and petroleum can also be burnt, if preferred, though at a somewhat greater cost. Such economy in use, of course, makes it many times cheaper than elec- tricity, gas, or any other artificial light, and no other is employed on any section of the works.
THE SWEATING SYSTEM: MEN'S SUITS

FOR TWO SHILLINGS.-PICTURES OF DEPRAVITY. 1 he Lancet, concluding its special report on the sweat- ing system. in Glasgow, complains of the proximity of the sweating workshops with the haunts of vice and crime. Yet in this villainous district and court, ten, sometimes twenty ot thirty, young girls have to go to narn the scanty wages the sweater chooses to give them. 'rile only sanitary accommodation existing they have to share with tenants of so low class a character that they are made to pay their rent nightly and in advance. There had been fights and riots the three nights previous to our visit. The tailor's girls, as they go to work, are in danger of being insulted by The hrawnv and half-drunken women who listlessly stand about in the court, vieing with each other in the use of obscene and violent language. To be over- worked, poor, half-starved, in ill-ventilated, insuffi- ciently lighted, over-crowded, over-heated, and badly- Irained workshops is evil enough: but to be compelled to work in the same courts, to pass under the same nar- row, dark, low passages, rendered historical by the seri- ous records above referred to, to be surrounded by vice which, in Glasgow, has reached the last expression of degradation and bestiality, is a danger, a humiliation, an insult against honest workers and against womankind at large, which should evoke the indignation and shame oF the entire community. We went to a workshon where as many as 600 gar- ments have been made in a week, where thirty girls have been employed, and where, nevertheless, there was no sanitary accommodation whatever. The premises are now, we are glad to say, closed. Another Jew on whom we called had also removed. He had been en- eagod makino• entire suits for boys for the sum of lid.! lie employed ten or more persons, and has been kriawn to turn out men's suits for 2s.

Ia Glasgow, as elsewhere, the order shops also want ictive sanitary superintendence. For instance, we visited the workshop of a high-class and one of the Adest-established tailors in the town. It is tbe sweaters, and net the properly qualified and properly paid jour- neymen tailors who profit by this growing prosperity of their employer. The public, on the other hand, have no suspicion that a portion ot the clothes they order at this shop are sent out to the places where the sweater em- ploys unskilled labour. There are several wholesale sweaters at Glasgow. One of these we found employing some fifty workers, for the most part girls, and they were nearly all engaged making soldiers' red coats. here the closet was in the workshop, against tile wall, with no window, surrounded only by few boards, and therefore ventilating in among the workers. Some of the tables were so crowded that the girls had to sit sideways when sewing. Close by, the brother of this Jew sweater had an equally large establishment. The first Scotch home worker on whom we called was sewing in her kitchen. In another tene- ment we found great misery. Some old women were sitting round a dirty kitchen table. There was a power- ful odour of fish, and the furniture was so scanty that one person was working on the box used to collect ash and domestic refuse. The women, who were unwashed and unkempt, explained that formerly they earned enough to live with fair comfort, but now the Jews had beaten down the prices, and they were obliged to make waistcoats for 6d. each. They were themselves dressed in soiled rags, and looked utterly wretched. The stand- ing space remaining is barely four feet square, and yet here work is done, for the other and front rooms of this *n fAin chrir

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

This season, so far as it has gone, has been a very favourable one for the Warrington Cyclihg Club. The number of members now enrolled reaches the very res- pectable total of fifty-four, and the runs of the Club show a good average of attendance. In returning from an afternoon's run to Hoo Green on Saturday evening, the members of the Club, as they rode up Bridge-st. in "Indian file" behind their captain (Mr. R. Bennett), presented a very creditable appearance, and attracted a good deal of attention. At Derby, on Tuesday, the Australian cricketers de- feated Derbyshire by an innings and 79 runs, and the Gentlemen beat the Players at Lord's, by five runs. The matches. Yorkshire v. Warwickshire and Staffordshire v. Cheshire were drawn.

The sports of the Warrington Football Club, which are to be held on August Bank Holiday, will include a 100 yards race for members to be run in full costume. Each competitor, after running half the course, will have to pick up a football and carry it past the tape. Another event which should be of great local interest is the bicycle race confined to riders living within six miles of Market Gate. There will no doubt be a good entry of local *heel- men, and Warrington is just now pretty well favoured with creditable riders. We are informed that a well-known member of the Warrington Football Club and a couple of companions had quite an adventure while on a visit to the Isle of Man lately. Among the places visited was "Derby Castle," near Douglas, and as it aame on to rain while there, went into a cave to shelter. This, however, turned out to be a very unsatisfactory place of refuge, for they had not been in the cave long when they were surprised by a huge wave dashing into the entrance. As the wave ebbed they naturally made a. rush for the open air, but before they could get out they were met by another inrush of the briny element, which forced them back again. There was now clearly no chance of getting out in the face of the advancing tide, and in fact, in- stead of getting out they were driven further and further in by the encroaching waters. After spending a very miserable time of it they were at length relieved by see- ing the tide beginning to sudside, and in the end they came out of their unpleasant adventure not much the worse, but with no desire for a repetition of the escapade. An inquest was held at the Cheadle Asylum, on Wed- nesday. on the body of Percy Cromwell Jackson, aged 18 years, who while playing with the Bolton Football Club against the Free Wanderers Football Club, at Fallowfield, on the 14th April, received injury which brought on epileptic convulsions, the cause of his death. The de- ceased had been " tackled " by the throat, but it was stated that the game was "a quiet one," and that the best of feeling existed. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

EXPLOSION ON A STEAMRI2.—WhiIst the Board of Trade steamer Cockchafer was proceeding' out of Queenstown Harbour on Thursday morning with the principal medi- cal officers of tile Board of Trade to clear the Transatlan- tic liner British Princess, an explosion occurred on board the Cockchafef, which blew off the cylinder valve and enveloped the vessel in steam. Luckily no lives were lost, and after much trouble the Cockchafer was brought to safe anchorage. Subsequently another accident oc- curred alongside the British Princess. When she was getting under weigh her propeller struck a whaleboat which was towing astern, shattering the after part of the boat and filling her with water. The occupants, five in number, were rescued.

div.head: ANCIENT POMPEII IN MODERN
div.p: ANCIENT POMPEII IN MODERN
LONDON.

TN these days of increasing activity, rapid change, 1_ and wondrous developments, all things are brought into kinship, more or less. Art no longer looks down on utility, science asserts its magic power over the most ordinary affairs of life, and beauty breaks its old bonds of exclusiveness and unveils itself to the whole world. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the streets of London. Sentiment, it is true still gathers round the ghosts of a dead past, and would fain revivify them, but little by little, new forms arise, superseding ugliness by beauty, and creating fresh landmarks that speak to present times with far greater eloquence than did the now displaced evidences of a bygone day. The artistic spirit is abroad, and affects the aspect of all mundane matters, and here and there some leading power exerts its influegce with special force and application, lifting into the serene atmosphere of eternal art things which had previously been hidden away in the obscurity of every-day surround- ings. A touch of art, like a touch of nature—for art is but reflected Nature—" makes the whole woild kin." _ _

Such a touch of art has recently been given to a portion of Oxford Street, by the enterprising firm of Messrs. A. & P. Pears who have erected a veritable palace of art there, dedicated to the service of soap. At the first blush, the relationship between soap and art may not appear altogether of the strongest; but a moment's reflection will suffice to demonstrate that, soap is a very fundamental element of art. Soap suggests purity, and the lesson of purity Is taught by all the highest art. How much the world is indebted to soap could only be estimated, indeed, if we Were able to realise what a world it would be without soap! Be that as it may, Messrs. Pears have, in the building of their new palace, displayed an artistic instinct which cannot fail to produce a corresponding artistic appreciation on the part of the public They have presented the thousands who daily pass up and down Oxford Street with a perpetual vision of delight—a dreamland of fancy reduced to fact--a glimpse of the antique world, with the t4dded brightness of a modern setting. The imposing frontage, with its striking architec- tural features, its spacious windows and noble door- way, is enough in itself to command wonder and attention, but it is the interior view that constitutes the great attraction. The by-passer, as he saunters up Oxford Street, becomes suddenly aware of a brightness and a glow shining through the windows of this palatial edifice, and stops and looks, and looks again, and if he can by any means obtain per- mission to enter the palace he is not likely to neglect the opportunity. What he would see when he found himself within we will endeavour briefly to describe. _

Having passed the portals and the watchful com- missionaire on duty there, he would set foot within a noble hall which would remind him of one of Alma lemit's pictures. Whether or not that distin- guished artist has had anything to do with suggest. lug the form and leading features of this magnificent interior is more than we can tell; but certainly it might be so. The scene is a reproduction of a Pompeian Court, and although some of the details may not be in strict accordance with Pompeian decoration, nothing has been introduced that would mar the general harmony of the picture. The floor is inlaid with mosaic in quaint and curiously wrought designs the walls repeat the glories of the buried city in all their pristine freshness. columns'of the rarest marbles stretch from floor to oeiling, and a broad marble staircase, veined with many dainty markings, winds off at the western corner to the mysteries of loftier regions, stiggesting" endless vistas of marble delights beyond. At thu foot of these steps a rectangular bath is carved, as it were, out of the mosaic, and with its luminous ground, its leaping fountain, and its marble borderings forrns a very beautiful feature. At the head of the bath, in a niche whose dark backgraund throws the white marble into charming relief, stands the statue 'of Venus--a replica of Thorwaldsen's famous master- piece—as the emblem of purity and beauty. This however is only temporary, we believe, a more elaborate piece-of sculpture-7a group more sugges- tive of ablutions—being in course of execution for this prominent position. Suspended by chains from the delicately-ornamented ceiling, with its white rarion -pierre enriehmentsj are several exquisite repro- ductions of the old boat-shaped Roman lamps, which, at the touc.li of a spring or the turn of a tap, burst into electric radiance, filling the marble ball with a flood of light, and suffusing the stately columns, the snow-white statues, and the crystal floor with s,vriads of magic hues and scintillations. 'Dm visitor %lomat seems to profane such an in- wviot with his nineteenth century costume and nineteenth century manners. Here surely we should have maidens in sandals and garments of clinging draperies, and fillet bands;l youths with flowing locks and robes of dainty workmanship, not ladies wearing modern bonnets and mantles, and gentle- men with chimney-pot hats and suits of sinning shoddy. One feels abashed and humiliated in the. presence of so much that is chaste and beautiful— so much that recalls fairer climes and a more poetic people. The sculptured marbles are in keeping and harmony with the scene, however, if the every-day visitor is not. Venus looks placielly down upon it; "The Bather," to whom Mr. Lewes has given stony embodiment and ideality, seems at home there; and even those _happily oontrasted statues, "The Dirty Boy" and "rho Clean Boy," known as they are to all the world by their manifold artistic repro- ductions, do not appear out of place, for white mirble always conveys the idea of purity, no matter what the story may be that it has to tell. After having taken the measure of those various ajects of art and beauty the visitor, bent on ex- ploring further, will be conducted up the marble staircase to the floor above, where he will find other matters of moment to engage his mind. If he be desirous of seeing Mr. Barrett, who is the wonder worker of this place of many rtunniflcations, the probability is he may have to wait a while, for the demands upon the time of the master-mind of a business whose range is the universe are endless. The tedium of waiting is usually an infliction that a business man greatly resents, but in the waiting- room provided by Messrs. Pears there is a danger that, instead of weariness a luxurious forgetfulness will be experienced, add weariness, when the time comes for the visitor to be ushered forward into Mr. Barratt's sanctum he will be reluctant to leave. Such will assuredly be the ease if he be a 'lover of art, for on the walls of this elegant room, with its exquisitely decorated carton-pierre ceiling of classical design, hang works of art by celebrated modern masters to the value of many thousands of pounds. Of course, they all illustrate one text, and testify indirectly to the honour and glory of Pears' Soap; but they are works of great merit ,nevertheless, and would be an ornament to any art gallery in the Kingdom. In studying Millais's charming ''Bubbles," or its com- panion picture, "More Bubbles," by Fouard Frere, tao soap connection is not thrust upon you; for, although in the millions of reproductions of these paintings which have been scattered broadcast over the universe the name and virtues of the ,soap are conspicuously printed, so that those who run may read, the pictures as they hang in this waiting-hall or gallery appeal to the eye simply yet emphatically as works of art. The same may- be said or the pic- tures which Stacy Marks and other ,well-known artists have executed for 'A-Aiwa. Pears... First of all, tite.y serve the cause of art in the strictest sense; then they are utilised for the purposes of advertisenient. Thus the announcements of Pears' Soap may be said. to go mairing on the wings of art to all the ends of the earth. The artists represented in this room may be at least grateful for one mercy—they us' an Lung " ou the line."

When the signal is given, Ole visitor passes into M. Barratt's office, and while the interview proceeds has the privilege of observing not only a further display of artistic objects, but certain business ac- cessories of a very notable character. A series of speaking-tubes and electric bells at Mr. BM-raft's elbow, labelled according to countries and depart- ments, places him within conversing distance of the different departments and divisions, and whether he wants to know the latest transactions with a par- ticular customer in Melbourne, the quantity of stock in New York, how a certain, advertising contract is being fulfilled in California, or how many coolies have been put on duty in Calcutta for diurnal per- ambulation with pasteboard effigies of " The Dirty Boy," he has only got to whistle and ask, and the answer will be immediately forthcoming. Here Mr. Barratt is in touch with every part of the world! here he retains a sort of bird's-eye view of the whole of the firm's operations, from the busy labours constantly in progress at their huge factories at Isleworth to the acknowledging of the most recent report from some public analyst who has bought his sample of soap for himself in his own locality and reported thereon. Here, if you press the point, you can have shown to you advertisements emanating from this firm so far back as the beginning of the present century, including one in the Times of the Waterloo year. Then, if you happen to be of an inquisitive turn, and ask Mr. Barratt whether all the taking ideas which they put forth are, like their soap, of their own manufacture, he will perhaps send word through one of the tubes for the "notions" that have come by that morning's post to be brought to him. What a medley they present! Ideas for puzzles, suggestions for pictures, verses by John Jones aged thirteen, a map of the world showing Pears' Soap cleansing every oontineut. and offers of various kinds

from poets, painters, lithographers, newspaPer prietors, ladies of fashion, sculptors, chemists' , tors, and what not. But Mr. Barratt is coraPf: to confess that out of the hundreds of thongs:les suggestions which an industrious public sends firm there is rarely one to be found that cos utilised. Some self-confident notion-mongers coolly a 4 a thousand pounds for the right of 11' an idea that is only worthy of Bedlam. If fortunate enough to get Mr. Barratt to tali firm's operations generally, you will hear miles will astonish you. How could it be otherwise an annual expenditure in advertising of r £100,000? Orders are given out from this for tons of this and millions of that, for once the firm has decided upon doing a do it thoroughly; and if a printer or a lit gets an order for ten or twenty millions of a certain pictorial sheet, it may surprise him fb and cause him to reflect that the world is verf and that Messrs. Pears' business is a gig,toatie but the transaction will only be an ordinal far as Messrs. Pears are concerned.
From Mr. Barratt's °Moe the inspection • continued to loftier heights and lower (Iva?, room to room and floor to floor; but from Os the evidences are all of a business oharacter.

large counting-house, with its rows of desks its gleaming electric lights, and ita clerks and ponderous ledgers: there is an prosperity that is decidedly exhilarating ; IA" constant click-click of a row of type-writers t" ferring to perfect legibility the letters which been taken down in shorthand from Mr. dictation is a sound that is music to the

div.head: Letter 5 to the Obitor.
div.p: Letter 5 to the Obitor.

HALF HOLIDAYS IN WARRLNGTON. Sir.—There being a strong desire of the majority of 1 the boot and shoe trade of Warrington to have a half- day, closing on Thursdays, lam very glad to see already that two of the trade have taken advantage and have at once closed at one o'clock, namely, Mr. Frisby and Mr. Fleming; all credit to them. Trusting others will come to the same agreement, I remain, yours, &c., A. P.

CHARGE AGAINST AN INFIRMARY OFFICIAL. Sir,-1 observed in your last issue one of those flimsy charges which are so often made against House Surgeons I of Charitable Institutions. As one of the Honorary Staff visiting the Infirmary at all hours, I have always found the present House Surgeons kind and polite to the patients, and upon inquiry in reference to the charge of Mr. Hawthorne, I found in the Accident Book, in the column for remarks, "Father impertinent," so that one tale is good until another is told.—Yours truly, - JOHN FL GOILNALL. Warrington, 13th July, 1888.

HEALTH OF THE RURAL DISTRICT. Sir,—ln your last issue I noticed that this district was stated to be in a very healthy condition. As I have fre- quently pointed out, when scarlet lever is epidemic in the borough, it is of necessity i prevalent in the parts ad- joining. The present time s no exception to the rule, for lam daily receiving information of its existence in many streets on the boundaries of the municipal dis- trict. As a medical friend said to me the other day. "Your efforts to arrest the spread of scarlet fever in the borough are entirely frustrated by the utter carelessness that exists in the rural district." lam aware that the Rural District does not possess the same compulsory powers of notification, isolation, &c., and for this the legislature is to blame ; but I think it will not be in vain if I appeal to parents, and those having the care of children, to carry out the precautions and directions given them by their medical advisers.— Yours, &c., THE MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH FOR THE BOROUGH. Warrington, 13th July, 1888.

div.head: GAS QUESTION.
div.p: THE GAS QUESTION.

Sir,—So unaccustomed have Town Councillors been to criticism, that when their actions are challenged they know not what to do. Instead of meeting criticism, like men—and profiting by it—they adhere to their old ways most tenaciously; and when they find their policy con- demned and a new one called for, they meet the demand by quitting the work. As with the Markets Committee, so with the Gas Committee. The members seem incapa- ble of devising a policy in accordance with the wishes of the ratepayers, and it is, perhaps, for the best that the Gas Committee should retire. New brooms are said to sweep clean, and if we can get a new committee that will give us cheaper and better gas, so much the better for the consumers. If they don't, we must agitate until we get a committee that will do what is wanted. It is intolera- ble that we, on theborders of a vast coal field, should have to pay nearly double for our gas than consumers in towns far and near have to pay. I was in conversation with a Widnes gentleman the other day, and he was completely astonished at the price Warrington people pay for their gas. He said that it was time we had a change, and instanced what had occurred in Widnes. They had there a gas manager who made them a loss of £l,OOO a year, for several years, but they cleared him out and got a first-class man who saved the sum mentioned the first year. It was all done in management, and it is time we in Warrington had a little of the same sort: Rates of all kinds are at their highest pitch, and I for one will support any movement that will tend to reduce them .—Yours truly,
ECONOMIST.
TRIUMPHANT .DEMOCRACY.

Sir,—l have just react with great pleasure and no small amount of profit a shilling book entitled "Trium- phant Democracy," which I commend to the thoughtful attention of all young Radicals. In its pages they will find enlightment as to the lines upon whica reforms in this country must go, and encouragement to held fast in these perilous times their views upon liberty in all its phases. I confess that my politi6al opinions—advanced though they be—have been greatly strengthened and enlarged, and my ideas of government and war elevated and intensified. Would that every man in this country, Liberal and Tory, would read this deeply interesting and and wonderfully informing book ! This fair land of ours would then soon be in reality, which it is now only in name, "The land ot the happy, the home of the free." No more would Ireland cry aloud for her rights, no more would the people be dominated by a privileged class, no more would the nation be committed to foreign wars and entanglements against its will. We should have freedom in its widest—yes, if you will, its wildest—sense, for the democracy would be triumphant. The Government would be what every true Liberal is striving for—" Of the people, for the people, by the people." There would be no vast army and navy suck- ing the life blood out of the nation, no religious system seeking self-agrandisement over others, no vast monopoly like the beer interest exercising its deadly sway over an unwilling people. Our people must be, sober for the conditions of life demand it. Oh, that I could urge every young man to read and ponder this entertain- ing, this enlightening, this ennobling volume t It is worth its weight in gold. The author has done his country a real service in putting it face to face with the true facts, and it behoves every Briton, in whom the writer of the book has unbounded confidence, to profit fr it be too late,—Yours, &c., Warrington, July 12th, 1888,

div.head: RADICAL.
div.p: A RADICAL.

SWEET (?) ODOURS IN THE STREETS. Sir,—Can anyone tell where the smells come from? , Those OdoUrs far from sweet that so often offend the nos- trils of Warringtonians ? They are. perhaps, not con- tinually with us, else might we all take fevers and die ; but they crop up sufficiently often to make their oc- casional presence known and felt; as 'much as to say that in case of a hot season and an epidemic they will not be found wanting. They are most aggressively in- clined during the beautiful mornings of summer. I have met them in Winwick-st., Buttermarket-St., and Church- st., and in Scotland-road I have turned tail and fled, a very coward, frightened by a stink. But then—is:pat a stink it was! It is not very pleasant to perambullite in the rear of a Corporation " honey-pot " chariot, but that would not make me flinch. Some people say that the sanitary :system of the borough is the cause of these perfumes, and scents, and things, and others aver that they are the natural accompaniment of life in Warrington, and I must put up with them. I suppose I must, and philosophically make the best of it; but I hope I may be allowed to grumble, if there is RO bye-law against grumbling. Perhaps, however, when those Town Council fellows have got through withlisten- ing to long speeches that they do not comprehend. with admiring their own little oratorical efforts, and endeav- ouring to smuggle in neat little bits of jobbery, the' will put their noses to the stink—l mean grindstone— and endeavour to clear away these pestilential aromas from off the face of Warrington. If those very talkative Council swells Will but do away with these'dreadful smells. They will be very handsome swells indeed. And may treat themselves to a—Council feed. At the public expense; too. At least, no objection would be raised by the one who is childlike and bland.— Yours, &c., Warrington, July, 1888.
therl

A SHAM CLERGYMAN. The Rev. George Frederick Wilfrid Ellis was indicted at Suffolk Assizes, on Tuesday, for pretending to be in holy orders, and for illegally solemnizing matrimony at Wither- ingsett. He was further charged with obtaining the living ef Witheringsett by forging the name of the Roman Catholic Bishop of Salford to a certi- ficate of tonsure. The prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. THE TWELFTH OF JULY.—Upto a late hour on Wednesday night all was tranquility in Belfast, but in some quarters there was much excitement. The Glasgow Orange- men celebrated the twelfth of July on Thursday in glor- ious weather.
