div.head: CORPORATION • SERVANT'S LAMENT'.
div.p: A CORPORATION • SERVANT'S LAMENT'.

An oldish man, with a furrowed face, and a tired limp in his walk, I met in the Park the other day, and joined him to have a talk. It was Saturday, when work was done, and I felt inclined for a chat, So I spoke to him in a friendly way—meanwhile he touched his hat. "Well, sir," he said, " I've worked for the town— Corporation, you know, I mean; "For nigh on forty year, I may say, a servant o'theirs I have been. "Mi wages is eighteen bob a week, and little enough, you will sax. "When you've got a wire and family to keep its a held job to pay your way. "I live on plain vittles most o' days, with on Sun- days a bit o' meat : "An it's rather hard do's i' winter, for us to get enough to eat. " I in getting to feel rather shaky, an a bit tottery on mi legs. "Afore long I must go to t' Workus—it's as sure, Sir, as eggs is eggs. "If I drew a few hundreds a year, like some fine coves I could mention, "I'd have brass in t' bank, and they'd give me— why, what d'ye think, a pension. "Seems funny, dont it, but it is so ; 'to him that bath shall be given.' "While us poor chaps, though we works as hard, to t' big House at last are driven. "It seems to be t nateral order o' things: we are poor, they are rich; that's all • "But if I were a chap wi brass, and took a pension, I woad feel small. "From him that bath not shall betaken; the poor, they must go to the wall; "But what say's t' precious old book, Sir, what says Him as is Ruler of all— "In Heaven the rich shall be humbled, the poor there exalted will be There'll be no such thing as a pension, and—well, if you get there you'll see." I left him and pondered the questi, n. ! what he had told me was true; Poor wages are given to the many—but pensions to only a few. 11. S.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) MOORE,_ &c.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) MOORE,_ &c.

The work in the cutting at Moore is advancing rapidly, the German excavator being kept pretty constantly at work, while blasting operations are also being carried on. Of late, mainly in consequence of the heavy rain, the bottom of the cutting has been covered with a consider- able depth of water, which will have to be pumped out. The work at Acton Grange also is going on satisfactorily, and at Walton there is no cessation in the activity that has prevailed there for some time past. During the week three navvies of the American type have been engaged in the cutting here, and the second lift has been com- menced. The cutting now extends to within less than fifty yards of some of the buildings at Lower Walton, and beyond, in the direction of Wilderspool, surface earth has been removed in readiness for further advances. The cottages at Lower Walton are now all occupied, and a commencement has been made with the building of additional ones. THELWALL AND STATHAM. There is little that is new to be recorded about the work at Thelwail and Statham. About 800 men are em- ployed along this length of canal, and these, aided by the numerous mechanical appliances on the ground, con- tinue to push operations rapidly forward. Perhaps the most effective work is just now being done in front of Morris Brook Farm buildings, where three powerful steam navvit.s are regularly at work, and as the soil here is sandy and easily displaced, trains of waggons are rapidly filled and as rapidly hauled away by locomotives. More in the direction of Statham, Priestman's " grabs" are in use for the lifti of the clayey soil. Pumping is kept up along the length, but the workings do not at present seem to be much interfered with by any excess of the watery element, which at times has been so troublesome.

div.head: ECCLES AND BARTON.
div.p: ECCLES AND BARTON.

The operations on the Eccles and Barton "sections are being pushed on with great vigour, notwithstanding the unsatisfactory state of the weather. At Stickings Island the required depth has almost been reached. An Ameri- can navvy has also arrived at this point, but it is not yet fitted up. On Thursday a• large bed of rock was dis- covered, which is of considerable thickness, and men are engaged boring holes preparatory to blasting. This week the engineer has obtained the land formerly used as a sewage farm by the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority, and a large quantity of plant is in course of delivery. The contractor has now full possession of the land for the completion of the works from Manchester to East- ham. At Barton blasting operations are in full swing, men being engaged shaping the blocks of rock for future use in the constructive works, and also to form the new entrance to Trafford Park, now in course of operation leading from Dumplington-lane, Barton, through the fields, °Ter the canal, and into the park.

div.head: STRETFORD.
div.p: STRETFORD.

At I Meeting of ratepayers held in Stretford Town Hall on Thursday evening, a resolution was almost unanimously adopted approving of the action of the Stretford Local Board in sanctioning the alteration of boundary between Salford and the township of Stretford, as proposed in the new bill of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company. MORE LEVEL CROSSINGS: At the meeting of the Daresbury Highway ROard, on Thursday, an application was made by Mr. Walker, junr., on behalf of the Ship Canal contractor, for permis- sion to lay a tram line'across the Chester road at Lower ' Walton, the Stretton-road at Stockton Heath, end Acker's- ' lane and Common-lane at Latchford. The application was granted subject to similar conditions to those agreed upon with regard to the level crossings over Grappen- hall-road and Knutsford-road at Latchford.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

BAPTIST CHAPEL, CHERRY-LANE.—TWO sermons were preached in this chapel, on Sunday afternoon and even- ing, by Mr. S. F. McKee, of Manchester. There wers large attendances at each service, and about £l4 was raised by the collections. POLICE NEWs.—On Monday afternoon, before Mr. C. Lister, Peter Murphy was charged by Sergeant McHale with being a tramp, and on suspicion of being a deserter from the Army. The evidence was not considered strong enough to justify a remand, and prisoner was discharged with a caution.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY MEETING.—A meeting of the officers in connection with Lymm Mutual Improve- ment Society was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Rush I Green, on Monday evening, to consider the best mode of I raising the outstanding liabilities, incurred by the Society during last session. Although several gentlemen pronr- ised subscriptions, it was thought advisable to make a collection among all the members, and to call a meeting of the society for that purpose. 1 LOCAL BOARD.—A special meeting of this Board took place on Thursday night. Mr. H. Cameron presided, and there were also present Messrs. R. Dutton. William Brazendale, J. Gibbon, S. Appleton, H. Harrison, T. J. Ridgway (law clerk), W. Mullard (clerk), J. Mort (sur- veyor.) The meeting had been convened chiefly for the consideration of certain plans. Plans for some new cottages at Fleatley were referred back in order that cer- tain alterations might be made. Plans submitted by Mr. Richard Griffiths and Mr.' Thomas Griffiths were passsd. VISITORS. —On Saturday afternoon special trains brought to Lymm 600 adult and 1,500 juvenile members of the Manchester Rechabites, who were accompanied by the Fairfield Temperance Brass Band, which played through the village to a field in Pepper-st., belonging to Mr. John Leigh, where dancing and games were en- joyed till the return journey commenced. Many other smaller parties also came by train and in various vehicles byroad. On Wednesday from 80 to 100 tradesmen of Iles- wick, near Manchester, came by conveyances to the Plough Hotel for the afternoon. ACCIDENT TO A HORSE AND TRAP.—On Saturday last, as Mr. Colin Maclver, of Lymm, with his man had driven to the station, at Thelwall and there left some empty boxes, Mr. Kite brought a small bag and dropped it into the back part of the trap. This, it is supposed, frightened the horse, which is young. It at once rushed •off round the enclosed station yard with the owner hold- ing on to its head. When in the corner nearest the en- trance gate, however, it managed to shake him off, and he fell, fortunately rolling out of the way of the wheels. The horse continued its career across to the back of the old station room, and then to the rails at the west end of the yard, where, probably, seeing its danger, it made a rapid turn, but was carried by the impetus through the, rails, and it fell on its back with the conveyance attached into the road beneath, a distance of 15 or 18 feet. The trap was completely smashed, but, strange to say, the horse is not much the worse for its escapade. MEETIND7OF FUSTIAN CUTTERS.—A meeting of the recently appointed committee of 'fustian cutters, took place in the clubroom of the Millstone Inn on Monday night, for the purpose of meeting and conferring with the master cutters as to the best mode of relieving the fustian trade, which is at present in a very depressed state.—After waiting for some considerable time the Chairman of the committee said they had now waited for some time after the appointed hour, and none of the masters had put in an appearance. This was not very encouraging to any expectations theymight havehadthat the masters were anxious to enter into some amicable arrangement by which the interests "of master and man would be alike improved. Any im&ovement that they desired in their condition must therefore be undertaken without any assistance from the employers.—lt was stated that the next general Meeting will take place in a fortnight, when a new conamittee and officers would be appointed, as the numbers who had joined the society gave an earnest of success.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1888.

MEETING OF THE ORDER OF FORESTERS. —The quar- terly meeting of the Altrincham and Lymm District of the Ancient Order of Foresters was held at the Royal Oak, Baguley, on Monday last. Besides the officers of the district there were also present delegates from the Courts at Altrincham, Lymm, Hale, Dunham' Bowden, Ashton-on-Mersey, and Baguley. The quarterly ac- counts, which shewed the number of old members re- turned to be 1479 were passed. The funeral account showed a total income of £2OB 7s; total disbursements for ten funerals, £95; balance, £ll3 7s. Management fund: Contributions, etc., £l3 Is lid; balance in hand, £4 12s 6d. District distress fund: Contributions, etc., £36 is 7d; no disbursements. The following were nomi- nated officers for the ensuing year :—Bros. John Barnes, Court 1391, D.C.R. ; William Kinsey, Court 2098, D.S.C.R ; James Pownall, Court 1198, district secretary; E. G. Fairhurst, Court 229, district treasurer. No noti- ces of alteration of rules were brought forward. It was resolved that the district secretary, Brother Pownall, should be granted a credential to attend the High Court meeting to be held at Ileading next month. This was all the business of importance. ACCIDENT TO A LYMM GENTLEMAN. At Manchester, County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Russell, Mr. J. Svranwick, of Lymm, carrying on busi- ness as a commission agent in Manchester, brought an action against Henry Fidler. a cab proprietor, of Thomas-1 st., Rusholme. The action was brought to recover damages, laid at £5O, for injuries sustained by being knocked down by a cab. Mr. A. E. Paterson (Messrs. Dendy and Paterson) appeared for the plaintiff.—The Judge said it was clear, from the evidence given by a witness for the plaintiff, that there was no tramcar near at the time of the accident. He (the judge) had noticed that drivers of cabs in Manchester, and especially dri- vers of hansom cabs, drove in a most reckless manner. They got possession of the road, and they did not care a single straw about foot passengers; and then, if an accident happened, they came forward and said they were driving at five miles an hour, were taking all pre- cautions, and that what had occurred was in no way at- tributable to them. He had no doubt that the acci- dbut in question was due entirely to the reckless dri- ving of the defendant, and the only matter of sur- prise to him was that more accidents of the kind did not occur. He gave judgment for the plaintiff for £l5 and costs.
THE WA.RRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.

The Ist Volunteer Battalion (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment has is week been represen- ted at the Wimbledon Rifle meeting, several mem- bers of the corps having taken part in the competi- tions with a creditable result, especially when it is borne in mind that their facilities for shooting prac- tice have only been limited. In the shooting for the Queen's Prize Sergeant Watmough headed the Warrington contingent of riflemen, totalling 89 ' points, and two of his comrades succeeded in making 82 points each. It is the protracted competition for the Queen's Prize that takes most of the marksmen to Wimbledon,and every man whose chances survive to the last of its three stages, has a right to think that he has done remarkably well. The con- ditions for shooting during the first stage of the " Queen's " have been very favourable, with the result that nothing below 86 points would find a place in the list of the three hundred who shoot in the second stage. Below are the scores of the Warrington Volunteers who shoot in the "Queen's " Competition :

200 500 609 To- yds. yds. yds. tat. Sergeant Geo. Watmough 3.3 28 28 89 Sergeant T. Jolley J 31 25 26 82 Corporal Sloane Sergeant J. Dobson Sergeant Dolan Sergeant G. Painter 26 29 14 69 Lance-Sergeant Fitzgerald 25 12 14 51 Bugler-Major Phaeton l7 24 14 55 Pifteen competitors making 86 points were counted out of the 300, because of their inferiority at the longest range, compared with the 61 other scores of this amount who are included. Sergeant G. Watmough took a prize of of .£2 in the Alexandra competition, with a score of 54 points. It is proposed, if found practicable, to form a body of cyclists in connection with the corps, and the commanding officer, Colonel Greenall, has issued a notice to the effect that he strongly desires that such a step should be taken, in time, if possible, for the proposed meet of volunteer cyclists at Crewe.
_WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., presided, and there were present Messrs. T. Handley, D. Wright, W. W. Gossage, J. Midwood, R. Cook, F. Heyes, Taylor, J. Houghton, S. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (engineer), T. lligginson (suri eyor), J. Dickson (nuisance inspector).

A. FLOUR WAREHOUSE FLOODED. Mr. Richard T. Fairclough writing on behalf of the firm of Messrs. Jas. Fakelough and Sons, millers, War- rington, on July sth, asked M. Gossage, as chairman of the Local Board, to inspect the damage done at the firm's warehouse in Widnes. They had written to Mr. Allen twice about the grids in West-st. being stopped, but the question had been ignored altogether. The firm would be obliged if he (Mr. Gossage) could put the matter right, as the firm did not wish to commence legal proceedings. —The Clerk said the Surveyor stated that the flood was not the fault of the gullies, but was caused by a thunder- storm.—The letter was referred to the Highway Com- mittee.

posed by Sir Lyon Playfair respecting the qualification and appointment of medical officers—the county coun- cil to have full power instead of the local authorities as at present. The Clerk was instructed to request Mr. Moos to oppose the clause. Mr. Moss had replied that both matters should have his careful attention. It was further recommended that Mr. Moss, M.P., be asked to support the bill to be introduced by Captain Cotton to amend section 156 of the P. IL Act, 1875, so that new buildings may not be brought beyond the line of fron- tage.—The minutes were then passed, on the rnotion.of Mr. Handley.

div.head: ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT HALTON CASTLE.
div.p: ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT HALTON CASTLE.

The Orangemen in the neighbourhood of Liver- pool having decided to celebrate the 12th of July this year at Halton Castle, the people of Runcorn had an opportunity of witnessing the demonstra- tion of the brethren. Between nine o'clock and half-past ten, five special trains arrived at Runcorn Station from Liverpool, and discharged their freight of human beings wearing the orange lily and sashes of gay colours and design. The number of arrivals would be about 2,000. At eleven o'clock they were formed into processional order in Lowlands-road, and marched, by way of High-street and Bridge- street, to the Castle. In front was a coach (sup- plied by Messrs. Yarwood), drawn by four grey horses, with postilions. The occupants were the Grand and Provincial Lodge officers,with the regalia of the Grand, Lodge—namely, Bros. W. Touchstone, D.G.M , G.S. of England; J. Ballard, D.G.M., P.P.G.M. ; F. Soperville, D.P.G.M. : H. Thomas, D:G.M., P.G.M. ; and J. Lynch, P.G.S. The members of the various lodges, headed by large banners, and in about eight instances also with a rife and drum band, followed after in this order :—Johnston True Blues, No. 244 (with a new banner, made by a member and used for the first time); Lady Claud Hamilton, No. 94; Loyal Female Lodge, No. 20; Rose of England, No. 182; St. Nathaniel's, No 466; Sons of Enniskillen, No. 265 : Kelsey's Lodge, No. 311; Primrose of England, No. 605; St. Stephen the Martyr, No. 337; Pride of Old Brunswick Female Lodge, No. 11; Garston True Blues, No 14; Widnes Invincibles, No. 429; Lord Claud llamilton, No. 105; Star of the North, No. 36; England's Glory, No. 293; Ulster Royal Blues, No. 543; Prince of - Wales, No. 50; Bootle's Glory, No. 131; Kirkdale's Glory, No. 113; Churchill's Purple Guards, No. 620; No Surrender, Birkenhead, No. 148; and Derry Walls, Birkenhead, No. 367. Halton Castle was reached at twelve o'clock, and every preparation had been made for their reception. In the shape of food and liquids there was most ample store, provided by local tradesmen and publicans, and the usual paraphernalia were there in great variety for the amusement ot the loyal visitors. The Parish Church and the ancient library were also thrown open for inspection. About two o'clock Mr. Howard, of the Castle Hotel, provided lunch in a tent erected by Mr. Cooper, and the Grand Lodge Officers, together with the Rev. J. Lockwood (vicar of Halton), the Rev J. 11. Skewes, vicar of Holy Trinity, Liverpool, and Bros. F. Morgan, D.M. ; W. Shaw, D.G.M. ; T. Garrett, D.T. ; J. Davies, D.M. ; J. Mc. Lean, D.M., Sze. Afterwards there was an informa- gathering on the Castle Green. Brother J. W. Bal- lard presided. Brother Touchstone delivered an ad- dress in which he referred to historical events, in- cluding the Armada. He was afterwards thanked, on the motion of the Rev. J. 11. Skewes, seconded by Brother Harry Thomas, and supported by Bro- ther F. Somerville. Brother Thomas said a com- plaint had been made about the absence of local members of Parliament. The blame was upon him; he had concluded that coming a long distance from Liverpool to historical place whore there was much to see, that they would not want to hear two or three ;hoard' speechifying.--Brother Somerville remarked that members only came to them when they wanted their votes, and he advised the Orange- men to stick to their rights and show the members that they could do without thorn.— Brother Touchstone, in responding to the vote, said there was every excuse for the absence of the members of Parliament, for it was well known that they were expected to be in their places ready to give their votes against the Parnellites and Glad- stonians—men who for place and power would sell their Queen and country. (Applause.) The lodges commenced to leave Halton at four o'clock, and by half-past six they had all departed for Liverpool in special trains. The demonstration was highly favoured as regards the weather, and it is gratifying to be able to record that the affair passed off without any serious disturbance.

div.head: TRIPS FROM WARRINGTON.
div.p: TRIPS FROM WARRINGTON.

WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH SCHOOL. On Monday last the annual trip in connection with this institution took place, Blackpool being the destination of the trippers. The excursionists reached Blackpool at 8-30, after a pleasant and quick run of about one hour and twenty minutes. Passing Buxton, where the London and North- Western Railway is joined by the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway from Manchester, the two lines then running side by side to Preston, a train on the latter line came pp at the same moment as the ex- cursion, and a race, which continued for a mile or more, was commenced, causing not a little excite- ment amongst the excursionists. Alth6ugh the weather up to no:n was rather unpromising, after that time it cleared up and became on the whole favourable. The various places of entertainment, including the Winter Gardens. the entertainments at which are particularly good this year; the Royal Palace Gardens (late Raikes Hall), where Mr. Bart Taylor, who is the responsible manager, has struck a happy idea in introducing a grand Indian village ' and fair; and the Aquarium, where a splendid col- lection of curiosities is on exhibition, received a I large proportion of visitors. At the latter place. I to further enhance the attractions, the proprietors have now set apart a certain portion of the interior for dancing purposes, and, judging from the num- bers who took part in the favourite pastime there, the addition will prove an attractive one to the visitors. The return journey was coi.menced at eight o'clock, and Warrington was safely reached at 9-30 p.m., all evidently well pleased with the days excursion. The members of Christ Church choir, I together with their friends, to the number of about 40, accompanied the excursion to Blackpool. Din- ner and tea were partaken of at Mr. Longbottom's, in Talbot-road. Everything passed off favourably, and the opinion was general that the trip was as enjoyable as any previous one.' MESSRS. RYLANDS' BROS. The employes of this firm, with their families and friends to the number of about 400, journeyed to Southport for their annual trip on Saturday. As the works stopped on the previous Tuesday for a week, a number of the men did not accompany the excursionists, having gone away to spend the whole week at some of the popular pleasure resorts. Start- ing from the Central station, Warrington, soon after seven o'clock on Saturday morning, the Southport excursionists were conveyed by special train to that popular watering-place. On arriving there they separated to the various places of amusement, to many of which they were admitted (by previous arrangement) at reduced rates. Throughout the day the weather was all that could be desired, and the excursionists appeared to thoroughly enjoy their trip. The return was made about eight o'clock, Warrington being reached soon after nine. A few extension tickets had been sold, and from forty to fifty of the excursionists took advantage of them, remaining until Tuesday night. It may be men- tioned that the Railway Company had supplied most comfortable carriages for the journey, a special saloon carriage being added to the train for the committee.

div.head: MANCHESTER EYE INFIRMARY!
div.p: MANCHESTER EYE INFIRMARY!

A letter was read from this institution asking for a sub- scription from the Board.—The Chairman remarked that there were sufficient people in Widnes who subscribed to the Liverpool Eye and Ear Infirmary to enable them to send all their patients there without reference to the Manchester Ilogpital.—The letter was ordered to lie on the table.

Mr. John Rolinson, of Elizabeth-terrace, Ditton, wrote stating that last year he made arrangements with Mr. Whitfield, the collector, for a supply of water to use in his garden at so much per quarter, the payment to be discontinued at the end of any quarter. He had given notice before the 30th December last, but Mr. Allen then wrote that the supply was yearly, and he would have to pay for the succeeding quarters. 'He did not use 1,000 gallons during the year. and it was preposterous to charge 4s 8d per annum, and he declined to pay for a further supply at such an exorbitant rate.—The Chair- man (sarcastically) : I think we had better pass this on to the Water Committee. It is a very serious matter.

div.head: SUPPLYING WATER TO LIVERPOOL.
div.p: SUPPLYING WATER TO LIVERPOOL.

Mr. J. Parry, water engineer to the Liverpool Cor- poration, wrote under date July 4th that he had reported the result of his interview with the Water Committee of the Widnes Local Board to the Supplementary Water Supply Committee, and had stated that the WidnesCom- mittee were prepared to recommend the Local Board to supply water to Liverpool at 4d per 1,000 gallons. The Sub-committee agreed subject to confirmation by the Water Committee in Council to take a supply from the Widnes Local Board's six inch pipes at Gateacre on these terms, leaving the question of laying a main to Netherley to be dealt with when the fifteen inch pipe line now in hand had been completed. As this decision was in ae- cordance with the views of the Widnes Water Com- mittee he should feel obliged if they would take the earliest opportunity of submitting it to the Board. In the meantime he was pushing forward as rapidly as possible witil the pipe-laying from Huyton to Gateacre.—The Board resolved into committee to consider the question. It was decided to accept the offer of the Liverpool Cor- poration. The quantity of water to be supplied was not fixed, but it was stated that through the six inch main mentioned that half a million gallons per day could be easily obtained. The jitori of a further supply through a large main was held over.

div.head: 'QAE ANb WATER CORM- ITTEE.
div.p: 'QAE ANb WATER CORM- ITTEE.

The Engineer reported that the accumulation of sand in the bore hole at Stocks well had not up to the present affected the yield of water. He recommended that the existing 21n and 3m mains in Deacon-road, Appleton Vil- lage, and Birchfield-road be enlarged to a 9in main. The distance is 1,000 yards, and the estimated cost £4BO. Station Governor at Gas Works.—As the 12in governor is becoming much too small for the maximum demands in the depth o! the lighting season, and as the pressure in the low laying portions of the town is at these times in- sufficient, he would recommend that an additional 14in governor be erected and connected on to the portions of the town by means of a new 14in main from the Gas Works to Ann-st. crossing. The town would then be divided into :two districts, high and low, which would enable a more uniform pressure to be maintained throughout the township. At present, working from one governor as we do, the pressure in West Bank dis- trict is insufficient, while that in Farnworth is excessive. The estimated cost of the governor, valves, and connec- tions is about £9O. The estimated cost of 274 yards of 14in main along Ann-st. east is £l4O. The mean rain- fall for the past month was 2445 inches, and the water in stock was 1,297,842 gallons. The water delivered during the month was 57,692,131 gallons. TheTas de- livered was 4,765,000 cubic feet. The illuminating power of the gas had averaged 1781 candles.—The Com- mittee recommended that the governor and main sug- gested by the Engineer should be fixed. They also re- commended that the seal of the Board be attached to the agreement with the Dinsmore Gas Company Limited for the use of their patent for the making of gas. The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Wright, who said it was expected that the Dinsmore patent would be at work in about a month.
FLUSHING SEWERS. . _

On the proposal of this committee it was decided to purchase a tank for flushing the sewers at a cost of £BO. A. DISGRACEFUL STREET. 31r Handley drew the attention of the Highway Com- mittee to the disgraceful condition of Pitt-st , off Water- loo-road. One side of the street had been built upon for 20 years to his knowledge, and under a recent Act of Parliament the Board could make one side of the street and charge the owners with it. He thought the Board should make and adopt the street.—Mr Sadler promised that the committee should consider the matter.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

To this committee the Medical Officer of Health re- ported that during June they& were 112 births and 43 deaths, being at the respective rates of 43.03 and 18-64 per 1,000. The deaths included nine children under one year, and nine children between one and five years. There had been six inquests. The Nuisance Inspector reported that there had been two fatal cases of diarrhea, and one each of measles and diptheria.—Mr Wright moved the confirmation of the minutes. IRE WASTE INSPECTOR. . . .

Mr. Sadler inquired what had become of the Inspector of Alkali Waste. He had never seen one of his reports since he was appointed.—Mr. Wright replied that the committee had the inspector's report before them each month, but it was not thought necessary to have it printed. If that was the desire of the Board it could be done.—Dr. O'Keeffe : There is not a single opinion in the bninutes as to whether the report is favourable .or not.—Mr. Wright: We might have stated.that it was quite satisfactory.--Dr. O'Keeffe : People are still corn- plaining.—Mr. Cook said he had paid a weekly visit to the waste heaps in company with the inspector. He be- lieved the inspectoAi was doing his work very well. The men laying the waste did not pay as much attention to the inspector's instructions as they should do, but the inspector was now writing to the proprietors themselves, and the course had proved very effectual. There was a very great improvement perceptible during the past four monthsi It would be a very good thing if there were several rules laid down for the deposit of the waste, as the men in charge did notifulfil their duties as well as they might do. However well the waste might be laid, they were so near to the town, that complaints were sure to arise. The committee would be glad to print the inspector's report.
FINANCE.
On the recommendatiO.n-aThe Finance Committee, ac- counts, amounting to £3,126 17s 6d, were passed for ). payment.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

At the Oval the Gentlemen's first innings closed for 76, and they had to follow on. The Naval Lords of the Admiralty on Friday inspec- ted the mobilized squadron at Spithead. A well-known character' named Richard Nash, a centenarian, died on Wednesday at Bishop's iStortford, completing his 100th year on the day of his death. The directors of Bryant and May's matchworks decline to give way on any point to the work girls on strike. A strong force of police is kept in reserve in the neigh- bourhood of the works.

Mr. McHugh, Mayor of Sligo, was arrested at Sligo, inserting yesterday, adhaomnpt charge innt.kidsedptar ntimi- date certain persons. He was remanded on bail. Sir Thomas Grove, M.P., has written to his consti- tuents justifyinr, his secession from the Liberal Unionists, Mr. justifying having now accepted the principle of retaining the Irish members at Westmins- ter,

Frederick George Life was yesterday indicted for the murder of Martha Charles, a charwoman, at Kingsbury, on the 23rd March. The jury found prisoner committed tie crime whilst insane, and he was ordered to be de- tained during Her Majesty's pleasure. THE SEVERE WEATHER.—The Welsh farmers, on Friday, reported heavy losses of sheep in consequence of the severe weather. Large flocks of sheep had just been sheared on the mountain sheepwalks, when the hills be- came enveloped in snow, and large numbers of the flocks perished. ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.—RochdaIe: Professor Hopkin- son, of MancheAter, has been invited by the Liberal Unionists of Rochdale to contest the seat against Mr. Potter.—Wet Bromwich: Mr. Edward Strachey (Glad- stonian) was on Thursday night selected by a majority of the West Bromwich Liberal Six Hundred as their can- didate. _ _

BRUTAL MURDER OF A WlFE.—Alice Delany, a young woman 28 years of age, died on Thursday evening , in Chesterfield Infirmary, from injuries inflicted upon her by her husband, Arthur Thomas Delany, a fitter. It is alleged that Delany strnck his wife many times over the head and face with a poker, breaking her nose, smashing in her forehead, and entirely destroying the sight of one eye. Delany is in custody, and will be charged with wil- -1 ful murder. _ . _

TEE WIMBLEDON MEETING.—GeniaI sunshine on Fri- day morning restored warmth and cheerfulness in the camp. There was very little wind, and a good light. The principal objects of competition oni Friday were the St. George's Challenge Vase, an the accompanying dragon cup, gold and silver jewels, and £745 divided into 155 prizes. Range 500 yards. Bombardier M`Laffie, Galloway Artillery, made 34. Quartermaster-Sergeant Grier, Renfrew, has won the Henri Clicqoot prize. Lieu- tenant Dalglish, 3rd Lanark; Private Fulton, 2nd West- minster; 'Sapper Bratherton, of the 2nd Cheshire Engineers; Sergeant Keating, Ist V.B. Liverpool; Bom- bardier NPHaffie, Galloway Artillery, have each made 34 in the St. George's. In the tie shots Keating made the highest possible scoring, three bull's eyes.

COACHING EXTRAORDINARY.—WINNING £l,OOO. A sensational coaching trip was made yesterday. A wager of £l,OOO to £5OO was made, at last Ascot races, that James Selby, the famous "Whip." would not drive the "Old Times " four-horse coach from London to Brighton an 4 back (104 miles) in 8 hours. The wager was accepted by the proprietors of the coach on the understanding that if Selby perfoimed the feat, he should have the £l,OOO. The event came off yesterday morning, the party on the coach consisting, besides the owner and guard, of several gentlemen and Press-men. The start was made at exactly ten o'clock, and the first stoppage was made at Streatham, where the horses were changed in forty-seven seconds. The roads were some- what heavy near London, but inlproved on getting into the Chalk Districts. Brighton, was reached at one fifty six. The return journey was commenced immediately, and the coach finally drew up in Piccadilly, amid loud cheers at five-fifty, Selby thus winning the bet by ten minutes.
POLITICAL DUEL IN FRANCE.
GENERAL
BOULANGER. SERIOUSLY WOUNDED.

-- After the insult offered him in the Chamber on Thurs- day by General Boulanger, who called him a liar, M. Floquet commissioned two of his friends, MM. Clemen- ceau and Perrin to go to the General and ask him to name his seconds. They arrived at General Boulanger's house Rue Dumont d'Urville, at seven o'clock, and found the General had left home at half-past six. They were, however, informed that they would find him at the office of the " Presse "at half-past twelve o'clock last night. MM. Clemenceau and Perrin said they would not fail to be there at the time named.

PARIS, FRIDAY, 11-50 A.m.—Tile duel with swords be- tween M. Floquet, the Premier, and General Boulanger, was fought this morning, as arranged. At the second en- gagement between the combatants, General Boulanger was slightly wounded in the leg. M. Floquet receiving a slight wound in the right hand. On the third renewal of the combat M. Floquet was very slightly touched in the left breast, while his adversary was wounded in the throat.

div.head: M. FLOQUET'S WOUNDS.
div.p: M. FLOQUET'S WOUNDS.

PARIS, FRIDAY.—M. -filo-cluet's-;;;;Is have been dressed by a surgeon, and do not now cause him any in- convenience. He will keep his appointment to assist at the inauguration of the statue to Gambetta to-day, and it is expected he will be accorded a great popular ova- tion. General Boulemger's friends now express some anxiety, as it is now certain that his wound is serious, if not dangerous. •

SERIOUS CONDITION Or GENERAL BOULANGER. PARIS. FRIDAY, 3-30 P.M.—A bulletin issued this after- noon, signed by Dr. Monod, states that Generalßoulanger has a deep wound on the right side of his neck, causing
a marked difficulty of respiraltion. The_doctors abstain at present fro giving an opinion regarding the turn which the case may take. ?1.

AFFAIRS IN ZULULAND.—REINFORCEMENTS ORDERED OUT. • On Friday morning some excitement was caused in camp by a sudden Horse Guard's order to withdraw the 2nd King's Own Scottish Borderers from the field column for the purpose of preparing then for immediate embarkation for Egypt, whence it is understood they will replace a battalion ordered to proceed to South Africa (Zululand). The 2nd Yorkshire Regiment will take the place of the Borderers at Aldershot. TERRIBLE MINING ACCIDENT.—SUPPOSED LOSS OF 500 LIVES. A telegram received in Capetown from Kimberley . 1 states that a fire occurred on Wednesday night at the en- trance to the shaft of the De Beer Mine at that place. lEight hundred miners were entombed, and the work of rescue was proceeding. It was feared that 500 have perished, including Mr. Lindsay, the manager, and a number of other white men. A London correspondent learnt on inquiry on Friday morning, at the London offices of De Beer's Mining Company, that confirmatory reports had been re- ceived there of the disastrous fire at their mine at Kimberley, Cape Colony. According to their advices, 224 lives have been lost, including 24 whites. It is further stated tbat rescue parties are exploring the mine. The cause of the fire was unknown. rhe nameEt of the white men killed have been telegraphed for.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at 4 o'clock. Lerd Ellenborough asked what steps were take. to put the militia in a more efficient state. After discussion, Lord Harris replied that the efficiency of the militi: was receiving the atteption of the authorities.— Lord Ashbourne, replying to Lord Fitzgerald, said the Government would not at present make a supplemental grant under the Irish Land 'Purchase Act.—The Limited Partnerships Bill passed through Committee, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Deputy-Speaker, Mr. Courtney, (the Speaker being indisposed), took the chair at three o'clock. The Liverpool and Birkenhead Subway Bill was read a third time.

OUR NAVAL STRENGTII.—Lord GeorgelLuovrow stated,in answer to Mr. Caleb Wright, that his attention had not been specially called to the speech of Mr. Forwood in Liverpool, in which he said that Admiral Hornby had suggested an increase in our Navy of 144 cruiser, the cost of which was estimated at £33,500. The Govern- ment had no intention of making such .an addition to Our naval strength. • CORRUPTION IN PUBLIC Boores.—Lord R. CHURCHILL gave notice that on Monday he woidd bring in a bill to make it a misdemeanour for a member or servant of any public body to corruptly give or receive fees. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL. The House then went into committee on the Local Government Bill, taking up clause 38, which deals with the re-arrangement of quarter sessions in the metropolis, and the payment of chairmen and deputy-chairmen.— Mr. ROBERTSON proposed the omission from the clause of the words enipowering the County Council of London to increase the salary of chairman and deputy-chairman.— This was agreed to.—Mr. PICKERSGILL moved an amend- ment to provide, in future' that the recorder,. common sergeant, and Judge of the City of London Court, should be appointed by the Queen, Instead of the Court of Aldermen and , Common Council.—A long discussion ensued.—Lord R. CHETacrin.x. spoke in favour of the prin- ciple of the amendment.—Eventually Mr.W. Smith accep- ted the amendment, and it was agreed to amid cheering.— On clawse 39, which provided for applications of the Act to certain special counties, Captain HEaTacorE moved that the district of Staffordshire potteries, com- prising the municipal boroughs of Hanley, Stoke-upon- Trent, Longton, and Burslem, and the Urban Sanitary districts, the Fenton and Tunstall Local Board of Health should be a separate county.—Mr. RITCHIE said the case was a peculiar one, and promised to introduce a pro- visional order bill next year, dealing with those special circumstances. The amendment, on that intimation, was withdtawn. An amendment moved by Sir W. BARTTELOT, that the Eastern and Western division of Sussex should be separate counties for plirposes of Act, was agreed to. —On the motion oi Captain SELWYN, it was agreed that Isle, of Ely and the residue of the County of Cambridge, should be respectively separate administrative counties for the purposes of the Act —Mr. RITCHIE then, in accordance with an inti- mation previously given proposed to withdraw the Dis- trict Council clauses.—After discussion the clauses were omitted, Mr, W. SMITH promising that a bill dealing with District Councils should be introduced next session. —Other clauses were afterwards considered and agreed , to.

ANOTHER DEPARTURE FOP, AMERICA. On Thursday, Mr. James Winstanlev, of War- rington, with his wife and three children, sailed from Liverpool in the Parisian (Allan Line) for 7imerica. Mr. Winstanley is well known in War- rington as a skilful joiner, and has worked in con- junction with his brother, Mr. W. Winstanley. plumber, for a number of years. He has for some time acted as honorary auditor of the Warringtol Football Club," and as treasurer of the joiners' organisation, and below we give some details of presentations made to him by both of these bodies, I which reveal the high esteem in which he is held. Mr. Winstanley has booke I right through to San Francisco, via Vancouver City, but it is his inten- tion to settle in Vancouver if he finds a favourable opening there. He has been in communication with Mr. William Porter, formerly a builder in War- rington, who has settled in this thriving western city, and has thriven greatly himself. Mr. Win- Stanley has an idea of engaging in either farming or building, or in a combination of both, and as he is exceedingly handy and intelligent there is every prospect of his making his way. He will reach his destination by way of the Canadian Pacific Rail- way, of which Vancouver is the western terminus; and, largely in consequence of this, the rise and progress of the town has been phenomenal, even for the west of America. We need hardly say that we join in the good wishes of Mr. Winstanley's townsmen for his future prosperity.

div.head: PRESENTATION BY WORKMEN,
div.p: PRESENTATION BY WORKMEN,

On Mon-d-a-iwiJiii-wg-;.—pi:eseVatiO'n—;;;; made to Mr. Winstanley, by the Warrington Lodge of the General Union of Carpenters and Joiners, whose treasurer he has for some time been. The gift, which consisted of a sil- ver pencil case and sleeve-links, had been subscribed for by the members of the Association. The presentation was made by the chairman of the evening, Bro. R. Bur- rows, who "alluded to his long acquaintance with Mr. Winstanley, who had been his apprentice. He said that the members of the lodge had shown the esteem in which they held Mr. Winstanley, by unanimously 'sub- scribing to the present he had that 'night to make him, on behalf of the members of the lodge. He hoped Mr. Winstanley, when far away, would remember the com- rades he had left behind lum in Warrington. Bro. T. C. Brookes, Bro. Lea, and Biro. Dyson also gave testimony to the active work which Mr. Winstanley had done for the lodge, and expressed their sorrow at parting with him. Mr. Winstanley, who was re- ceived with applause, in reply said that he could hardly find words in which to express his thanks for the kind words which had been said to him that night. The presentation had been wholly unexpected by him, and he was therefore unprepared for it. He thanked the members of the lodge for their good wishes, and assured them that in the United States, as well as in Warring- ton, he should endeavour to uphold the principles of a trades unionist, which had been taught him in that lodge. (Applause.) The proceedings soon afterwards terminated.

PRESENTATION BY THE FOOTBALL CLUB. On Tuesday evening a presentation was made to Mr. Winstanley on behalf of the members of the Warrington F.C. who wished in that way to express the esteem in which they hold him, and to give a token of their re- cognition of his services to theclulias honorary auditor for the last three years. The present took the form of a handsome travelling bag and a knife. The bag had on it the inscription :—" Presented to Mr. James Winstanley as a token of esteem by the members of the Warrington Football Club for services faithfully rendered during his term of office as honorary auditor for seasons 1886-7-8." The gifts were presented to Mr. Winstanley at a meeting of the committee of the club, which was held at the head- quarters, the Roebuck Inn, Bridge-st,,, and which was presided over by Mr. J. Evans, in the absence of the President, Councillor W. Pierpoint.—The Chairman said that the reason of that meeting being held was of a very pleasant character. It was simply in order that they might acknowledge the services of Mr. James Winstan- , ley as auditor to the Football Club. He would ask the treasurer, who had been best acquainted with Mr. Winstanley's work, to make the presentation on behalf of the members of the club.—Mr. T. Pemberton said that I during the last few years Mr. Winstanley had worked with him on Saturdays, and if he (Mr Pemberton) had to be away,he had only had to let Mr Winstanlev know and he had then been ready to take his place. Mi. Winstanley had done a great deal of work for the club, and had I carried out his duties in as efficient a manner as any auditor could do. He hoped that he would have a pleasant voyage to America, and that he would be suc- cessful in his new undertaking. He thought that Mr. Winstanley would succeed, and he wished him much prosperity. Mr. Pemberton then made the presentation. —Mr. J. E. WARREN said that, as secretary of the club, he should like to add his testimony to what had already been said. Mr. Winstanley had done very valuable ser- vice for the club. The bag was not presented to him as a recegnition of those services, because that would be poor recognition indeed for what he had done. The presentation was made simply as a token of the respect and esteem felt for Mr. Winstanley by the members of the club, who had seen and appreciated the good work

that be had done for them. He hoped that in the to which he was going—and he could wish 1111000 t better—Mr. Winstanley and his family would enjoY health. If he had health and strength his energy command success. He sincerely hoped that Mr. stanley would have a good time in America, and would come back some time with the bag laden, gold. (Laughter and applause.)—Mr. Gaonos said that they all felt sorry Mr. Winstanley was lea, them. When he heard of his approaching depart urea felt a certain amount of dismay, because he knew they would have to lose his services as auditor to, club. This was the third year that he (Mr. Smith) had the honour to sit upon the committee, mid he e' bear testimony to what thq secretary and treasurer said—that Mr. Winstanley had done his and done it well. (Applause.) He felt that he was speaking the opinion of atri members of the club when he said they wur wishing well to Mr. Winstanley. He hoped, ho"' that what would be their loss would prove to he,A Winstanley's gain. They would at any time be gmr,al acquaint him as to the doings of the club, both finalltiji and inthefield.—TheChairman joined inthe expressi,",' good wishes, and said that he had seen nothing e' Winstanley but what he could admire, He reg that l at the club were about to lose his services, hl,' should be very pleased to hear of Mr. Winstanley s cess in America.—Mr. W. Dillon, captain for the eel season of the first team, also spoke of the service-4 dered to the club by the recipient of the present, he said, had been very much liked by all the meol It would be difficult to replace Mr. Winstanley, find someone who would serve them as well as lee, done. He trusted that Mr. Winstanley would hs' safe and pleasant journey, and that he would pros, his new home. (Applause.)—Mr. C. R. Adainsen 3 with the previous speakers in wishing Mr. Wing. success.—ln reply, Mr. Winstanley said that he done his best during the time he had been core'° with the club, and he was very thankful W that his services had been so highly appreciate far as payment was concerned, he had been pa P „SI had gone along by the pleasure he had had in wituT struggles for victory in the field. The love ho he" the club was sincere, and he was sure that if the were going on now he should find it a far more task to tear himself away. He sincerely hoped club would prosper, and he should be very h3t,. hear of them climbing step by step to the topmost'', of the ladder in the football World. He tiaankeu members of the • club very much for their Ichadlit Amongst the few pictures he was taking away with was one that he should not prize the least—it vr,,,,,a^4. picture of the football team, and lie should cer' hang it in a prominent position. (Applause.)—The ceedings then terminated.

A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Office at half-past twelve on Thursday. The Duke of Rutland was absent. The Rev. Canon Harrison, vicar of St. James's, Bury St. Edmunds, was on Thursday elected Bishop of Glas- gow and Galloway. Mr. Michael Thompson, solicitor, Kendal, was drowned in Morecambe Bal, at Arnside, on Thursday, through the capsizing of a small sailing boat. Three ladies who, were with Mr. Thompson reached the shore. A fatal quarrel occurred on Thursday afternoon be- tween two brothers named Talbot, butchers, of Watney- st., Commercial-road, London. The younger brother, aged 16, stabbed the elder, 21, and th& latter died on the way to the London Hospital. CoLLislO IN THE MERSEY.—The steamer Wasp, of Glasgow, coming up the Mersey on Wednesday night, came into collision with the barque Hypatia at anchor. She sank in ten minutes, her crew barely escaping to a tug. The Hynatia sustained severe damage. A fishing boat was also swamped in the river, and two of her crew were drowned. MUNIFICENT GIFTS TO BURY.—At a special Council meeting on Thursday morning, the Mayor of Bury an- nounced that Mr. Thomas Ormerod, Openshaw, who had already given £9,000 to the Rochdale-road Recreation Grounds to be opened by Prince Albert Victor on the 21st inst., had given another £5,000 to be invested for the maintenance of the grounds. TERRIBLE SUICIDE.—A shocking case of suicide has oc- curred at the Infirmary at Peterborough. A man named Shacklock jumped out of bed and cut his throat with a razor in the presence of a number of other patients. They were so terrified that they were unable to call for assistance for some time, but at last one of them managed to crawl along the floor and pull the nurse's bell. LORD HARTINGTON Os TECHNICAL EDUCATION.—Lord Hartington presided on Saturday at the first annual meeting of the National Association for the Promotion of Technical Education, and expressed a hope that the effect of the discussions which had taken place, and of further discussions, might be to secure the passing of some measure without much further delay. He feared the Government Bill would not pass this session because of the several controversial questions it raised, but he trusted it would not be delayed beyond another session. Referring to statements as to the extent to which tech- nical education had been adopted in other countries and as to the increasing severity of the competition to which we are exposed, Lord Hartington said they did not ap- pear to attract as much attention in this country as their importance deserves. A resolution was passed declaring that legislation on the subject of technical education on satisfactory lines ought not to be longer delayed, inas- much as a continuance of a state of uncertainty as to the nature of that legislation is likely to paralyse local effort and indefinately to postpone all action in many towns. A a conference of representatives of local branches and members of the Executive Committee, a general opinion was expressed in favour of Sir \H. Roscoe's Technical Education Bill as against that of the Government.
